en: The Scripture on the Stages of Cultivating the Path, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter One: On Accumulation and Dispersion (1). Chapter One: On Accumulation and Dispersion.

Its origin arose from the manifest and sublime; its brilliance surpasses the light of the sun. Its accumulated virtue is most majestic, excelling even the lineage of emperors and kings. That the various devas and transcendental beings achieved their states through single-minded devotion and exposure to the elements—this is truly marvelous. How could it not be so? It is because he has attained the Way that he is able to bring about such transformations. How much more so for one who has perfected the Way! This is why the Buddha’s virtue is so vast and profound. He is the Honored One of the World, the Teacher of Gods and Men. His radiance illuminates all things, and his majesty is supreme. His wisdom is peerless, and his power is incomparable. His fame spreads throughout the ten directions, and his renown reaches the ends of the earth. He is the Great Sage, the Most Honored One, the Peerless One, the One of Unobstructed Wisdom. He is the One Who Knows All, the One Who Sees All, the One Whose Virtue Pervades the Ten Directions. He is the One Who Is Fully Awakened, the One Who Has Transcended the World, the One Who Is Truly Enlightened. He is the One Who Has Reached the Other Shore, the One Who Has Attained Liberation, the One Who Has Realized the Truth. He is the One Who Is Free from Defilement, the One Who Is Pure and Stainless, the One Who Is Utterly Tranquil. He is the One Who Is Unshakeable, the One Who Is Immovable, the One Who Is Firm and Steadfast. He is the One Who Is Unassailable, the One Who Is Invincible, the One Who Is Supreme and Peerless. He is the One Who Is Worthy of Offerings, the One Who Is Honored by the World, the One Who Is the Field of Merit. He is the One Who Is the Refuge, the One Who Is the Protector, the One Who Is the Guide. He is the One Who Is the Lamp, the One Who Is the Light, the One Who Is the Eye. He is the One Who Is the Sun, the One Who Is the Moon, the One Who Is the Jewel. He is the One Who Is the Ocean, the One Who Is the Mountain, the One Who Is the Tree. He is the One Who Is the Medicine, the One Who Is the Remedy, the One Who Is the Savior. He is the One Who Is the Boat, the One Who Is the Bridge, the One Who Is the Path. He is the One Who Is the Door, the One Who Is the Gate, the One Who Is the Entrance. He is the One Who Is the Source, the One Who Is the Root, the One Who Is the Foundation. He is the One Who Is the Beginning, the One Who Is the End, the One Who Is the Middle. He is the One Who Is the First, the One Who Is the Last, the One Who Is the Eternal. He is the One Who Is the Ancient, the One Who Is the New, the One Who Is the Ever-Abiding. He is the One Who Is the True, the One Who Is the Real, the One Who Is the Ultimate. He is the One Who Is the Empty, the One Who Is the Signless, the One Who Is the Wishless. He is the One Who Is the Non-arising, the One Who Is the Non-ceasing, the One Who Is the Non-dual. He is the One Who Is the Non-self, the One Who Is the Non-existence, the One Who Is the Non-grasping. He is the One Who Is the Non-birth, the One Who Is the Non-death, the One Who Is the Non-suffering. He is the One Who Is the Non-joy, the One Who Is the Non-grief, the One Who Is the Non-fear. He is the One Who Is the Non-desire, the One Who Is the Non-hatred, the One Who Is the Non-delusion. He is the One Who Is the Non-anger, the One Who Is the Non-resentment, the One Who Is the Non-affliction. He is the One Who Is the Non-attachment, the One Who Is the Non-clinging, the One Who Is the Non-obstruction. He is the One Who Is the Non-bondage, the One Who Is the Non-liberation, the One Who Is the Non-action. He is the One Who Is the Non-doer, the One Who Is the Non-feeler, the One Who Is the Non-knower. He is the One Who Is the Non-seer, the One Who Is the Non-hearer, the One Who Is the Non-smeller. He is the One Who Is the Non-taster, the One Who Is the Non-toucher, the One Who Is the Non-thinker. He is the One Who Is the Non-mind, the One Who Is the Non-consciousness, the One Who Is the Non-perception. He is the One Who Is the Non-form, the One Who Is the Non-sound, the One Who Is the Non-smell. He is the One Who Is the Non-taste, the One Who Is the Non-touch, the One Who Is the Non-object. He is the One Who Is the Non-eye, the One Who Is the Non-ear, the One Who Is the Non-nose. He is the One Who Is the Non-tongue, the One Who Is the Non-body, the One Who Is the Non-mind. He is the One Who Is the Non-earth, the One Who Is the Non-water, the One Who Is the Non-fire. He is the One Who Is the Non-wind, the One Who Is the Non-space, the One Who Is the Non-consciousness. He is the One Who Is the Non-past, the One Who Is the Non-present, the One Who Is the Non-future. He is the One Who Is the Non-beginning, the One Who Is the Non-middle, the One Who Is the Non-end. He is the One Who Is the Non-cause, the One Who Is the Non-condition, the One Who Is the Non-result. He is the One Who Is the Non-karma, the One Who Is the Non-retribution, the One Who Is the Non-defilement. He is the One Who Is the Non-purity, the One Who Is the Non-impurity, the One Who Is the Non-emptiness. He is the One Who Is the Non-sign, the One Who Is the Non-characteristic, the One Who Is the Non-nature. He is the One Who Is the Non-arising, the One Who Is the Non-ceasing, the One Who Is the Non-abiding. He is the One Who Is the Non-going, the One Who Is the Non-coming, the One Who Is the Non-staying. He is the One Who Is the Non-moving, the One Who Is the Non-shaking, the One Who Is the Non-fluctuating. He is the One Who Is the Non-changing, the One Who Is the Non-altering, the One Who Is the Non-transforming. He is the One Who Is the Non-decaying, the One Who Is the Non-perishing, the One Who Is the Non-vanishing. He is the One Who Is the Non-disappearing, the One Who Is the Non-appearance, the One Who Is the Non-manifestation. He is the One Who Is the Non-hidden, the One Who Is the Non-revealed, the One Who Is the Non-concealed. He is the One Who Is the Non-secret, the One Who Is the Non-open, the One Who Is the Non-covered. He is the One Who Is the Non-bound, the One Who Is the Non-free, the One Who Is the Non-restrained. He is the One Who Is the Non-loose, the One Who Is the Non-tight, the One Who Is the Non-fastened. He is the One Who Is the Non-fast, the One Who Is the Non-slow, the One Who Is the Non-speedy. He is the One Who Is the Non-high, the One Who Is the Non-low, the One Who Is the Non-equal. He is the One Who Is the Non-superior, the One Who Is the Non-inferior, the One Who Is the Non-middle. He is the One Who Is the Non-white, the One Who Is the Non-black, the One Who Is the Non-color. He is the One Who Is the Non-long, the One Who Is the Non-short, the One Who Is the Non-square. He is the One Who Is the Non-round, the One Who Is the Non-flat, the One Who Is the Non-uneven. He is the One Who Is the Non-smooth, the One Who Is the Non-rough, the One Who Is the Non-hard. He is the One Who Is the Non-soft, the One Who Is the Non-rigid, the One Who Is the Non-flexible. He is the One Who Is the Non-bright, the One Who Is the Non-dark, the One Who Is the Non-luminous. He is the One Who Is the Non-obscure, the One Who Is the Non-clear, the One Who Is the Non-translucent. He is the One Who Is the Non-solid, the One Who Is the Non-void, the One Who Is the Non-substantial. He is the One Who Is the Non-existent, the One Who Is the Non-nonexistent, the One Who Is the Non-dual. He is the One Who Is the Non-one, the One Who Is the Non-many, the One Who Is the Non-ind
Having studied extensively and mastered manifold meanings, they all pay homage to the Most Peaceful One.
Gods, humans, dragons, and spirits, exerting themselves while in the world,
welcome the World-Honored One, who is peerless throughout the three realms.
Delivered by incomparable wisdom, the fear of birth and death is utterly eliminated;
the Buddha, the True Dharma, and the Saṅgha—these three virtues are unsurpassed.
One should contemplate this eye of the Path and truly expound the Dharma of equality.
Intent upon collecting and proclaiming the Honored One’s teachings,
it is as if nectar has emerged. Some are dedicated solely to practice,
observing the world of convention with its manifold clamor and the instability of birth and death.
Immersed in the worldly sense-faculties, like a rotting cart sunk in mud, one cannot extricate oneself;
therefore, one should follow the essentials of the scriptures.
Just as one gathers various flowers, I have expounded this out of compassion for the world.
Listen attentively as I expound the *Xiuxing daojing* (Sutra on the Practice of the Path), which eliminates existence and leads one to the state of non-existence.
Now, therefore, I shall lecture upon the *Xiuxing daojing*.

Birth, death, old age, sickness, grief, anxiety, weeping, and the assembly of all such disagreeable afflictions—those who practice with single-minded devotion, whether lay or ordained, desire to bring about the ultimate dharma of complete purity; their resolve shall not turn back, they will eventually reach the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), and all sufferings shall be severed.

For those who have no protection and no one to rely upon, they should only abandon all seeking; therefore, those who practice with the desire to leave suffering behind should always diligently and respectfully uphold this sutra.
Then he spoke in verse:
Falling into birth, old age, and death, one suffers grief and distress; The body and mind give rise to manifold sufferings.
Desiring to attain deliverance and never return, One should study and practice the Path without weariness.
What is meant by non-practice?
What is meant by practice?
How does one cultivate practice?
How does one practice the Path?

That which is called "non-practice" refers to: being mindful of lust, anger, and the desire to harm one's kin; [being preoccupied with] celestial realms and lands; associating with evil friends and violating the precepts; habitually practicing coarse speech and listening to what is unwholesome; having no fondness for study and being self-deprecating and arrogant; giving rise to attachments and conceiving false views of permanence; craving the existence of the body and the places where it dwells; associating with women and indulging in negligence and indolence; clinging to sensual desires and not departing from anger and delusion; frequently seeking out crowds of people while avoiding those who would offer refuge; being licentious and self-righteous, letting the mind run wild and sinking into doubt; losing diligence and constantly harboring fear; having the sense-faculties unsettled as they chase after various worldly matters; being talkative without moderation; delighting in long journeys and instead propounding heterodox doctrines; enjoying speaking of perverse matters and following along with what is contrary to the Dharma; and being far removed from the Way and its meaning—this is called non-practice.
This cannot be applied to the unconditioned.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Harboring hatred, greed, and thoughts of harming life, Always delighting in the body while conceiving notions of impurity,
With perverted wisdom following various faults— The Buddha says that such things are not to be practiced."
What is meant by that which is to be practiced?
It is to refrain from giving rise to anger and not harbor thoughts of inflicting harm; to draw near to virtuous friends and maintain the purity of the precepts;
to always speak according to the Way and receive instruction through study; and to not disparage oneself, while contemplating impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

Abiding in a suitable dwelling, he does not habituate himself to female forms, thereby eliminating his dissipation; he constantly resolves upon diligence to extinguish the afflictions of dust and toil;
he eats little and knows moderation to govern his physical conduct; he remains awake through the night, withdrawing his mind so as not to forget;
he is free from doubt and harbors no fear; his sense-gates are stilled in concentration, devoid of manifold external conditions. Regarding all things...
Whenever one speaks, it is always for the sake of right, impartial liberation; one delights in dwelling in seclusion and contemplates according to the truths.
One should aspire to attain those dharmas not yet obtained, firmly uphold and never forget those dharmas already reached, and joyfully adopt the essentials of the Dharma-transformation.
Regarding food, clothing, and shelter, one knows contentment; with the mind set upon the Way of the Sūtras, one never grows weary.
To the utmost, one practices the contemplation of impermanence and takes no pleasure in worldly, defiled thoughts regarding food.
The Way of non-action (*wuwei*) is characterized by stillness; such dharmas as these approximate non-action and are therefore called "practicable."
Where does this practice reside?
It is called Nirvana.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
With pure precepts and a mind delighting in the absence of self-conception, listening only to the meaning of the sutras and following virtuous friends;
seeing with discernment and practicing according to the teaching—this, the Buddha says, is the path of the unconditioned.
All mental applications toward the various phenomena one encounters, with a concentrated and focused mind free from suffering or weariness—this is called the accumulation of the virtues of discourse;
to restrain the faculties through concentration is what is meant by "practice."
What is meant by "cultivation" (bhāvanā)?
What constitutes "practice"?
It refers to being able to act in accordance [with the teachings], cultivating and reverently following them; this is cultivation.
That which is cultivated and practiced is called "practice.
What is meant by "practicing the Path"?
Single-minded diligence in the path of tranquility is what constitutes practicing the Path.
That cultivation consists of three grades: first, the ordinary person;
second, those training toward the Way; and third, those who have nothing further to learn.

Regarding what is called the cultivation of the ordinary person—whether newly initiated or long-practiced but not yet perfected—for such individuals, one preaches the Sūtra on the Path of Cultivation.
As for those who do not study, they consider themselves to have attained full understanding; what more need be discussed?
It is because of this that it is said in the *Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*: "One observes in profound stillness."
What is tranquil contemplation?
It is the pursuit of the fruits of the four virtues of a śramaṇa.
What are these four virtues?
This refers to what is called the realm of nirvana with remainder.
Why is it called "with remainder"?
It means that one is destined to reach the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
How should one reach the realm of the unconditioned?
It means that all roots of suffering are completely eliminated.

Therefore, a practitioner who wishes to abandon the afflictions of all intense sufferings should always be single-mindedly diligent and not engage in divergent practices; they must not violate the prohibitions of the teachings but should cultivate tranquil contemplation.
If a practitioner violates the precepts and harms the teachings, failing to reach tranquil contemplation, their efforts will be in vain.
It is like a person drilling wood to seek fire who repeatedly rests and lacks single-mindedness; they will never produce it, and having failed to obtain fire, their labor is wasted.
One with a lazy mind who wishes to seek the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is just like this.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Always attain tranquility and practice meditative concentration; One should abandon arrogance and frivolous play.
Dedicate yourself to cultivation without fail, Like one walking with eyes open in the dark of night."
Thus the practitioner perceives the destination; with wisdom such as this, they advance with diligence.
Devoting themselves to the True Transformation without ever flagging, they shall reach the path of tranquil stillness and non-action.
Having thoroughly perceived the profound and subtle mysteries, and having observed and gathered the teachings spoken by the Great Virtuous One—
this sūtra’s grand instruction is named "Quiescent Contemplation"— I have excerpted from various scriptures to expound it here.
Gathering the essential meanings from various sūtras, I have established these words of the nectar of non-aging and death;
what is heard by the ear is the practice of the wise, and through pure wisdom, the darkness of defilement is removed.

Entering into stillness like the light of the sun, Like the moon’s course illuminating the myriad stars, Having attained transcendence, one should receive the teaching; This abundance is immeasurable, like the autumn moon.
I reverently serve the Arhats and bow my head; I prostrate with face and forehead before the Muni, who is like space.
Taking refuge in the Exalted One, I obtain the nectar that eradicates the various desires—the roots and sprouts of worldly existence.
Various kinds of fruits are produced, with joy and sorrow as their branches;
the Buddha understands that the five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent—one should contemplate the various sutras according to their source.
One who practices the Path should further contemplate the basis of the five aggregates (skandhas) of the body:
form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are called the five aggregates.
It is like a city composed of many households; it is through the combination of the east, west, south, and north that it constitutes a city.
Form (*rūpa*) is likewise: it is not a single form that constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are also thus.

It is not that a single consciousness alone is called the aggregate of consciousness; it possesses ten bases, some of which are material forms and others mental phenomena—these constitute the aggregate of form.

Eight hundred types of painful and pleasant sensations are termed the aggregate of sensation. The aggregates of perception, formations, and consciousness each likewise possess eight hundred [subdivisions], and only then are they designated as "aggregates."
One should understand that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are fundamentally like this as well.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness— These are the origins of the five aggregates.
It is like a great city, consisting of various households of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
It is not a single form that constitutes "form"; in total, there are ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
There are eight hundred [types of] feeling and pleasure; the same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The wise person understands this dharma: that which is manifold is called an aggregate (*skandha*);
discerning it as not being one, the practitioner reflects upon it.
When various phenomena are collected and linked together, those who lack wisdom abandon the Buddha’s teaching.
Habituated to ignorance, one lacks clear understanding; it is like a tree with many branches and leaves, its five parts growing and spreading out. Those lacking skillful means are also like this;
one should understand that the five aggregates are just so, for the wise person who understands through wisdom clearly knows this.
Thus he grows upon the ground of his clan; the Dharma words he expounds are like honey-smeared [tongues].
The bhikṣu is like a bee gathering the nectar of flowers, just as a lotus flower unfolds its petals.
His wisdom awakens and excels the rising sun; the Buddha further transcends and surpasses the lotus flower.
The Buddha’s purity is free from all attachment; therefore, I bow my head and take refuge in the Honored One.
His marks are serene and reach unimpededness; in silent stillness and thoughtlessness he attains concentration.
Never once does he regress or fall away, for through his deliverance he reaches the unconditioned.
Holding fast to his intention, he manifests guidance; he instructs all living beings according to his own practice.
Out of compassion for me, he has spoken thus, for the sake of future generations of sentient beings.
That practitioner should understand the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
How does one know the characteristics of each of the five aggregates?

That which possesses luminosity is form (*rūpa*); that which possesses the characteristic of an image is also form; that which is grasped or held by the hand is also called form; and that which is shown to others is likewise form.
The cultivation of pleasure is suffering; that which is neither pleasant nor painful is likewise suffering—this is the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*).
The characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is perception (*saṃjñā*); whether it be a man, a woman, or any other object, this is called the perception of ideation (*saṃjñā-saṃjñā*).

That which involves volitional activity is called "formations" (*saṃskāra*); whether one performs wholesome actions, unwholesome actions, or those that are neither wholesome nor unwholesome, these are what are termed formations.
To discern perceptions is "consciousness" (*vijñāna*); whether they are wholesome, unwholesome, or neither wholesome nor unwholesome, such discernment is consciousness.
Thus, each clearly understood the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Form is unstable and full of defilements; The Buddha’s teaching of the sūtras is truly as it should be."
Acting in accordance with what he has taught, he discerns the various characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
With the nectar of immortality, he extinguishes the blazing fires; he eliminates the root of all suffering within the five aggregates.
His wisdom-light is like the light of the sun; the three realms universally revere him, and I too take refuge in him.
The Buddha, the Honored One of Capable Benevolence, possesses the power of profound wisdom;
having realized the purity of clear intelligence, he manifests the meaning according to what he knows, gathering the teachings of the Buddha-Dharma and expounding them as appropriate.
One should listen to his discourse with analytical understanding;
now he guides others toward compliant concentration, discerning the original arising of the five aggregates, and skillfully contemplating them by extensively citing various meanings.
That practitioner should discern and understand the fundamental nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
What is meant by "clearly understanding the root of the five aggregates"?
It is like a string of pearls dropped at a crossroads; someone seeing it feels joy in their heart and wishes to go and pick it up.

That person’s visual perception of the string of pearls is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); their fondness for and mental approval of it is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*); the initial consciousness that recognizes the strung pearls is named the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*); the mental intention arising in that person to take up the strung pearls is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); and the discernment of the strung pearls is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Such are the five aggregates.

These five aggregates are like beads on a single string, moving together at once; they perform various actions, whether emerging from the mind like beads on a string arising simultaneously, or receding back into the five aggregates.

It is the same for all people: the five aggregates follow whatever forms are seen by the eye; likewise with sounds heard by the ear, odors smelled by the nose, flavors tasted by the tongue, tangibles felt by the body, and mental objects perceived by the mind. Among these, the four aggregates within the mind constitute the formless aggregate.
Thus, in order to distinguish the roots of the five aggregates,
a verse was spoken:
"The boundless virtues are explained through differentiation, Just as their meanings were taught within the sutras."
The greedy are deluded and do not accept the teaching; I now follow the Dharma and receive this discourse.
The World-Honored One’s essential wisdom is peerless; through disciplined compliance, one attains the ultimate limit.
Having transcended all realms to reach the boundless shore, I prostrate to the World-Honored One, whose virtues are immeasurable.
His teaching is like the brightness of the sun, illuminating his disciples in this way;
he thoroughly understands worldly afflictions and removes fear as one discards withered flowers.
He beholds all arising and ceasing, and fully comprehends the formation and dissolution of the five aggregates.
I pray that I may bow my head to that Buddha and hear his venerable words.
One who practices the Way should know the transformations of the arising and passing away of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
What is meant by "knowing the arising and passing away of the five aggregates"?

It is like when a person’s life is about to end; because their lifespan is drawing to a close, four hundred and four diseases gradually afflict their body from all sides. They then encounter many dreams and behold strange and ominous portents, harboring fear and alarm:

they dream that bees, crows, magpies, eagles, and vultures perch upon their heads; they see crowds dwelling in halls above them, amusing themselves; the clothes they wear are blue, yellow, white, or black; they ride a wild, unruly horse and cry out in lamentation;
they dream of resting their head on a large dog, or again on a monkey, as they lie upon the bare earth.
In a dream, he eats from the same vessel as dead people, executioners, and latrine-cleaners; they travel and sightsee together.
Or else, he pours sesame oil, fat, and clarified butter over his own body and consumes them, doing so repeatedly.
He sees a snake coiled around his body and, struggling, is dragged headlong into the water.
Some, seeing their own bodies, leap for joy and strike their thighs with laughter;
some, seeing their own floral ornaments fall into ashes, smear their bodies with that ash and then take it up to eat;
some see ants and leap over them.
Or one may see them chewing salt; dogs, hounds, and monkeys, upon seeing this, will chase after them and each bite back at what they have taken.
Or one may see the taking of a wife, or the worship of household deities, or see the collapse of a house and the destruction of various shrines.
In dreams, one may see plowing, or the plow falling and cutting off one's beard and hair.
At times, one's own teeth may fall to the ground, or one may be dressed in white robes;
or one may see oneself walking naked and barefoot, with sesame oil smeared on the body, wallowing in the dust;
or one dreams of wearing garments of hide, grass, or tattered rags.
He dreams that others mount a dilapidated carriage and arrive at his gate, intending to take him away;

or he sees various flowers, *kunkuma*, and other perfumes being taken by his kinsmen to adorn their bodies; or he sees his ancestors appearing with dark-blue complexions, calling to him from before and seizing him to drag him along—he has such dreams repeatedly.
He wanders among burial mounds and tomb mounds picking up flower garlands, and he sees red lotuses falling upon his neck, or he falls into a great river and is swept away by the waters.
In dreams, he falls headlong into the waters of the Five Lakes and the Nine Rivers, unable to reach their bottom;
or he sees his own body enter various groves that bear neither flowers nor fruit, where his frame is mangled by thorns and brambles, while tiles and stones are piled upon him;
or he sees withered trees entirely devoid of branches and leaves, dreaming that he climbs them to frolic and play alone, or dances and beats his breast at shrines and altars.
Sometimes they see a grove of trees and, finding solitary joy therein, laugh with exuberant mirth; they break off withered branches, bind them into bundles, and carry them away on their backs.
Sometimes they enter a dark chamber and do not know how to exit through the door;
again, they ascend mountains and peaks or enter among crags and caves, unaware of the way out.
Furthermore, they may see a mountain collapse and press down upon their bodies, causing them to wail and cry out in grief;
or they may see a herd of elephants suddenly arrive and trample over them;
or they dream that dust and soil cover their bodies and heads, or that they wear tattered clothes as they walk through a vast wilderness.
In a dream, one sees oneself riding a tiger and galloping violently, or riding a donkey or a dog while traveling south;
entering a cemetery to gather charcoal, claws, and hair, one sees oneself wearing withered flowers upon the head, being led into a great mountain where King Yama appears and questions him.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"While dwelling in the world, there is much peace and joy; But when the confrontation with death arrives, one is struck with fear.
Stricken and wounded by illness, One is oppressed and constrained, no longer at ease."
With a mind burning with distress and affliction, he sees a dream and harbors fear, as if being pursued by an evil person; his anxiety and dread are just like this.
Once the man has awakened from his heart, he harbors terror within and his body trembles; he reckons that his life is about to end, certain of it without doubt:
"The dream I have just had is unprecedented since time immemorial.

Because his mind was filled with dread, the hair on his body stood on end; his illness became grave and he trembled with unease. It was as if a fierce elephant were trampling a plantain tree underfoot as a vast multitude arrived; his condition worsened until he was confined to his bed, just like that simile.
Desperate and without recourse, he sought out a physician. Seeing him in such distress, his brothers and kinsmen sent someone to summon a doctor—the very person who was dispatched.

His body was covered in much filth and impurity, and his robes were tattered and worn out. His hands and nails were long, and he wore a cracked parasol; his feet were shod in sandals made of split wood that were torn and broken. He rode a dilapidated carriage, his complexion was pitch black and his two eyes were blue, and he frequently rubbed and wiped his beard and hair with his hands.
The oxen yoked to it were either blue or black, and there was also one that was pure white.
"Quickly call for a physician and seize him to place him upon a carriage.
Thereupon, he recited this verse:
"When people go out for excursions and sightseeing, They take pleasure only in things that are of no benefit."
Indulging unrestrainedly in one's desires, one never thinks of a physician.
Only when the body is afflicted by illness and one lies bedridden in severe distress does one then summon a physician, wishing to have that ailment cured.
At that time, the physician examined the matter with his mind and concluded that the patient would surely die.
Why was this? He observed these strange omens:

he looked at the person who had come to call for him and saw his clothing and speech, as well as his broken umbrella; his beard, nails, and hair were disheveled. Furthermore, the day was inauspicious—whether it was the fourth, sixth, twelfth, or fourteenth day. Those who arrive on such days are all considered ill-omened; the physician was thus displeased, as the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) was unfavorable, the auspicious hour had been lost, and it was a day forbidden by the immortals and former sages.
The physician thought to himself:
"Even though one encounters such strange constellations and their auspicious or inauspicious influences, they may still be treated. Why is this so?"
Although one may employ skillful means to treat the sick and expect recovery as long as their allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted, if the time for their end has arrived, they cannot be cured.
From this it is clear that it is not necessarily dependent on auspicious days or the good or bad fortune of the constellations; therefore, the wise do not seek favorable times based on the calendar.
The transcendents often say:
"One should seek skillful means.
Even in cases of wind-cold illnesses where life has not yet ended, if there is the possibility of an untimely death, such a person may still be cured.
"If his life is destined to end, there is nothing that can be done;
nevertheless, it would still be better to go and treat him than not to go at all.
Having thought this, the physician immediately rose with the intention of departing.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"It is like two people who set out together to enter the sea;
one may reach the further shore, while the other is cut off midway."
Falling into the ocean of disease is likewise illustrated by this analogy:
even if one should occasionally recover from an illness, there may still be those who die again.

Thus, when the physician has arrived at the patient’s home, he encounters evil omens and hears ominous sounds—such as reports of loss, burning, destruction, severing, flaying, being dragged out, threats of execution, being hauled away, setting out on a journey, or imprisonment; based on these signs, he determines that the patient cannot be cured and is already dead.

To the south, foxes howl; one may hear the cries of crows and owls, or see small children scattering soil at one another, standing naked and pulling each other’s hair, and breaking jars, bottles, basins, and various vessels.
Having witnessed these omens, one goes before to visit the patient, who lies weak and exhausted upon their bed.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"The physician examines the patient's features; The man is struck with alarm and dread, ill at ease.
Whether sitting, rising, or returning to his bed, He is distressed and feverish, as if his skin were being scorched."
Seeing this, the physician thought to himself:
"As I have examined the beginning and end of various medical scriptures, these are the signs of death:

the facial expression is terrified, the eyelashes are disheveled, the body is withered and yellow, saliva flows from the mouth, the eyes are dim and clouded, the nostrils are parched and yellow, the complexion has lost its luster, one cannot perceive sounds or scents, the lips are cracked and the tongue is dry; his appearance is like the earth, the hundred vessels are vividly blue, and all the hair stands on end. When his hair is grasped or his nose pinched, he has no sensation at all; his breathing is uneven, sometimes slow and sometimes rapid."
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"The complexion of his face has changed, The hairs upon his body stand erect;
His gaze is fixed as if lost in thought, And strange signs have already appeared, stiffening his tongue."
The patient possesses these omens; his remaining life is but a trifle.
Enveloped by the fire of illness, he is like grass and wood being consumed by flames.
Furthermore, another sutra describes the various strange portents that occur when a person is about to die:
Even if he is provided with bathing, or even if he does not bathe;

even if fine incense—such as *agaru*, *candana*, root-incense, flower-incense, and various blended perfumes—is burned, these fragrances, though truly excellent, will smell to the sick man like the stench of burning human bones, hair, body hair, nails, skin, fat, marrow, and excrement; they will further smell like the stench of owls, vultures, foxes, dogs, rats, snakes, and vipers.

The patient’s voice changes, sounding like broken tiles; its quality is as if the throat were constricted. The sound may resemble that of a crane, a wild goose, a peacock, an ox, a horse, a tiger, a wolf, thunder, or a drum.

The person’s temperament and character undergo constant shifts and are no longer stable: at times they appear dignified and their body becomes supple, while at other times it becomes coarse and rigid. The body frequently changes, becoming sometimes light and sometimes heavy, thereby losing its original state.
These various portents are encountered by those whose lives are destined to end; each person experiences several, though not necessarily all.
Thus, it is said in verse:
Beholding such various transformations, The multitude of afflictions assails the body.
With a mind harboring fear, one encounters such calamity as this.
Human nature is thus ruined; the body undergoes manifold transformations, just like the fruit of the bamboo or reed, which perishes spontaneously of its own accord.
According to what I have studied and as I have heard and known, when a person approaches death, various strange transformations appear:
the mouth no longer perceives flavors, the ears no longer hear sounds, the tendons and veins contract and tighten, and the breathing becomes irregular;
the body aches and groans, the blood and vital energy become faint, the body grows emaciated and thin, and the tendons become prominent.
Or his body suddenly becomes bloated, with the veins protruding and the jaw hanging down; his head trembles, he is loathsome to look upon, and his movements are sluggish.
The pupils of his eyes are much darker than usual, his gaze is fixed, his bowels and bladder are obstructed, his joints feel as if they are coming apart, and his faculties are unsettled.
His eyes and mouth are entirely blue, and his breath is constricted and gasping.
All manner of strange portents and transformations appeared in this way.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"His ailments and afflictions are beyond counting; The blood, veins, essence, and vital energy are all exhausted."
"Just as water gnaws at the roots of a tree, one must pity [the patient] as if they were being cut down.
At that time, the physician thought to himself:
"One who has such an illness will surely die; of this there is no doubt."
"In ancient times, there were skilled physicians who composed sūtras, known as:

Yu-bi-chu-kong (At-that-removes-fear), Chang-er-hui-zhang (Long-ear-ash-palm), Yang-yen-chang-yu (Nourishing-speech-rearing), Ji-jiao-duo-ran (Urgent-instruction-many-beard), Tian-you-chang-gai (Heaven-also-long-canopy), Da-shou-tui-zhuan (Great-head-retrogression), Jiao-cui-da-bai (Emaciated-great-white), Zui-zun-lu-mian (Most-honored-road-face), Tiao-niu (Ox-tamer), Qi-bo (Qi-bo), Yi-hui (Yi-hui), and Bian-que (Bian-que). Such individuals as these all treated physical illnesses."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Among those of such a kind— The Honored Dharma, the Brahmins, and the Sages;
Those who provide true salvation and their fruits, As well as other kings and skilled physicians."
This is the primary cause of success or failure; one who possesses broad knowledge can deliver others from calamity.
To save lives through the compassion of the sutras is just like the Brahmā-creator fashioning the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is another physician who specializes in treating the ears and eyes, named:

Yanxuan-dongyao (Eye-twitching-shaker), Hedou-lingming (Battle-quarrel-bell-sounder), Yuèzhī-yīngzǐ (Moon-clan-hero-child), Qiècáng-shànjué (Casket-store-well-awakened), Tiáoniú-mùjīn (Taming-ox-eye-gold), Tuliáo-lìshì (Bald-owl-power-clan), and Léimíng (Thunder-sound)—these are the names of eminent physicians who specialize in treating the ears and eyes.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The physicians such as Akṣika and others, Who prepare their medicines with clarity,
Remove the darkness of disease, Just as the sun destroys all gloom."
Furthermore, there were physicians who treated various sores, named:
Dharmadatta the Younger Brother, Priyadarśana the Concise, and Suvarṇavākya; these were the physicians for sores.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Whoever is able to heal and treat The hundred kinds of wounds and sores,
And can eliminate all calamities and ailments, Is like one who levels the ground with their feet."
The reason the wealth of the Dharma is brought forth and scriptures are composed in this world is precisely to treat the maladies of affliction,
so as to cause all beings to leave behind suffering and hardship.
Furthermore, there is a physician for infants, whose name is:
The Venerable Kāśyapa and Jīvaka were respectful yet swift and agile; these individuals all treated the ailments of children.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as there might be a servant boy Who abandons his worldly tasks and eliminates arrogance,"
Therefore, born into the mundane world, he took pity on those who treat children.
These venerable ones, such as Kāśyapa and others, practicing benevolence through the True Dharma,
out of compassion for the young, have composed this medical scripture.
Furthermore, there are spirit-doctors named Daihua (Wearing Flowers) and Bushi-huo (Not Serving Fire); these are those who ward off spirits and ghosts that come to harass people.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
As the various constellations revolve in their cycles, so too it is with human life;
when one is gripped by fear, many perils arise.
This sūtra was composed to completely resolve those afflictions.
Just as the Buddha, by means of the True Dharma, removes ignorance and causes one to see the light;
even if all these aforementioned physicians were assembled together, along with those of illusory arts, sorcery, and incantations, they could not effect a cure or prevent one from meeting their end.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Committing sinful defilements, One undergoes diligent toil while harboring manifold afflictions.
Sickness and pain disorder one's will; With much impurity, life’s span is shortened."
Swept away and submerged by illness, one sees the evidence of death and is struck with fear;
even the Lord of Devas and the various gods cannot rescue or bring peace, much less I.
The physician thought to himself:
"Before my life is cut short, I must withdraw!
he said, and then addressed the assembly:
"If this sick man should request any food, drink, or delicacies, give him whatever he desires; do not oppose him!"
"I have an urgent matter and must leave you; once my business is concluded, I shall return.
Having made this pretext, he then departed.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
When life is about to be severed, one contracts a disease of extreme severity;
joined with the afflictions of worldly toil, one does not realize that retribution has arrived.
Strange transformations arise spontaneously, and one encounters the utmost heat of the five aggregates.
Even were one to hold a vajra, they could not save his life.

At that time, the members of the sick person’s household—men and women, both old and young—hearing what the physician had said, immediately abandoned their decoctions and medicinal herbs as well as all incantations and rituals. The family, kinsmen, clansmen, neighbors, close friends, and acquaintances all gathered together, surrounding the patient, wailing and weeping in sorrow, contemplating the gravity of his illness.

It is like when a butcher’s flock seizes a pig, leading it away to slaughter; the remaining pigs all gather together in alarm and fear, pricking up their ears to listen for the sound, staring about in terror and consternation.

It is like when a fierce tiger seizes an ox from among a herd; the other oxen, seeing this, flee in panic—some entering mountain caves, some throwing themselves into deep valleys, and others entering the thickets of trees, leaping and bellowing.
It is like when a fisherman holds a net to catch fish; the other fish, seeing him, scatter in fear, sinking down or hiding among the rocks, the shores, and the depths of the grass.
Furthermore, it is like a hawk swooping down upon a flock of birds; as it seizes its prey, the other birds see it and each flies away in dispersal.
So it is with this person: when impermanence confronts them, their body disintegrates and scatters, and their household and kinsmen grieve over the impending separation with such sorrow.

When life is about to be severed, the messengers of King Yama naturally arrive; having arrived, they see them bound and pierced by iron arrows, being drawn along by their transgressions onto the boat of birth and death, and are on the verge of departing.

His family members surrounded him; with their hair disheveled, they were overcome with grief and lamentation. Dust covered their faces as they wept and sighed in sorrow, tears streaming down their cheeks, all saying:
"How painful! How tragic!"
"How can you abandon me?
He beat his breast in deep distress, extolling the various virtuous qualities of the sick man while his heart was filled with anguish.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
When a person is afflicted by illness and suffering, their body grows cold and fades away from heat;
the members of the household all gather together and raise their voices in lamentation.
One creates karma that results in further suffering or joy, just as a bee gathers the nectar of flowers.
The mind then succumbs to grief, bringing distress to the entire family.
Such is the person's illness: the "sword-wind" arises within the body, causing the joints of the patient’s bones to dislocate.
There is a wind named Kṣepa, which severs the joints;
there is a wind named Spandana, which causes the tendons and veins to slacken;
there is a wind named Asthibheda, which consumes the marrow of the sick person.

There is a wind named *Kṣaya* (Diminishing) that alters the complexion of the face; the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and throat all turn blue; the various orifices for inhalation and exhalation are severed and destroyed, and the body is flayed and stripped.

Furthermore, there is a wind called *Pārśva-stambha* (Paralyzing the Sides) which causes everything within the body—the knees, shoulders, sides, back, spine, abdomen, navel, large and small intestines, liver, lungs, heart, spleen, and all other internal organs—to be completely severed.

There is also a wind called *Āvarta* (Whirling) which obstructs the flow of fat, blood, feces, urine, the raw stomach (*āmāśaya*), and the cooked stomach (*pakvāśaya*), as well as whatever has been eaten; it dries up both cold and heat entirely.

There is a wind named "Between the Joints" that causes all the limbs and joints to either contract or extend, making one raise the hands and feet as if wishing to grasp at empty space. One becomes agitated when sitting or rising; sometimes one laughs and plays, while at other times one sighs deeply with a piteous sound. The joints feel as if they are breaking one by one, the tendons and veins become slack, and the marrow and brain waste away. The eyes no longer see forms, the ears no longer hear sounds, the nose cannot distinguish fragrances, and the mouth no longer perceives flavors. The body grows cold and the breath ceases; there is no further consciousness, yet the heart remains warm and the soul persists. The body is as rigid as wood, unable to move or shake.
Thereupon, it is said in verse:
When the wind of the sword arises, the body moves with much unease;
as all conditions arrive together, one is entirely unaware of them.
Having encountered manifold afflictions, his life is brought to its end;
like the string of a bow or crossbow, it is no longer functional whether slack or taut.
At that time, all the four elements within that person’s body are utterly decayed; though a faint breath remains, it is like a lamp about to go out.

Within this person’s mind there exists the faculty of mental consciousness; during their lifetime, regarding whatever good or evil they have done, the mind itself knows by its own nature the resulting calamities or blessings, misfortunes or auspiciousness, and all that has been performed in both this life and future lives. Those who practice virtue possess a serene and harmonious countenance, while those who commit evil have a displeased expression.
If a person’s mind is joyful and their facial expression is pleasant, one should know that they will find their destination in the good realms;
if their facial expression is foul and their thoughts are unwholesome, they will head toward the evil realms.

It is as if an old man were to look into a clear mirror and see his own form: his hair white, his face wrinkled, his teeth fallen out, his body scarred, covered in dust and grime, dark and ugly, his skin sagging, his back hunched, and his old age trembling;
upon seeing this, he would feel ashamed and contemptuous of himself, closing his eyes and setting down the mirror, thinking, "I have already lost my youth!"
As old age approaches, the mind harbors sorrow and anxiety; having departed from peace and security, one reaches the ultimate extremity.
Those who have habitually practiced evil, at the time of their death, perceive terrifying transformations; filled with grief and dread, they reproach themselves deeply, thinking:
"I shall surely return to the evil realms; of this there is no doubt."
It is also like an old man looking into a mirror; seeing his own body, he knows that decay has arrived.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Things made of gold, jewels, and the like, Differ in quality according to whether they were crafted skillfully or clumsily."
If there are those who commit evil deeds, they shall sink into the deep abyss.
Though they may rise again after having sunk, they look about for no support;
like one being swept away by water, such is their state even at the point of death.

Among those who practice goodness, there are three classes: they restrain their body, speech, and mind; they purely cultivate all virtues; and they take the Dharma as their wealth. When the time of their death approaches, their hearts are filled with joy and exultation, thinking:
"I shall surely ascend to heaven."
It is like a merchant traveling far away to conduct his business, who, having traversed perilous paths and acquired great wealth and profit, returns home with immeasurable joy;

or like a farmer who, having plowed his fields at the proper time and encountered timely wind and rain, harvests a bountiful crop of the five grains and stores them in granaries, his heart filled with great delight;
or like one who recovers from a debilitating illness or finally settles a heavy debt—their hearts leaping with exultation are just like this.
Just as bees gather flowers to produce honey, so too is the accumulation of merit; his mind was filled with great joy, thinking, "I shall certainly ascend to heaven!
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Those who are learners and true men, having accumulated the practice of the True Dharma,
cross over all manifold afflictions and personally attain the Way of Clarity.
They are like those dwelling in seclusion, gazing down from a high mountain.
When that person’s life comes to an end, they see the path to the good realms as follows:
At that time, when the person’s life has ended, the faculties of body, sense, and consciousness cease, and they immediately undergo the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
It is like a scale: according to its lightness or heaviness, it rises or falls; such is the case with goodness and evil.
When the spirit departs from the human body and dwells in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it possesses all five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) without any deficiency.
At the time of death, the aggregates of the intermediate state do not reach [the new birth], yet the aggregates of the intermediate state do not depart from their original basis.
It is like using a seal to stamp clay: the seal does not adhere to the clay, nor is it separate from it.
Just as when the five grains are sown, the sprouts, stalks, and fruit arise; these are not the original seed, yet they do not depart from it.
In the same way, when a person dies, their spirit, essence, soul, and breath are not identical to the five aggregates, yet they do not depart from the original source.

Each receives their respective retribution according to what was originally sown: those who have performed virtuous deeds abide in the midst of goodness, while those who have practiced evil abide in the midst of transgression; only those with the eye of the Way can perceive this.
While abiding in the state of cessation (nirodha), there are three kinds of nutriment:
first, the nutriment of contact (sparśāhāra); second, the nutriment of mind (mana-āhāra); and third, the nutriment of mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna).

Those who abide in this cessation may remain for one day or as long as seven days; thereafter, according to their past karma, they either follow toward the union of their parents or proceed toward the three miserable realms, the human world, or the heavens.

Those who have committed much evil, while dwelling in the intermediate state, see a great fire arise and surround their bodies, just as a wild fire consumes grass and trees. Dust and rain fall upon their forms. They see crows, vultures, eagles, and other such malevolent beings, all with long claws and teeth and hideous faces; their clothing is tattered and ruined, and fire blazes upon their heads. Each brandishes weapons and strikes them with clubs, piercing them with spears and hacking at them with knives, leaving them filled with terror.
Seeking rescue and protection, they see a grove of trees in the distance and run toward it, but at that moment they vanish, ceasing within the five aggregates of the intermediate state.
As for those who enter the hell of the sword-leaf trees and fall into the hells, their spirits perceive it as such.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Deluded like an intoxicated elephant, They have violated and lost the teachings of the Noble Dharma."
Turbid with defilement like muddy water, the mind is as agitated as this;
constantly abandoning the Right Path and letting the mind wander into evil ways,
such a person encounters manifold sufferings and, at the end of life, falls into hell.

Those who have committed minor evils see fire, smoke, and dust swirling and filling their bodies; they are pursued by lions, tigers, wolves, snakes, vipers, and herds of elephants. Furthermore, they see old canals, springs, deep waters, collapsing mountains, and great ravines; filled with terror, they rush toward them and immediately lose [their former state], ceasing within the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
Falling into the realm of animals, one who sees these transformations knows they have received the body of a beast.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"By habituating to delusion and abandoning wisdom, One may become intoxicated and fall into the dark path."
Those who speak with harsh and coarse words, who delight in beating and striking others,
who further bring about the calamities of their own transgressions, and who take pleasure in unwholesome deeds—
such as these, lacking in compassion, are reborn among the beasts.

If one's offenses are slight, hot winds will arise from all four directions; the body will become stiflingly hot and naturally experience hunger and thirst. One will see people approaching from afar, all bearing swords, staves, spears, halberds, bows, and arrows, surrounding one. Seeing a great city in the distance, one desires to enter within it;
as soon as this thought arises, the five aggregates (skandhas) currently experienced therein are immediately lost.
Born among the *pūtana* (hungry ghosts), their appearance undergoes such transformations; one should know that they have fallen into the realm of the hungry ghosts.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Harsh and corrupt, delighting in slandering others, They distance themselves from the precepts and do not follow the Dharma."
Those who commit forbidden and defiling acts, Greedily eating alone;
Falling into realms of pus and blood, Where the afflictions of hunger are extreme—
Know that such people as these Will certainly enter the state of hungry ghosts.

Cultivating pure conduct and virtuous goodness, cool breezes blow from all four directions, their fragrance most exquisite; various kinds of incense rain down upon his body, while the sounds of various musical instruments resonate in harmony. Beholding the gardens, groves, trees, flowers, and fruits, he finds them all flourishing and lush.
As soon as he forms the intention to go there, he immediately loses that thought and ceases within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); his spirit naturally ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Practicing the Dharma leads to the Noble Path; planting meritorious karma brings rebirth in heaven.
There, one delights in music and song, wandering amidst the various flowering trees."
A multitude of beautiful and radiant jade maidens, upright, luminous, and composed,
constantly observe with joyful hearts as they dwell upon the summit of Mount Tai.
If one’s conduct is not uniform— whether good or evil— one shall reach the human realm.
When the parents unite and the vital essence is released at the proper time, the child is destined to be born.

If the parents possess virtuous thoughts and are in harmony, and if the mother’s womb is open and unobstructed, her heart filled with joy and free from improper thoughts, then she will be supple and not stubborn; being free from illness, she is capable of receiving the child.
She shall not be negligent nor act contrary to the way, following the True Dharma without being defiled by turbidity, immediately casting off all dust-like impurities.

That essence is neither impure nor turbid; it is moderate and not excessive, neither putrid nor dark red, and is not corrupted by the various poisons of wind and cold. It separates from the urine, and when it is time for rebirth, the spirit immediately enters it.
She thought to herself:
"If this man does not unite with a woman, I wish to have intercourse with him.

She gave rise to a mind of anger and resentment toward that man, while her heart harbored reverence for the woman; thus, manifesting both hatred and desire, she pushed the man aside and moved toward the woman.
When the father’s semen was emitted, his spirit rejoiced, thinking, "This is mine.
At that moment, it immediately loses the five aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and enters the womb.
Once the parents' essences have united and it is within the womb, it leaps with redoubled joy; it is no longer the five aggregates of the intermediate state, yet it is not separate from them.

Entering the womb is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*); the time of joy is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*); the time of mindfulness regarding the semen is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); entering the womb due to the conditions of past demerit or merit is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); and the spirit dwelling within the womb corresponds to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). This such conjunction is called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Seeking [the state of being], while still in the womb, one immediately acquires two faculties: the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and the body faculty (*kāya-indriya*).
During the first seven days of abiding therein, these remain without increase or decrease;
after another two weeks, the embryo begins to transform slightly, becoming like thin curd.
At the end of three weeks, it resembles raw curd;
at the end of four weeks, the essence coagulates like mature curd;
by the end of five weeks, the fetal essence undergoes transformation, becoming like fresh butter.
Furthermore, after six or seven days, it changes like a polyp;
at the seventh week, it turns into a piece of flesh;
and after eight weeks, its hardness becomes like unbaked clay.
Upon reaching the ninety-seventh day, five blisters transformed and emerged from his two elbows, two thighs, and his neck;
after another seventeen days, there were again five blisters that emerged from his wrists, ankles, and his head;
after eleven more days, twenty-four blisters continued to emerge, from which his fingers, toes, eyes, ears, nose, and mouth appeared.
In the twelfth week, these fetal membranes further develop and take shape;
in the thirteenth week, the form of the abdomen appears;
and in the fourteenth week, the liver, lungs, heart, spleen, and kidneys are produced.
In the fifteenth week, the large intestine is formed;
in the sixteenth week, the small intestine appears;
in the seventeenth week, the location of the stomach is established.
In the eighteenth week, the receptacle for undigested food (āmāśaya) and the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya) arise from these two locations;
in the nineteenth week, the thighs, calves, intestines, bones, palms, insteps, arm joints, and tendons are formed;
in the twentieth week, the genitals, navel, breasts, chin, neck, and physical features are produced.

In the twenty-first week, the skeletal elements are each differentiated according to their respective positions: two bones are located in the head; thirty-two bones are attached to the mouth; seven bones are attached to the neck; two bones are attached to the thighs; two bones are attached to the elbows; four bones are attached to the upper arms; twelve bones are attached to the chest; eighteen bones are attached to the back; two bones are attached to the hips; four bones are attached to the knees; forty bones are attached to the feet; one hundred and eight minor bones are joined with the body's flesh; and eighteen bones are situated on the two sides of the torso, while two bones are attached to the shoulders.

Thus, these bodily bones total three hundred in number and are interconnected; at this stage, the bones are as supple as a freshly harvested gourd. In the twenty-second week, the bones become somewhat firmer, like an unripe gourd.
After twenty-one days and seven nights, the bones become increasingly firm, like walnuts; these three hundred bones are each interconnected:

the foot bones attach to the feet, the knee bones to the knees, the ankle bones to the ankles, the thigh bones to the thighs, the hip bones to the hips, the vertebrae to the spine, and the breast bones to the chest.
The ribs are joined to the ribs, the jawbone is joined to the jaw, and the bones of the neck, chin, arms, wrists, hands, and feet are all interconnected.
This collection of bones is like a magical illusion, or like a chariot constructed with its bones as the walls;
it is bound together by sinews, drenched in blood, and enveloped in skin, flesh, and thin membrane.
It is covered over; thus, according to one's original sins and merits, one obtains this fruit. There is no conscious thought that relies upon the fundamental source of the mind;
rather, it is led and moved by whatever direction the wind takes it.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
This accumulation of five bones, Following the mind’s whims and indulgence,
Manifests as sudden jerks within the body, Just like the dragging of a snake.
The deeds performed in previous lives, the dharmas arising from good and evil,
are like a person traveling a road— sometimes level, sometimes thorny. In the twenty-fourth week,
seven hundred sinews are produced, connecting throughout the body.
In the twenty-fifth week, seven thousand channels are produced, though they are not yet fully formed;
in the twenty-sixth week, all the channels are completely penetrated and fully perfected, like the pores of a lotus root;
in the twenty-seventh week, the three hundred and sixty-three sinews are all completed.
In the twenty-eighth week, the skin begins to form;
in the twenty-ninth week, the flesh and muscles become somewhat thicker;
in the thirtieth week, there is just skin and the semblance of form.
In the thirty-first week, the skin becomes thicker and firmer;
in the thirty-second week, the skin and leather further develop;
in the thirty-third week, the ears, nose, lips, fingers, and the various joints of the knees are formed.
In the thirty-fourth week, ninety-nine thousand pores are produced, though the hair follicles are not yet formed;
in the thirty-fifth week, the pores are fully developed;
in the thirty-sixth week, the nails are formed.
In the thirty-seventh week, various winds arise within the mother’s womb. There is a wind that opens the child’s ears, eyes, nose, and mouth;
there may be a wind that colors the hair and body hair, making them either handsome or ugly.
Furthermore, there is a wind that forms the complexion of the body, whether white, red, or black, and whether beautiful or ugly—all of which result from past actions.
During these seven days, the winds of birth arose, bringing chills and fevers, and the channels for excrement and urine were opened.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
This body is bound together by sinews, And is composed of various blood vessels.
Impurities fill it and rot accumulates within; the various orifices leak as if washed by water.
The mind is thus deceived by its own delusions, skillfully joined together through artifice.
Like a wooden puppet operated by machinery, it is exceedingly difficult to find when sought.
In the thirty-eighth week of being in the mother’s womb, winds arise spontaneously according to one's past conduct (*pūrvacaryā*).

For those who have practiced virtue in previous lives, there arises a fragrant wind that makes their body and mind supple and flawless; it aligns their bones and joints so they are upright and handsome, such that all love and respect them.

For those who have practiced evil in previous lives, there arises a foul wind that makes the body uneasy and contrary to the mind; it blows upon the bones and joints making them hunched and crooked, rendering them unattractive and incapable of male virility, such that people do not delight in them.
This constitutes thirty-eight weeks.
When nine months are less by four days, the child’s body and skeletal joints are fully formed as a human being.
Thereupon, a verse says:
When a person has been in the womb for nine months, all the bodily constituents and channels are complete, and the bones and joints are fully formed; everything is perfected without deficiency.
Within the belly, they gradually develop of their own accord, growing little by little.
When the time arrives, everything is fully complete, like the moon on the fifteenth day.
That infant’s body consists of two parts:
one part from the father, and one part from the mother.

Among the various parts of the body—the hair of the head, the body hair, the cheeks, the eyes, the tongue, the throat, the heart, the liver, the spleen, the kidneys, the intestines, and the blood—those that are soft derive from the mother;
the nails, teeth, bones, joints, marrow, brain, tendons, and veins, which are hard, derive from the father.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
The human body is joined together, All born from father and mother;
When its various joints are disassembled, It is established through the transformation of causes and conditions.
Depending on these, one’s complexion fades; all shall surely come to decay.
Just as various materials are joined to construct a chariot, so too is the reckoning of the body.
There are two things prior to its making; the establishment of the person is like this.
Only through the karmic retribution of the parents can one subsequently be born.

When the infant is within the mother’s womb, it dwells below the raw receptacle (āma-koṣṭha) and above the cooked receptacle (pakva-koṣṭha). A male child has his back toward the exterior and his face toward the interior, situated on the left side;
a female child has her back toward the mother and her face toward the exterior, situated on the right side.

It is a place of suffering, foul-smelling, filthy, and impure; all the joints are contracted and cannot be extended. Cast away within a leather bag, it is entangled by the network of the abdomen; stained with stored blood, its dwelling is cramped and confined, and it depends upon such impurities as excrement and urine.
Regarding these remaining four days of the ninth month, he had previously cultivated wholesome conduct; on the first day and the last day, he resolved his mind and thought:
"Whether I am in my garden pavilion or in the heavens, [I am here]."
Those who have committed evil deeds are said to be "in the prisons of the hell-world.

Within three days, they become distressed and unhappy; by the fourth day, winds arise within the mother’s womb, moving the child’s body up or down and causing it to hang upside down with its head toward the birth canal.
Those who possessed virtue would then think to themselves:
"As I cast myself into the bathing pool and sport in the water, it is as if I have fallen from a high bed onto a place filled with flowers and incense!"
Those lacking merit will think to themselves:

"I have fallen from the mountain and cast myself into trees, riverbanks, ditches, or pits; or perhaps into a latrine, or into something like hell, a net, upon thorns, into a wilderness, a stony ravine, or amidst swords and halberds!"
He was filled with sorrow and found no joy.
"The retribution for good and evil is as different as this.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Like casting oneself into a blazing, scorching fire, surrounded by swirling smoke,
this is brought about by the fruit of heedlessness; dwelling within a body like boiling water,
the origins of suffering and joy are all produced through transgressions and merits.
Whatever one has done in each successive birth, such is the body one receives.

When the infant’s body is about to emerge from the birth canal, and upon falling to the ground, it is struck by the external wind; then, touched by the woman’s hands and washed with warm water, the agonizing pain is like that of a festering wound.
Due to these afflictions, fears, and dread of death, one becomes deluded and confused; thus, one is bewildered and does not know where one originally came from or where one is now going.

As soon as one is born upon the earth, amidst the foul place of entangled blood, malevolent spirits come to surround one, one is struck by the wicked and depraved, touched by flying corpses, and beset by those who practice sorcery with insects or by epileptic demons, each waiting for an opportunity to assault one.

It is like a piece of flesh fallen at a crossroads, where crows, ravens, vultures, and wolves each come to contend for it; likewise, various malevolent spirits and ghosts, seeking an opportunity against the child, surround him on all sides.
Those who have practiced virtue in past lives cannot be harmed by malevolent spirits; however, those who have committed evil in past lives are immediately possessed by various demons.
When a child is first born, it survives through the mother’s milk; as it gradually grows, it becomes established through solid food.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"While dwelling within the womb, one encounters manifold sufferings;
once born and having attained human form, the pains are a hundred thousandfold."
When the sense faculties have fully developed, one emerges from this fragile and precarious body;
that which is born must inevitably age and die—this is the ultimate lack of reality.
Once the child has grown and the body has been nourished with food and drink, as soon as it receives the essence of grain, eighty kinds of worms immediately arise within its frame.
Two types are located at the roots of the hair:
the first is named Tongue-Licking, and the second is named Repeated-Licking.
Three types are located on the head, named as follows:
Solidity, injury, and destruction.
One type resides in the brain, while two types reside on the surface of the brain:
the first is named *nṛtu*, the second is named *khāra*, and the third is named *saṃkula*.
Two kinds are located on the forehead:
the first is called "lowly," and the second is called "putrid.
Two kinds are located in the eyes:
The first is named Tongue-Licking; the second is named Repeated-Licking.
Two types reside in the ear:
the first is named Discerning-Flavor; the second is named Manifesting-Flavor-Essence.
Two types are located in the ear-organ:
the first is named Chi (Red), and the second is named Fu-chi (Re-red).
Two types are located in the nose:
The first is named "Fatty" (Pīna), and the second is named "Further Fatty" (Punar-pīna).
Two types reside within the mouth:
the first is named "Shaking" (Kampa), and the second is named "Moving Shaking" (Prakampa).
Two types reside within the teeth:
the first is named "Corrupt," and the second is named "Violent.
Three types reside at the roots of the teeth, which are named as follows:
Panting, pausing, and grasping and tearing.
One type resides on the tongue and is called "sweetness";
one type resides at the root of the tongue and is called "softness."
One type is located in the upper gums and is called "coming and going.
One type is in the throat and is called "gurgling the throat.
Two types are in the pupils:
The first is called "arising," and the second is called "unripened.
Two types reside on the shoulders:
the first is called "hanging down," and the second is called "hanging down again."
One type is on the arms, called "standing firm" (sthāpana);
one type is on the hands, called "revolving" (parivartana);
and two types are on the chest:
The first is named "Forehead Pit" (Āṭi), and the second is named "Extensive and Universal" (Viśāla).
One type resides in the heart and is called "Variegated" (Pāṇḍu);
another type resides in the breasts and is called "Manifesting Milk" (Kṣīradarśin).
One is located at the navel, named Parivāra.
Two are located at the flanks:
the first is named Candra, and the second is named Candrānana.
Two are located on the spine:
the first is named Moon-Walker (Candravāhin), and the second is named Moon-Form (Candrarūpa).
One is located between the back and the chest, named Abundance-Settled (Sthirapauṣṭika).
One type is within the skin, called "Tiger’s Claw.
Two types are within the flesh:
the first is named "Skin-Destroyer," and the second is named "Tree-Burner."
Four types reside in the bones, named:
extreme poison, habitual poison, fine-bone poison, and miscellaneous poison.
Five types reside in the marrow, named as follows:
The "slaughtered," the "unslaughtered," the "destroyed," the "separated from flesh," and the "white bones.
Two types reside in the intestines:
the first is named *śālābha*, and the second is named *śālābhaka*.
Two types reside in the small intestine:
the first is named Sūnu, and the second is named Punarvasu.
One type resides in the liver, named Papphāsa.
One type resides in the raw receptacle (āmāśaya) and is called *paittika*.
One type resides in the cooked receptacle (pakvāśaya) and is called *tāksika*.
One type resides in the anal passage (guda) and is called *gauravika*.
Three kinds are found within the excrement, namely:
sinew-eyes, knot-eyes, and matted-hair.
Two kinds are found in the anus:
The first is called the flowing stream; the second is called the heavy stream.
When the five types [of elements] reside within the womb, they are named:
lineage, evil clan, lying in sleep, non-awakening, and protecting the fluids.
One type is on the thigh, called *Ghāta-daṇḍa*;
one type is on the knee, called *Prakāśavraṇa*;
and one type is on the ankle, called *Sūcī-nāsika*.
One type dwells on the toes and is called *Jiāorán* (Scorching);
another type dwells in the soles of the feet and is called *Shípí* (Eating the Skin).
These constitute the eighty types of worms that reside within the human body, consuming its flesh day and night.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"From the hair on the head down to the feet, Throughout [the body] dwell worms that consume one's food;
To contemplate it as a source of defilement Is like the metaphor of turbid water."
To turn upon oneself what one has produced is like a knife or an enemy that harms and injures;
it constantly comes to bite and wound one's own body, just as flowing water erodes both its banks.

Within the bodies of those people, diseases arise due to wind; there are one hundred and one such types. Cold, heat, and their combination each have one hundred and one varieties; when these are all totaled together, there are four hundred and four diseases within the human body.
Just as fire produced from wood returns to burn that very wood, so too is illness:
arising originally from the physical body, it in turn endangers the person.
Furthermore, the eighty kinds of worms within the body agitate it, causing the person unrest; how much more so, then, are the afflictions of external sufferings!

When one calculates the body in this way, it is constantly accompanied by sorrow and affliction; yet ordinary people consider themselves secure, neither hearing nor understanding [this truth]. Why is this?
Because they do not see the Truths.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Head hair, body hair, nails, and teeth; Heart, flesh, skin, and bones joined together;
Produced by semen, blood, cold, and heat; Marrow, brain, fat, raw, and cooked."
All manner of cold mucus, spittle, and tears, along with constant leakage of excrement and urine—these are impermanent and impure, yet the foolish deem them precious.
Consider the human body: it is covered by a thin skin, like a date or a pear; the skin is exceedingly thin and scant!
It is covered over so that people do not know [its true nature]; even if one were to strip away the skin like a piece of dull, lifeless flesh, how could it still be called a human body?

Its bones and joints support one another like a linked iron chain; if one sees it clearly in this way, it is not even worth treading upon, let alone approaching it or looking at it with one's own eyes!
Thereupon, he praised him with these verses:
"Consider the body as fundamentally defiled, Like a putrid and rotting corpse, Or like various dust and grime;
The same applies to its relationship with the worms within."
Just as a painted likeness must eventually return to decay, so too, by seeing clearly that [the self] is fundamentally non-existent, how could one draw near to it?
Calculating the misfortunes and blessings people create in this world, they do not exhaust their full lifespan; there are also those who die prematurely or suffer injury before their time.

It is like a potter making various earthenware vessels: some break at the very beginning; some break while being shaped with the knife; some break on the kiln bricks; some break when being lowered; some break upon hitting the ground; some break while being struck; some break when the clay has dried; some break within the kiln; some break after firing; and some break while being moved. Even if they are not used, after a long time they will inevitably break!

Human beings are also like this: there are those who have first conceived the intention [to live] but have not yet reached death; there are those with two organs in the womb, like raw curd, or like ripe curd, or like a mass of flesh, or like a piece of flesh; there are those who possess the six sense faculties, or those who lack them and yet die;
there are those who are about to be born, or have just fallen to the ground;
and there are those who die at one day, one hundred days, one year, or ten years of age while engaged in their studies.
Whether twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty years; from death at one year up to reaching a hundred years—though one may have a long life, it must inevitably come to an end!
