Thus, these five aggregates are reckoned as fundamentally empty; they depend upon one another in succession, arising for a moment and ceasing for a moment, such that every lifting and lowering of the foot is impermanent.

Foolish people do not hear or know [the truth], yet they contrarily calculate that there is a self; from youth until old age, they regard everything as "mine" and call it a single entity, failing to understand the transformation of impermanence!
The practitioner of the Path contemplates and calculates this: from this, that is brought about; without this, there is no that.
What is meant by "from this, that is brought about"?
It is because of the calamities and blessings produced by one's fundamental conduct that death occurs and one comes to abide in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

When the spirit enters the womb, the form is like thin curd, a fleshy mass, or a piece of meat; gradually it becomes firm flesh and the six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise. Once the six sense organs are complete, one is born. From the body of childhood through middle age, one reaches old age and sickness, and must eventually return to death. Thus the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) revolve upon the wheel of birth and death, constantly flowing like a river without rest. All things are empty, like illusions and transformations; such is this perversion that leads from old age, sickness, and death.

It is like a great city where a fire breaks out at the western gate; spreading from there, it burns all the way to the eastern gate until everything is reduced to ashes. One should consider that the fire at the eastern gate is not the original fire!
Yet that burning does not depart from its original fire!
Human beings are also like this: following their original causes and conditions according to their misfortunes or blessings, one should contemplate it thus—that existence arises from existence!
What is meant by "if this is non-existent, then that is non-existent"?

If there is no misfortune or fortune, nor any other afflictions (*kleśa*), then one does not return to death; since one does not return to death, one does not abide in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); and if there is no intermediate state, from what could birth arise?
Since birth no longer exists, how could old age, sickness, and death possibly arise?
Calculating the beginning and end of this flow of birth and death in this manner, those who practice the Path should contemplate the origin and dissolution of the five aggregates.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Clearly understanding the meaning of all wisdoms, The mind is pure like the full moon;
Maintaining a resolute and single-minded will, He takes pity on the beings of the three realms.
Like a lotus in water, sweet, pure, and exquisite—
what is proclaimed from his mouth is joyfully understood by those who hear it.
He analyzes and expounds upon the original occurrences [of phenomena], leading one to realize their ultimate cessation.
The Sage has reached ultimate perfection, out of compassion for all sentient beings.
Drawing from the Buddha’s scriptures and extracting their essence,
I have composed this *Sūtra on Practice* based upon the Buddha’s own teachings.
The Scripture on the Stages of Cultivating the Path, Scroll One.
The Scripture on the Stages of Cultivating the Path, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Six: Loving-kindness (2) A merchant traveling through a vast wilderness,
Hungry and thirsty on a perilous path,
Was rescued and protected by a guide, Who led him to a place of fruit and water.
By means of the Way of the Unconditioned, you extinguish all defilements and poisons;
having accumulated peace, you have attained an impartial mind—I bow my head to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Like a ship upon the great ocean heading toward the mouth of a makara fish,
When his ship entered the belly of a fish, he invoked compassion to rescue it.
In the brief moment before it was about to sink, he delivered countless hundreds of thousands of people and precious treasures;
he understood the suffering and joy from beginning to end.
Surpassing all former sages, his virtue is like Mount Tai;
the light of his wisdom exceeds the radiance of the sun. I pay homage to this Wisdom with my head bowed low.
Those who practice the Way should abandon anger and always uphold a heart of loving-kindness.

There may be practitioners who merely utter vows with their mouths, wishing for sentient beings to be at peace, yet do not understand by what causes and conditions they might rescue and deliver them to that state of peace.
Although such words are gentle and soothing, they do not arise from a mind of loving-kindness or from the meditative concentration of equanimity.

Those who practice the Way should not merely practice verbal kindness. Or perhaps a practitioner may give rise to the thought of mental kindness, wishing to bring peace to all classes of sentient beings; while possessing such a compassionate heart is indeed commendable, it is not yet the compassion that is fully endowed with the Way and its Virtue.
If you wish to practice the Great Way, do not give rise to this kind of benevolence.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Even if a seeker of the Way In heart, speech, and thought speaks of benevolence,"
Then one will have little peace and security, and will likewise obtain meager merit and protection.
It is like a craftsman fashioning an arrow who, having dropped it, lets it fall into fire;
how could he ever make that arrow successful and fit for use?
In practicing the stages of the path and establishing great, expansive compassion, how should one act?
Suppose a practitioner is in the heat and seeks a cool place before finding peace;
or is in a place of icy cold and seeks warmth before finding peace.
It is like a hungry person obtaining food, or a thirsty person obtaining a drink;
it is like one who has traveled a long road, utterly exhausted and weary, obtaining a carriage and thereafter finding peace and security;
it is like seeing someone standing and then obtaining a seat to sit upon.
It is like one who is utterly exhausted finding restful sleep;
like a person of naked form obtaining clothing for protection;
like one whose body is defiled bathing and washing themselves—the heart is filled with great joy as it becomes hidden in meditative concentration and tranquil.

Various kinds of suffering each find their relief; as his body and mind leap with joy and attain all forms of peace, he maintains an undistracted mind toward those he loves and respects. He brings peace and security to his parents, siblings, wife, children, kinsmen, friends, and acquaintances through the bonds of affection and kinship.

Furthermore, for all sentient beings who suffer various afflictions, he causes them to attain peace and security just as his own body has done; he seeks to deliver all people throughout the ten directions so that both body and mind may find peace, desiring to bring peace and security to his two parents and to all within his clan and lineage.
Next, one should direct thoughts of loving-kindness toward ordinary people, extending it universally to enemies without any distinction, so that all may attain liberation and peace just as I do.

If, while contemplating the people of the ten directions in the first thought-moment, one’s mind becomes distracted during the middle thought-moment regarding an enemy—such that the initial resolve cannot suddenly equalize the attitude toward the enemy, the friend, and those in between—one should perform this contemplation:

"The resentment and hatred I harbored for my enemy have already passed and are now abandoned. I shall regard him with even greater love than for my parents, my own body, my wife and children, or my kinsmen; I shall honor him in this way and no longer harbor any grudge."

Examine the source of one's existence within the cycle of birth and death across the five realms: one has perhaps been one's parents, spouse, children, wife, brothers, or friends; yet because these relationships extend so far back into the past that they can no longer be recognized or remembered, for this reason one should not harbor resentment.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"One should practice the arousal of a compassionate mind, Regard enemies as virtuous friends;
As we transmigrate through birth and death, All have once been our own kin."
Just as a tree produces flowers, which then transform into fruit without distinction,
so it is with parents, wives, children, friends, and kinsmen.
A practitioner of the Path reflects within his own mind:
"If one harbors anger toward others, it is an injury to oneself!
It is like wood producing fire that then burns its own body;
or like a plantain tree, which withers as soon as it bears fruit; or like a mule conceiving a foal, which brings about its own ruin."
I am also like this; if I harbor anger, I harm myself in just this way.
Should anyone give rise to anger toward others, they may, because of this transgression, fall among venomous snakes or enter the evil realms.
Contemplating thus, one should not harbor malice; if one feels hatred toward others, one should instead give rise to loving-kindness and compassion.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"If there be one who, out of anger, Directs hostility and harm toward another,"
In future lives one may fall among snakes and vipers, or become a predatory beast.
Just as splitting bamboo or trees, or as a she-mule conceiving a fetus, brings about its own destruction, so too is this [retribution];
therefore, one should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness.

Those who cultivate the Way should practice impartial compassion; toward parents, wives, children, brothers, friends, and even enemies—whether distant or near—they should be equal, without hatred or affection. Furthermore, throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions, they should universally direct their compassion toward all beings, never increasing it for some nor decreasing it for others.
One who acts in such a manner is fit to practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Thus, it is said in verse:
"One who practices a mind of loving-kindness Is even-minded, free from both hatred and attachment."
Without discriminating between near and far, one should practice great kindness;
with an impartial mind, one should exercise great compassion even toward those within the triple world.
One who practices such benevolence surpasses the merit of Brahmā.

Those who cultivate this path achieve a perfected mind of loving-kindness; they cannot be burned by fire, harmed by blades, affected by poison, nor can any malevolent forces find an opportunity against them.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The blade of a sword cannot harm him, Neither the government official nor the great enemy;
Nor can malevolent spirits, rākṣasas, Serpents, vipers, thunder, or lightning."
Lions, elephants, tigers, and all other predatory beasts do not dare to approach;
none are able to cause them harm. One who cultivates the Way and practices the conduct of loving-kindness should be thus.
One sleeps peacefully at night and awakens with joy; protected by devas and humans, one never has bad dreams. One’s countenance is harmonious and pleasant, and one lacks neither clothing nor food.

Born in the abode of the Brahma Heaven, one is always upright and handsome, with eyes clearly distinguished between white and black. The body is supple and rarely afflicted by illness, and one attains long life, being revered by the various devas.

Wherever one goes, one attains the Way and is praised by the Buddhas; one eliminates worldly toil and reaches the stage of non-retrogression. Having attained peace and security, one proceeds to the realm of Nirvana without remainder and achieves tranquil liberation—all this is due to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Those who practice loving-kindness Are handsome and have abundant food and clothing;
All people revere and look up to them, Living long and as radiant as the sun."
In lying down, waking, walking, and staying, one is at ease; deities and gods all provide protection;
one is revered by the Brahmā heavens and praised by the World-Honored One.
Therefore, in cultivating the Path, one should practice a mind of loving-kindness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"To practice a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, And to eliminate all anger and malice—this is called 'loving-kindness.
Now that I have manifested the roots of all virtues, I shall observe the Buddha’s sutras and transcribe their teachings."
All that is to be awakened to, he discerns and fully understands;
beholding all the Buddhas of the past, his clear penetration is such as this.
Because of his perfectly equal awakening, he is therefore called a Buddha.
The wise, as well as devas and nāgas, all take refuge in and revere him.
He teaches and transforms all realms, removing all defilements;
he transforms those who are evil and dwelling in darkness, causing their minds to attain illumination.
Having attained peace and liberation from all suffering, And having cast away all terrors, I prostrate before that Buddha And take refuge in the Most Victorious One.
The Buddha subdues the untamed; His lion’s roar resounds like a thunderclap.
Upholding his resolve, his fame is heard everywhere; all who emerge from it shall forever receive deliverance.
Though they were foolish and self-indulgent, running about like a torrential rain, he named the elephant Dhanapāla to subdue their arrogance.
As for the various dragon kings and spirits, who harbor venom and emit fire from their eyes, the Buddha transforms them through goodness and delivers them; their bodies remain eternally tranquil.
Being liberated and unimpeded, I now prostrate myself before him.
I take refuge at the feet of the World-Honored One, the supremely tranquil one.
Beholding Māra harboring the poison of wrath, he manifested transformations everywhere as fire;
he bore mountains and carried weapons, holding swords, spears, and halberds.
Serpents and vipers uprooted great trees, intending to bring peril to the World-Honored One;
all manner of spirits arrived in great numbers, yet he felt neither fear nor alarm.
Their bristles were like awls and knives as they surrounded him on every side.
Though the numbers are exceedingly vast, he feels no fear;
nor has he ever been startled or doubtful, for he is free from all delusion.
Having cast off all terrors and hardships, I pray that I may take refuge in the Most Victorious One.

If a practitioner of the Way, while dwelling in seclusion or in a secluded place, should happen to feel fear such that their hair stands on end, they should contemplate the excellence of the Tathāgata’s merits, his physical form and countenance, and the Saṅgha of the Dharma; they should reflect upon the precepts and the analytical understanding of emptiness, recognize the six elements and the twelve links of dependent origination, and practice loving-kindness and compassion.
Even if one is terrified, if one brings this matter to mind, there will be nothing further to fear.
Thus, it is said in verse:
"Or perhaps out of terror one falls to the ground, unable to stand upright by oneself in accordance with the Dharma."
The teachings command firm abiding in the dharma of precepts, Like a mountain that the wind cannot move.
Just as a bee gathers the nectar of flowers, So too have I excerpted from various sutras;
Though the text is very brief, what is established herein is vast, And I preach this in order to eliminate fear.
Having originally lost a precious jewel, it fell into the great ocean;
immediately grasping a vessel, he exhausted the sea in search of the jewel.
With diligence free from sloth, he held fast his resolve without wavering.
The Sea God, seeing this, immediately brought forth the pearl and returned it to him.
Just as he employed this skillful means, the Heavenly King Resting-Mind (Śailendra) transcended to the Great Jewel Mountain, never growing weary or indolent.
Able to exhaustively realize primordial non-existence, I bow my head to the one who is free from attachment;
To the one whose vows do not waver, I take refuge and pay homage to the Most Victorious One.
Like a dragon king coiled and knotted, He sits upright in the same manner.
Seeking the Way through diligence, he rose with great power to attain Buddhahood;
Walking alone for seven days, he was able to endure and transform women.
I bow my head to that Most Honored One, whose vision of faith never wavers.
The practitioner of the Path reflects within his mind:

"I have been in the cycle of birth and death for an incalculable time, and my cultivation of lust, anger, and delusion has continued for a very long period. Since human life is both short and one is often indolent, how could one possibly eliminate all faults within a single lifetime?"
If such a thought arises, one should form this contemplation:
"It is like an old house where no one has lived for many years and no lamp has been lit in the darkness; yet, when one enters holding a torch, the darkness immediately vanishes."
Although one has long been accustomed to the various poisons of defilement, these flaws are extinguished by means of wisdom.
Why is this? Because the power of wisdom is strong, whereas ignorance is weak.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Those who seek the meaning of the Path must not be indolent; By attaining the benefit of the Dharma, they remain free from decline.
Receiving the wisdom of the Buddha’s radiant light, They eliminate lust, anger, and delusion, so that all are forever extinguished."
Who is able to follow this compliant Way in such a manner?
Only those who possess faith, diligence, and wisdom, who are without flattery and resolute in their intent, can thus practice in accordance with it.
What is meant by faith?

It is to see and know that all things return to impermanence, that whatever body one receives is entirely subject to sorrow and suffering, that the three realms are entirely empty, and that all dharmas are reckoned to be without self. To understand in this way is called faith.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Those who practice the Way and cultivate the path, Realize that the world is not secure;
All things are impermanent, And whatever body is received is entirely suffering.
The three realms are entirely empty; all phenomena are without self.
To be able to accept and practice this wherever one is—for this reason, one is said to possess faith.
If one harbors the notion of a self, then one is a person of inverted views.
One who can fully comprehend that all things are empty, Should know that such a person is a Buddha.
Having attained the path of ambrosia, Those who awaken to this truth Cannot be shaken; This is what is called faith.
Regarding the practitioner on the path, what is called diligence?
If a practitioner is single-mindedly devoted to emptiness and non-existence, and their mind does not abandon or depart from it, this is called diligence.
Even if a wild fire were to burn and gradually approach their seat, and further burn their robes, reaching up to their head and face, they should maintain this thought in their mind:
"Even if fire burns my head, and even if it scorches and consumes my bones, flesh, skin, and muscles until my body dies, I shall never abandon this practice. Why is this?

Although burning my body is not worth mentioning, the fires of lust, anger, and ignorance within my inner being have burned my body throughout countless lifetimes as I transmigrated through birth and death within the three evil realms; yet I have not attained the ultimate state of the Way and its Virtue."

Though burning one’s own body is insufficient as a means of salvation, one should instead strive to extinguish the fires of lust, anger, and delusion; once nirvāṇa is attained, there is no further regression. Having become bodiless, one is then free from the afflictions of all internal and external fires.
"These [afflictions of] lust, anger, and delusion cannot be extinguished lightly; it is like attempting to melt copper or iron with chaff—it can never be done!
Only by holding the mind firmly and employing every skillful means can the diseases of lust, anger, and delusion be completely eradicated."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"For those who are single-mindedly devoted to the Way and its Virtue, At such a time, they do not spare their bodies;
It is like an elephant washing its body— Having bathed until it is clean, it then lies down in the dust."
Even if a sudden calamity should befall them, they would not be startled by thunder or lightning;
just as one does not begrudge a withered flower, they should likewise cast away worldly toil and affliction.
For one who practices the Path, what is meant by wisdom?

It is to clearly understand the time for tranquil concentration, to know the time for contemplation, to know the time for investigative discernment, to know the time for receiving the Dharma, to fully comprehend the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and right attainment (*samyaksamāpatti*), and also to know the time of emerging from concentration, whether slowly or quickly;
it is to distinguish between the good and evil within one's own mind, just as a skilled physician knows the ailment within the abdomen.

One should restrain the mind and not allow it to become unrestrained; just as when a powerful elephant is about to fall into a ditch or well, its keeper restrains and suppresses it so that it does not fall, so too should the practitioner of the Path restrain and sever external attachments.

To know the causes and conditions of the mind and that which all conceptions rely upon is like a wise person knowing what food is suitable for them, or like a cook who knows the master’s preferences regarding what he likes or dislikes!
One who understands skillful means attains all liberations; their progress and retreat are like a goldsmith distinguishing the quality of gold.

If a practitioner of the Way lacks clear wisdom, they will not understand the direction of the Path and will harbor fear, taking what is right for wrong and what is wrong for right, thereby failing to achieve wisdom.

Such a practitioner, even if they attain the first dhyāna or proceed to the second dhyāna, will become fearful and think they have lost the dhyāna, not realizing that they have merely entered a deeper state of tranquility.
He thought to himself:
"Alas! How deluded I am!"
"One originally possessed skillful application, yet through negligence it is lost and the mind wanders away!

Being in a state of joy and delight, one departs from meditative concentration; thus, the mind becomes self-limiting and cannot progress. Entertaining such doubts constitutes the loss of dhyāna: mistaking success for failure, and failure for success."
How does one thoroughly understand the meaning of meditative concentration?
With focused mind and resolute intent, one enters the first dhyāna with the mind abiding in the cessation-concentration; having performed this practice, one then enters the second dhyāna.

The reason they are deluded is that they have long practiced worldly matters and do not yet know the true reality (*bhūtārtha*) or the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); because they do not comprehend the truth, their will remains fixed upon that which is subject to outflows!
If one seeks the second dhyāna but cannot restrain the mind, then one does not possess that dhyāna; therefore, the practitioner should know this to be an error!
If the practitioner is clear-sighted and does not fall into such delusion, they will not lose the dhyāna—this is called wisdom.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"If one thoroughly understands all phenomena of the body, Then one knows where the mind tends toward;
By skillful means, one restrains the mind's inclinations, Just as with an iron hook used to tame a white elephant."
Those who clearly understand the concentrated mind, And likewise discern tranquil contemplation,
Always possessing wisdom without hesitation, Abide in the Way and its Virtue according to the Dharma teaching.
How is it that one who practices the Path is not crooked?
It means being without flattery or deceit, possessing a sincere and straightforward mind, applying oneself with diligence to the practice of the Path, and being steadfast in faith and integrity.

Even if one is engaged in practice, one does not treat it as mere practice; rather, regarding all the afflictions and improper matters, one fully discloses one's own flaws and defects to the Dharma Master.
For example, when a patient suffers from illness and pain, they should tell the physician everything with complete sincerity.
Likewise, the Dharma Master observes the practitioner’s disposition and preaches the Dharma for them according to their deficiencies and needs.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The practitioner harbors sincerity and straightforwardness; His mind is free from flattery and deceit.
Receiving the teachings of the Dharma Master, He severs all the defilements of worldly toil."
Abiding in peace and perfect purity, one should apply oneself with diligence to the cultivation of the Path.
One should revere the sutras as the Buddha’s teaching and follow the Dharma as if engaged in battle.
Even if a practitioner’s passions run high, one should preach to them the law of the impurity of the human body.
There are three grades of instruction:
first, visualizing the body and bones as a chain, with the members linked together;
second, immediately upon receiving the Dharma teaching, one contemplates the skull bone.
Third, having completed this contemplation, one further examines the forehead, fixing the mind upon the head.
If anger is intense and rampant, one should preach the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

There are four grades of loving-kindness: first, toward parents and kinsmen; second, toward neutral persons who are neither close nor distant relatives; third, toward the common masses of ordinary people; and fourth, extending this practice equally to bestow loving-kindness upon all.
If one protects even an enemy with a mind endowed with benevolence, then the nine afflictions and perverse anger will be eliminated.
To analyze this meaning: although there may be those who are close and dear, one should distance oneself from them [if they harbor such faults].
What are the nine grounds for resentment that lead one to give way to anger?
The first is when one thinks to oneself:
"This person has previously wronged me."
The second said:
"This man might perhaps encroach upon me later.
The third said:
"Now you have deceived me once again.
Fourth, he said:
"In the past, you wronged my close friends."
Fifth: "Lest they should later again encroach upon my relatives and friends. Sixth:
"Now, in the present, he has again deceived my kinsmen and friends.
The seventh said:
"In the past, that man revered my enemies."
8. "In the future, perhaps you will again show respect. 9. Said:
"Even though one currently holds such feelings of respect toward them, they must all be relinquished.
How can one prevent others from encroaching upon one's own person?"
I shall simply maintain my own integrity and refrain from encroaching upon others!
This is the retribution for my past misdeeds and unwholesome karma that has brought about these evil fruits!
My kinsmen and friends were originally guilty as well; it is because of this that such calamity has occurred!
Furthermore, my enemy has long been on intimate and close terms with that person; moreover, he possesses merit and virtue which cause others to revere him!
These three grades of affliction and nine types of resentment are not worth harboring as grudges.
What is called "sudden anger"?
It is when one has never met someone before, yet upon seeing them, one immediately becomes angry.
At that moment, one should reflect as follows:
"This person has never wronged my body, nor does he have any fault now, nor has he committed any transgression; for what reason, then, do you harbor ill will and look upon another with malice?
To give rise to an evil mind and unjustly inflict harm upon others is to return and receive punishment for oneself, just like raising dust against the wind only to soil one's own body."

If those who practice the path are unable to extinguish anger so that it does not arise, such people do not enter the factors of enlightenment; they are like a cracked vessel filled with water, which cannot carry it far.
One who can subdue anger is like water extinguishing fire; thus, there is no harm done. This is what one should practice to enter the discipline of the Path.

For this reason, even when encountering suffering and affliction, such as having one's body cut by knives and saws, one must not give rise to anger. Just as a withered tree being burned leaves no resentment, how much less should one harbor anger toward that which is spiritual!
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Contemplate your own body with equanimity; Ordinary people and enemies are no different.
Cast aside the nine afflictions, And resolve never to harbor groundless anger."
Controlling the mind so as not to harbor resentment, like a withered tree free from anger,
the practitioner of the stages of the Path is thus without blemish.
If a practitioner of the Path possesses much ignorance, they should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination to discern and understand them thoroughly.
From the causal conditions of birth, there is old age and death; if one does not come to be born, then there is no beginning or end.
Thus, it is said in verse:
Without delusion, there is no birth; Having eliminated the affliction of old age and death.
Beholding that the fundamental is without beginning, from what could decay and exhaustion arise?
It originates from the arousal of the six sense-faculties; through much turmoil, delusion is produced.
From delusion comes the web of fetters, which further develops into ignorant obscurity.

When a practitioner of the path entertains many discursive thoughts, they should then explain the counting of inhalations and exhalations. Once the breath is stabilized and the mind is tranquil and free from seeking, it is said in verse:
"Counting the breath seeks cessation and its following; By contemplating the true truths, the mind comes to rest."
Those whose nature is pure revere it in this way; sitting alone with many thoughts, they do not accomplish the practice.
To those practitioners who harbor much arrogance, he explains this meaning:

"There are three kinds of pride in a person: first, saying 'I am inferior to such-and-such a person'; second, saying 'such-and-such a person is equal to me'; and third, saying 'I am superior to such-and-such a person.'"
One who harbors such thoughts is conceited and should form this reflection: "In the burial mounds outside the city, there lie discarded skeletons;

heads and bodies are scattered in different places, devoid of veins and blood, with skin and flesh decayed and rotted away. One should go and observe that whether one is poor or wealthy, noble or lowly, male or female, large or small, handsome or ugly, these withered bones are all exactly the same—what difference is there between them?"

At the time of its final end, from beginning to conclusion, it is a mass of flesh clothed in skin, moistened with blood, and bound by sinews; yet it is adorned with garments, incense, flowers, and necklaces. Like a magical illusion produced by the convergence of skillful winds, it moves about through the activity of mind, intellect, and consciousness, traveling to cities, capitals, and villages, coming and going, advancing and halting.
Having made this contemplation, one is free from pride.
Originally there is no contemplator who perceives either the cemetery or all people as being equal and without distinction.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Whether one is noble, wealthy, or of high status, riding out from the city on a carriage,
or being cast away among the graves— when weighed, they are equal and no different.
If one dwells in seclusion beneath a tree and contemplates in this way, [one will realize this truth].
Practicing the Way with a resolute mind cannot be burned by the fire of arrogance.
When the Dharma Master preaches the sutras, he observes the dispositions of people, finding nineteen types in all.
By what means does he know this?
One comes to know them only by discerning the afflictions.
What are these nineteen?

First is greed and lust; second is anger and hatred; third is ignorance and delusion; fourth is lust and anger; fifth is lust and delusion; sixth is delusion and anger; seventh is lust, anger, and delusion; eighth is purity of speech but lust in the mind; ninth is gentleness of words but hardness of heart; tenth is wisdom of speech but delusion in the mind; eleventh is beauty of words while harboring the three poisons; twelfth is coarseness of words but harmony of heart; thirteenth is harsh speech and hardness of heart; fourteenth is coarse speech and delusion of heart; fifteenth is coarseness of speech while harboring the three poisons; sixteenth is delusion of speech and lust in the heart; seventeenth is delusion of speech and harboring anger; eighteenth is both heart and speech being deluded; nineteenth is delusion of speech while the heart harbors the three poisons.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Lust, anger, and delusion—these combined constitute the three poisons;
when these two by two are further intermingled, they are reckoned as four."
There are four types of verbal suppleness, and four types of verbal folly;
these were taught by the World-Honored One as nineteen kinds of human character.
How does one know when a person possesses the signs of greed and lust?
Adorned with literary embellishments yet self-deluded, playful and impetuous by nature, his resolve is restless and his character like that of a monkey;
he is prone to forgetfulness and error, his wit and guile are shallow and lacking in foresight. His actions disregard what lies before or behind him;
he initiates unnecessary affairs and causes alarm, speaking much and prone to weeping, easily deceived and easily subdued, [yet] finding peace.
He is easily led and cannot endure diligent effort; he rejoices greatly upon obtaining small gains for great use, yet becomes deeply distressed over losing minor things.
Upon hearing others praise him, he rejoices and believes it; he reveals all secret matters as if they were public.
His body is warm and excessively filthy, his skin is thin, and his person is foul-smelling; his hair and beard are sparse, with much white and many wrinkles.
He does not favor long beards or white teeth when setting out on a journey; he delights in clean and pure clothing and is fond of wearing ornamental decorations to adorn his body.
He takes pleasure in light garments, is highly learned in various arts and crafts with nothing he does not master, and frequently travels to observe and tour.
He always wears a joyful smile upon his face, adorns himself elegantly, upholds the precepts with a gentle nature, respects his elders, and is skillful at greeting others first when meeting them.
He was clever, elegant, and refined; by nature he was not perverse or stubborn, but possessed a sense of shame and much compassion.
He could discern between the beautiful and the ugly, and was skilled in taking and giving or trading. He was gentle, full of pity, and bestowed many favors;

toward his kinsmen and friends, he practiced total relinquishment and generosity, never contending with others over the amount of what he possessed. His gifts were vast and extensive, and he attended carefully to the physical forms and actions of all beings.

He is slow and sluggish, yet he understands worldly affairs and is capable of decisive judgment; when he sees a good person, he respects and honors them, but his perception of matters becomes swift and contrary.
He is skilled in speech, clever, and mild in conversation; though he has many friends, he cannot maintain long-lasting intimacy with them.
He harbors little anger and shows reverence for his elders, yet he is restless and uneasy in lying down, rising, walking, or moving about.
In detail, although they study the Dharma, their love for desires and material wealth makes them abandon their relatives and friends without firmness;
their friendships do not endure long, and upon hearing of matters concerning sensual pleasure, they immediately become greedily attached to them.
Yet, when these things are described as foul and impure, they soon grow weary of them, advancing and retreating with ease.
For this reason, it is the mark of lustful craving.
Thus, a verse says:
Violent and impulsive like a monkey, Constantly laughing with joy and also weeping with delight.
Great joy at gain and profound sorrow at loss; prone to much speech and easily subdued;
the will is deluded, restless, and filled with alarm; self-satisfied, easily deceitful, and trusting the words of others;
the disposition is forgetful and lacks foresight; yet fond of examining the precepts and possessing wisdom.
Gazing greedily at forms while intending to practice generosity, looking about with artifice while honoring friends,
having a relaxed and warm body yet being full of defilements— yet possessing joy, faith, shame, gentleness, and courage; regarding the Dharma,
wealth, beauty, and kin, one must not become suddenly estranged, lest one immediately regret it.
One who practices the trainings as they are taught can indeed attain them; yet though one may quickly understand them, one may also swiftly forget them.
Adorned with flowers and fine garments, such a person performs actions that are unnecessary and merely honors the aged.
The wise honor those whose will is set upon training, for they are proficient, clear-sighted, and harmonious.
He always delights in going out of the city to travel and sightsee;

he is eloquent in speech and enjoys listening, possessing a sharp tongue and skillful rhetoric with which he can discern things; wherever he stays, whether lying down or sitting, he cannot endure remaining for long.
Gentle and sincere, yet neglecting future consequences for the sake of trivial matters;
lacking endurance for hardship despite high aspirations, and fond of bestowing gifts upon friends;
hating long beards while delighting in short ones, and though self-satisfied, being foul-smelling.
Clever and skillful, with many wrinkles and white hair, he upholds the precepts with unimpeded wisdom;
when seeing others, he first greets them with inquiry; his robes are thin and his face and teeth are pure;
possessing compassion, he is easy to serve; and in his conduct, he does not begrudge wealth.
One who knows others' conduct practices loving-kindness; they are easy to teach and not perverse.
The Buddha has said that such a nature corresponds to the characteristics of lustful desire.
How then should one contemplate the characteristics of anger?

He understands profound meanings and does not harbor sudden resentment; though his anger may be difficult to resolve, he lacks a lack of compassion. His speech is sincere, yet his words may be harsh and coarse. He harbors universal doubt and does not seek to believe. He delights in seeking the faults of others, being wakeful for much and sleeping little. He has many enemies and hatreds, yet he forms friendships that endure to the end. Though difficult to reconcile with, he does not forget what he has received. He is not startled by those who cause alarm, nor does he fear them. Possessing great strength, he is stubborn and cannot be brought to submission. Full of anxiety, he is difficult to instruct. His body is large and tall, with a thick neck, a large head, broad shoulders, a square forehead, and fine hair. He is courageous and strong-natured, difficult to subdue. That which he hears and receives is slow to enter and difficult to grasp; once he has received it, it is likewise difficult to forget. Regarding the loss of Dharma-wealth or the parting from desired friends, he never feels sorrow or regret; he is neither easy to advance nor easy to retreat.
By this one knows it to be the mark of anger.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"With a nature firm and rigid, yet deeply understanding the meaning, One universally suspects others, seeking out their faults."
He requires little sleep and is difficult to subdue; by nature dull-witted, he is hard to teach yet hard to forget.
He can endure toil and hardship and is impossible to approach; possessing no fear, he does not suddenly become angry.
His body and speech act in concert, making him difficult to admonish or enlighten; he is courageous, powerful, and stubborn.
In youth there is little fear, few friends, and much resentment; in youth there is little peace, yet one’s own body grows vast.
Whatever one does, one does not regret; one abandons the wealth of the Dharma and turns away without a second thought.
Once one has abandoned those dear to them, they do not think of them again; they never turn back, nor do they submit.
Exerting effort and diligence to cultivate great matters—the Buddha says that such people exhibit the mark of anger.
How does one discern the mark of delusion?
It is said that their nature is pliant and they delight in self-praise; lacking compassion, they destroy the bridge of the Dharma and are constantly...
With eyes closed and a haggard countenance, he lacks wisdom and takes no delight in dark places; he frequently sighs to himself, being indolent and lacking faith.
He harbors hatred for virtuous people and always prefers to travel alone; possessing little insight, he considers himself great, yet is hesitant and wavering.
Unable to discern good fortune from misfortune or distinguish between good and evil, he cannot manage his own affairs when faced with an emergency.
Furthermore, he does not accept admonition; he cannot distinguish between virtuous friends and enemies; his actions are perverse and cruel like those of tigers or wolves;
he wears tattered clothing and his body is covered in grime; by nature he finds no joy, his beard and hair are disheveled and unkempt;
he is full of anxiety, prone to excessive sleeping, and eats without moderation; when others hire him for labor, he is the one they employ.
They are unwilling to do what they ought to do, nor will they employ or commission others to do it, yet they do it themselves;
they fear what they should not fear, and conversely fear that which they should not fear; they rejoice where they should grieve, and grieve where they should rejoice;
they laugh when they should weep, and weep when they should laugh; even when there is urgent business, they refuse to go, and as soon as they have departed, they call out for someone else.
They are unwilling to turn back and reflect, constantly encountering hardship and toil while forcibly enduring worldly defilements; in eating and drinking, they cannot distinguish the five flavors;
their speech is full of laughter and joy, and they forget what has been said before; they bite their tongues and lick their lips, yet they grind their teeth;
in walking, lying down, rising, or sitting, they never find peace or stability; in all their movements and actions, they know no fear or difficulty.
They do not know when to advance or retreat.
The Buddha says that such people possess the marks of folly.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
With a weak countenance and foolishness, devoid of compassion, he has a protruding forehead and praises himself;
his eyes do not blink, and he sighs repeatedly in distress;
walking alone without faith, he envies the worthy and is indolent.
Constantly anxious and full of doubt, they cannot distinguish between good and evil;
their bodies and faces are covered in dust and grime, and they do not know the difference between wholesome and unwholesome speech;
their actions are often confused and chaotic, and they are unable to bring anything to completion.
Those one commissions refuse to act; instead of being commissioned, they act on their own.
One should fear what is fearful, yet does not fear it; one does not fear what is not fearful, yet fears it.
One should rejoice where there is cause for joy, yet instead feels sorrow; one feels sorrow where there is cause for joy, yet instead feels joy.
One should weep but instead laughs; one should laugh but instead weeps.
Greedy for food and drink without satiety, failing to distinguish between kin and enemy, one’s disposition is perverse and stubborn;
lacking wisdom, one encounters suffering and affliction.
His beard and hair are perpetually disheveled; lacking faith, he delights in dwelling in darkness.
Unable to distinguish the five flavors, he sleeps much like a tiger or wolf.
Narrow-minded yet arrogant, he bites his tongue and licks his lips.
Fond of playing with his lips and delighting in gnashing his gums; speaking much and laughing frequently;
restless in his place of rest; unable to proceed when urgent matters arise;
calling back yet rushing forward—such a nature is the mark of a fool.
What are the characteristics of lust, anger, and delusion?
They are precisely those lust, anger, and delusion previously described!
The characteristics of lust-and-delusion and anger-and-delusion are likewise thus.
That which is conjoined with all worldly afflictions is called the mark of lust, anger, and delusion.
Thus, it is said in verse:
Abiding amidst worldly afflictions, One is fully joined with lust and anger.
One should contemplate the characteristics of lust and anger; these constitute delusion and a lack of wisdom.
All that has been previously described—the various defilements of craving, as well as acts of lust, anger, and folly—should be known as not being separate from delusion.
What is meant by "desire of speech" and "desire of mind"?

It means that one’s speech is gentle, compliant, and non-oppositional; one does not inflict upon others what one would not desire for oneself; and whatever one speaks or thinks is invariably wholesome, peaceful, and agreeable.
It is like a fine tree whose flowers are fresh and colorful and whose fruits are likewise beautiful; so too are the desires of the mouth and the mind.
On this, a verse says:
His speech is always gentle, And his compliant words are pleasing to others.
When words and deeds correspond, and the mind and body do not harm others;
it is like a fine flowering tree whose fruit is likewise sweet.
The Honored Buddha explained this as the mark of lust in thought and speech.
What is meant by one whose mouth desires while the heart is angry?

Their speech is gentle, yet their heart harbors poison; it is like planting a bitter tree: though its flowers are bright and beautiful, the fruit it bears is extremely bitter. To speak gently while harboring poison is exactly like this.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"His speech is gentle and soft, yet his heart harbors malice;
He looks upon others with great joy, appearing as one who is approachable and friendly."
The mouth speaks with gentleness and compliance, yet the heart harbors poison within;
like the tree whose flowers are bright and fresh, its fruit is bitter as venom.
How is one to know that the mouth desires while the mind is deluded?
Their speech is gentle, yet their minds are dark and obscured; they cannot benefit others, nor do they refrain from deceiving or harming them.
They are like a painted vase: its exterior appears excellent, but its interior is empty and dark; such is the nature of those whose mouths desire [the truth] while their hearts are deluded.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The mouth speaks with gentleness, Yet the heart harbors darkness and folly;
Know that such a person Is lewd in speech and foolish in mind."
Observe that their mouths are as bright as wisdom, yet their hearts are as dark as lacquer;
outwardly they are as fine as painted vases, but within they are empty and dark.
What is meant by "desire in the mouth" and "anger and delusion in the heart"?

What is said is soft and gentle, yet they have little mindfulness of the good; their nature is not disciplined or compliant. Sometimes they think of evil, sometimes they do not think at all; they cannot distinguish between good and evil, and their nature is difficult to fathom.

For example, when sweet medicine is mixed with salt and bitter flavors, they cannot be distinguished; so it is with those who have desire in their speech while harboring anger and delusion in their minds.
Thus, it is said in verse:
Those whose speech expresses desire, Yet whose minds harbor various forms of anger and delusion—
It is like ghee or honey mixed with pungent, bitter, or salty flavors.
What is meant by one whose speech is coarse while the mind is lustful?
Their words are harsh and impetuous, causing injury to others; they are loathed by all and no one wishes to see them, and there is no one who respects them.
It is like parents reprimanding their children: though their words may be harsh and urgent, their hearts still harbor love.
It is like a physician treating a wound: although it causes great pain at the moment of lancing and cleansing, one feels profound joy once the illness has been cured after some time.
Those who have harsh speech yet lustful hearts are also like this.
Thus, it is said in verse:
Some appear to speak with urgency, Yet harbor lustful desires in their hearts.
Just as the heat of a summer day causes its light to shine upon cold water, what is meant by one who is harsh in speech and angry in heart?
Such a person utters coarse and vulgar words; in their thoughts, they harbor no kindness or compassion and do not desire the welfare of others.

It is like bitter medicine mixed with poison: if one drinks it and the patient vomits it up and refuses to take it, that is one thing; but if one drinks it and it is digested, it will harm the person's life. So too is the case for one whose speech is harsh and urgent and whose heart is full of anger.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Their speech is urgent and lacking in kinship or respect; Their minds harbor evil thoughts and cherish poison.
They always delight in encroaching upon and wronging others; One should observe that such people’s conduct is a mixture of poisons.
What is meant by one whose speech is coarse while the mind is deluded?
Their words are constantly harsh and urgent, inflicting evil upon others; in their movements and actions, they are not self-aware, taking no account of another's goodness nor their wickedness.
It is like a thief who draws his sword to threaten others but cannot actually harm them; likewise, such a practitioner knows that while his speech is harsh and urgent, his mind is deluded.
Thus, a verse says:
"Though his words are harsh and urgent, his mind does not harm; He feigns fear toward others but inflicts nothing upon them."
For example, it is like drawing a sword that yields nothing; so too are those whose speech is coarse and whose minds are deluded.
What is meant by "coarse speech and a mind harboring the three poisons"?

It refers to one whose words are harsh and impetuous, who may speak kindly to others yet subsequently inflicts evil upon them, or who momentarily conceives unwholesome thoughts yet does not actually commit evil.

It is like a high-ranking official who has captured a thief. A subordinate official fears being held accountable for the thief's statements; another official entices him forward and questions him; a further subordinate official subjects him to flogging and torture; yet another official neither questions his good or evil deeds nor subjects him to torture or reprimand. This is what is meant by one whose speech is coarse while harboring the three poisons within.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Those whose speech is harsh and impetuous, Whose minds harbor the three poisons,
And whose dispositions are thus— They do not practice the unwholesome, nor do they commit evil."
One whose conduct is such as this is called a person of middle rank;
for them, hardship and ease are both mixed together.
What is meant by one who is foolish in speech but desirous in heart?
Having no discerning knowledge, when people speak with him, he understands nothing at all; he does not comprehend the meaning of good and evil or where they lead.
He constantly thinks to himself:
"How can I further benefit others!"
Regarding the pursuit of objects, they do not lose their original intent, just as one might think of them;
it is like clouds rising and rain falling in the darkness of night—their mouths, deluded minds, and desires are likewise so.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Those whose speech is dull and whose minds are lustful, Whose spoken words are indistinct—
Like a dragon that raises clouds but does not thunder, So too are those whose speech is dull and whose minds are lustful.
What is meant by having a foolish mouth and a stubborn mind?
One is unable to bestow kindness nor inflict harm; instead, one constantly thinks to oneself:
"By what means can I injure others?"
If they find an opportunity, they immediately bring harm to others.
It is like covering charcoal fire with ashes; when a traveler steps upon it, his feet are burned. So too it is with those whose mouths are deluded and whose minds are angry.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Stupid in speech and rigid in mind, Neither gentle nor free from harsh words,
Constantly harboring ill will toward others, One never considers the good or benefit of others."
What is called "unclear" refers to harboring evil within the heart;
it is like charcoal fire covered by ashes, which will burn one's feet should one step upon it.
What is meant by being dull-witted in speech while the mind harbors darkness?
One cannot bestow goodness upon others, nor can one inflict evil; the mind does not even contemplate the good or evil of others, remaining without increase or decrease. Why is this so?
Because it lacks power.

It is like a fire that has been extinguished and covered with ashes; if one were to place dry grass or dried cow dung upon it and touch or tread upon it with hand or foot, it would be unable to burn anything and would not bring anything to maturity.
Why is this? Because they lack the capacity for it.
The same applies to those whose mouths are deluded and whose minds are obscured by darkness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"With mouths of folly and minds shrouded in darkness,
They are utterly unable to contemplate evil, Nor are they able to contemplate good."
Unable to accomplish tasks, yet not incapable of acting;
like boiling water in a violent storm, nothing can reach maturity.
What is meant by "stupidity of speech and a mind harboring the three poisons"?
His mouth commits no offense that would benefit others; he rarely causes injury, yet day and night he reflects:
"By what means might I injure others?
Furthermore, he thinks to himself:
"What is it to benefit others? One might think to oneself:
"To neither harm nor benefit others."

It is like an old jar containing both pure and impure substances; though its mouth is covered, one cannot see what is inside, yet when the mouth is opened, it becomes manifest. The deluded mind harboring the three poisons is just like this.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"By nature prone to perversity, His speech is indistinct and fails to remove [defilements];
Yet he harbors lust, anger, and delusion, Filled to the brim with foul impurities."
For example, it is like a large jar that receives both pure and impure substances;
it cannot benefit people, nor does it cause them any harm at all.
As a Dharma teacher, one should observe the dispositions of others through these nineteen matters and preach the Dharma accordingly.
How is the characteristic of lust explained?
To teach the Dharma, it is said:

"Those who indulge excessively in desire fall into the realms of hell and hungry ghosts; only after emerging from there do they become lustful birds—parrots, blue jays, pigeons, mandarin ducks, geese, ducks, peacocks, wild men, and monkeys."
Even if one returns to human status, one will be prone to lust, dissipation, frivolity, and sudden violence.
You, O Benevolent One, should examine this while still in human form; observe and recognize the defilement of sin, its foul and impure nature, and do not indulge in sexual desire.
Thus it is said in verse:
Those who habitually indulge in lustful desires are swiftly scorched by the fire of pride;
whether among humans, animals, hell-beings, or hungry ghosts, [they suffer].
Born therein, they bring harm upon themselves, scorched by the fires of affliction;
wishing to liberate them from this, he speaks thus according to their conduct.
To those who are full of hatred, he preaches the Dharma in accordance with their own tracks.

"Committing many acts of anger leads to falling into the realms of hell or hungry ghosts. Emerging from those evil places, one shall become a venomous beast, a malevolent spirit, a rākṣasa, a *pratiśīrṣaka*, a female ghost (*piśācī*), or a type of latrine-demon; furthermore, one becomes a lion, tiger, wolf, serpent, viper, poisonous insect, mosquito, gadfly, stinging bee, or a centipede.

Should one eventually emerge from this path and return to the human world, one’s appearance will be ugly and unattractive to others; one will always be short-lived and plagued by many illnesses, with an incomplete physical form."
For this reason, the consequences of transgressions are clearly manifest.
One should constantly uphold a mind of compassion and eliminate all anger and resentment.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Many harbor anger and resentment, and are collectively loathed by all;
because of this, they fall into evil realms, suffer many illnesses, and lack peace and stability.
They fall among ghosts and venomous beasts, and even when reborn as humans, they are lowly and base.
One who is able to practice a mind of loving-kindness immediately eliminates the darkness of hatred.
To those who are mired in much ignorance, he preaches this Dharma:

"When delusion flourishes, one falls into death and onto the path of the hells and hungry ghosts; if reborn among animals, one becomes a foolish beast—such as cattle, sheep, foxes, dogs, mules, donkeys, pigs, and the like."

If they return to the human realm, their nature will lack clarity; their faculty of sight will be weak from youth, they will frequently suffer from illness, their six sense organs will be incomplete, and they will be born among the barbarians or the uncivilized, passing from darkness into darkness.
Teaching them in this way to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, he removed the root of their ignorance and delusion.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Those who habitually practice folly Have their faculties incomplete.
Born among cattle and sheep, one subsequently falls into hell;
if a practitioner of the Way wishes to cross this evil path and desires to escape its darkness,
they should contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
If one has much lust and anger, one should practice two things:
contemplate impurity and cultivate a mind of loving-kindness.
If one has much lust and delusion, one should expound upon two things:
He teaches emptiness and compassion.
Should anger and delusion be rampant, he explains two matters for them:
he guides them with a compassionate mind and leads them to realize the root of delusion.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Practicing loving-kindness and contemplating impurity, One subdues lust, anger, and delusion;
Yet those fools who teach the nature of form Do not understand the twelve links of dependent origination."
If a person’s anger is rampant, or their delusion is so profound as to obscure the light,
one should preach for them the mind of loving-kindness and the root of the twelve links of dependent origination.
If there is one whose mouth commits sexual misconduct while the heart harbors desire, one should explain for them the meaning of impermanence, emptiness, and stillness.
When the mind is angry and the mouth is resentful, one should preach only of loving-kindness and benevolence;
when the mouth is deluded and the mind is dark, one should preach the twelve links of dependent origination.
As for the remaining four types of afflictions, they are fully present.

First, those whose speech is lewd yet whose minds harbor the three poisons; second, those whose speech is angry and who possess lust, malice, and delusion; third, those whose speech is foolish and who inwardly harbor the three impurities; fourth, those who are simple-minded yet harbor the three poisons.
The Dharma Master Jie shall preach the Dharma and provide instruction for these people, causing them to tranquilly contemplate the root of causes and conditions.

Why is this? Because the afflictions of these types of beings are deep-seated and thick; they have accumulated various karmic calamities that entangle them from within. Although they practice the present dharma, they do not perceive the Noble Truths. One should therefore teach them to recite and exhort them to diligence; by means of this, their focus will be solely on the task of recitation, their afflictions will gradually thin out, and although they may not attain the Way, they can ascend to heaven.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Should there be those who commit sexual misconduct, And whose minds are afflicted by anger and delusion,
One should teach them to recite the sutras And encourage them to perform meritorious deeds."
Though the afflictions may flourish, by this one removes the veil of sin;
through these skillful means, one subsequently attains birth in heaven.

It is like a person who tends a grove of trees: he levels the high ground and fills the hollows, irrigates at the proper times, and pulls out thorns, weeds, and reeds. Whatever grows crookedly or sprouts perversely is all trimmed away and discarded beyond the fence so that the garden becomes orderly and beautiful.
The trees are unimpeded, their roots grow lushly, and they all protect them so that they are not broken or injured.
For this reason, the trees grow ever larger and their flowers and fruits flourish in abundance.

Those practitioners, having received the instructions of the Dharma Master, eliminate lust, anger, ignorance, desires, perceptions, and all defilements; for this reason, their practice gradually matures until they attain the Way.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The trees were crooked and twisted, growing askew and contrary to nature;
the thorns and all manner of impurities have now fallen away, and everything has been made orderly and well-governed."
By means of various skillful methods, one cultivates and repairs until completion;
in practicing the tree of the Dharma, honoring the sutras is likewise so.
Having eliminated lust, anger, and delusion, one receives hundreds of thousands of instructions from the Teacher.
To eliminate all defilements, one is like a gardener tending his trees.
When a Dharma master preaches the sutras, he examines them through four matters.
What are these four?
The first is to study extensively and attain the ultimate Way;
the second is to embrace and come toward the Way, yet being unable to discuss its principles through study and inquiry;
the third is to study the Way and its virtue extensively, yet failing to achieve full realization.
The fourth is ignorance and lack of the Way.
Furthermore, there are four other dharmas:
the first is that one initially receives instruction from a Dharma Master, through whom one comes to know the meaning and understand the Dharma.
Second, although they understand its meaning, they cannot do so with subtle profundity;
third, they analyze superficial dharmas but cannot reach the profound;
fourth, they neither know its meaning nor comprehend it clearly.
To train in the Dharma in such a manner is to practice in vain and suffer in vain.
It is like two people who both do not know how to swim; having fallen into deep water, they wish to rescue one another, yet instead they both drown.
It is like one blind person leading another blind person toward a destination; they become lost along the way and ultimately fail to reach it.
One who does not know the meaning likewise does not understand wisdom; yet to desire to preach the Dharma and to desire to save others is just like this.
Thereupon, a verse says:
For example, there is a person of vast learning, Whose manifold virtues are beyond measure.
Having attained the perfection of crossing over, like a person who has traversed the great ocean;
if a person is pure according to the Truth yet lacks wisdom,
they may grasp its essentials but cannot attain its profound meaning.
If one practices the entry into the Path, Following it without contravening the Vinaya,
And being able to respectfully receive the teachings, Such a person possesses constancy and reciprocity.
Just as by staying near a venerable one, One will surely obtain great benefit.
One who studies and practices the Path will surely advance in the meaning they seek.
Yet, if one only understands how to advance in that meaning but cannot attain its subtlety,
it is like a person eating empty broth without having any rice to eat with it.
Receiving the meaning from a teacher, yet not understanding its subtlety in this way,
one cannot comprehend the Great Way and shall not reach true and correct wisdom.
Even if one does not enter the Path, one will be unable to explain it through discernment.
Thus, one does not understand through wisdom, and the meaning remains unclear and indistinct.
Like a blind man attempting to lead another blind man, they cannot reach their destination;
likewise, when there is neither meaning nor wisdom, the analogy holds true for them as well.
There are three grades of such practitioners:

first, those who practice the Way with the body while the mind does not follow; second, those who practice the Way with the mind while the body does not comply; and third, those who cultivate the Way with both body and mind acting in unison.
What is meant by "the body acts while the mind does not follow"?

Suppose a practitioner sits in the full lotus posture, upright and with the mind composed, like a pillar or a tree that never wavers; yet, while manifesting this outward appearance, the inner mind flows and wanders, universally seeking after thoughts of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations—whether they have been experienced or not.

When the mind is dissolute and lacks self-mastery, it is like a corpse cast away in a cemetery, which tigers, wolves, wild beasts, birds, dogs, and foxes vie to devour; the state of physical concentration while the mind is inwardly chaotic is just like this—this is what is meant by one who practices the path of virtue having a concentrated body but a distracted mind.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Sitting upright in the full lotus posture, Immovable as Mount Tai, Yet his mind within is confused and distracted;
His state is like an elephant falling into a deep abyss.
Thus, for a practitioner whose body is concentrated but whose mind is distracted,
it is like a tree with wild blossoms that fall without bearing fruit.
What is meant by one who practices the stages of the path?

There may be a mind set upon the Path while the body does not follow; though the body sits upright to accomplish the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), at that time the mind is concentrated while the body is not at ease.
On this subject, a verse says:
"If the nature of the mind is naturally harmonized, Abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness without other signs,"
At that time, these are called the four foundations of mindfulness; though the body is not fixed, the mind is not distracted.
Regarding the stages of practicing the Way, what is meant by both body and mind being fixed?
The body sits upright and the mind is not negligent; the internal faculties are all tranquil, nor do they wander outwardly following various causes and conditions!
At that time, the body and mind are upright and settled, entirely immovable; by this one knows that the body and mind are equally concentrated.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
With both body and mind in samādhi, Neither internally nor externally lax;
Sitting cross-legged in profound stillness, He is as immovable as a pillar.
Seeing the truth of birth and death as being like trees on a riverbank swept away by the current, one’s body and mind act in harmony;
thus one swiftly accomplishes the Way and attains the fruit.
Practicing the stages of the Path with single-minded devotion to the Way without wavering, such quiescence leads swiftly to Nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Explaining various essential meanings, like mixing milk with rock honey for food;
Those who can receive the Dharma without flattery or deceit Shall use the Buddha’s teaching to discipline themselves."
*Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Two;
*Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Three.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Nine: Encouraging the Mind (3). Chapter Nine on Encouraging the Mind.
Regarding the stages of practicing the Way (*yogācārabhūmi*), by what skillful means does one rectify one’s own mind?
I have heard this before:
"In the past, there was a king who selected the wise and sagacious men of his realm to serve as his ministers.

At that time, the king employed skillful means and immeasurable wisdom to choose one individual who was brilliant and erudite, whose aspirations were noble and refined, who was majestic yet not violent, and who was fully endowed with both reputation and virtue."
The King, wishing to test him and to know his mettle, intended to inflict a grave punishment upon this man.

He commanded his ministers and officials to fill a bowl to the brim with oil and have the man carry it from the North Gate to the South Gate. Twenty *li* from the city there was a garden named Tiao-xi (Playful); he ordered that the man be taken there, decreeing that if anyone carrying the oil should cause even a single drop to fall, his head should be severed immediately without further inquiry.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Even if such a person enters a pleasure garden, If they follow my teaching and do not spill the oil, One should honor that person as one would myself;
But if they spill the oil midway, their head shall be severed."
"At that time, the ministers, having received the king's solemn command, filled a bowl to the brim with oil and gave it to the man.
Holding it with both hands, he was filled with great anxiety and thought to himself:

'The vessel is full of oil, the people in the city are many, and the roads are crowded with carts, horses, and onlookers; it is like a pool of water being blown by the wind, causing its waves to surge.'"
"Human beings are also like this, their minds lacking peace and stability.
He then withdrew and thought to himself:
"There is not a single person who encourages me by saying, 'Do not be afraid or terrified!'"
"If one cannot even reach seven paces carrying oil in such a vessel, how much less could one travel for many *li*?
This man was distressed and bewildered, not knowing where to turn, his heart filled with dread.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Beholding men, elephants, horses, and chariots, Like a great wind blowing across the water, my mind was thus;
With a heart filled with terror and dread of not reaching my goal, How could I have ever brought this matter to its ultimate conclusion?"
The man thought to himself:
"I am now certain to die; there is no longer any doubt!
Only if I can hold up this bowl so that the oil does not fall, and reach that garden, shall I live!"
"You must apply yourself with single-minded resolve; if you see right or wrong, do not waver, but keep only the oil bowl in mind with no other intent, and only then may you cross!
Thereupon, the man walked steadily and slowly.
At that time, the ministers, soldiers, and the multitude of onlookers—countless hundreds of thousands followed and gazed upon him, like rising clouds surrounding Mount Tai.
Thereupon, a verse was spoken:
That man held his bowl with a firm and resolute mind; On the road, he beheld various onlookers.
The multitude surrounded and followed him, like great clouds rising over rivers and seas.
At the moment that man held up his bowl, his voice spread everywhere so that none failed to hear it; countless people all gathered together, and everyone said:
"Look at this man’s robes, his physical form, and his movements—he must certainly be a condemned prisoner."
When news of this person reached his home, his parents and kinsmen all heard of it; they all rushed there in haste and, arriving at the place where their son was, wailed and wept in profound grief.

That man concentrated his mind so exclusively that he disregarded his parents, brothers, wife, children, and all his kinsmen; his thoughts were fixed solely on the oil-filled bowl, with no other thought in his mind.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The son wept and wailed, his tears like a spring, Wailing and lamenting for his father in many ways."
With a heart filled with dread, he did not recognize his kin; single-mindedly and with firm resolve, he held out his alms bowl.
The crowd discussed this, urging him to cry out, doing so repeatedly.

At that time, the people of the entire nation gathered together in a great assembly; the onlookers were so tumultuous that their shouts shook the air. They rushed about, chasing one another, falling to the ground and rising again, trampling over each other in such a crush that there was no room between them, yet in the midst of this, those at the center could not even see the multitude.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The multitude cried out without ceasing, Pursuing one another from front to back so that nothing could be heard;
Yet he held his oil bowl without looking at all, Like hail falling upon the sky, it caused him no harm."
The onlookers spoke again:

"A woman has come, upright and beautiful, her majestic and radiant countenance peerless in the entire kingdom. Like the full moon shining alone among the stars, her complexion is like a lotus as she walks along the royal highway. Her features are sublime and her beauty surpasses that of ordinary men; she is like a jade maiden, or perhaps like the queen of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven named Hārītī, who is so upright and beautiful that none among the devas or common people fail to revere her."
"Now this woman is so radiant that she can perform the eight kinds of dance, her voice pure and harmonious, bringing joy to all who hear it.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Her movements are composed and serene; In song and dance, she never transgresses the proper measure."
His heart harbors joy, moving all people to emotion.
His singing voice is mournful; his body moves with graceful ease.
Neither hurried nor slow, his robes are draped in accordance with proper decorum.
With seven kinds of subtle and wondrous tones, his marvelous discourse comprises fifty [aspects];
pure in three respects, the notes of *gong* and *shang* harmonize in rhythm.
From head to foot, his body is adorned with precious necklaces and ornaments.
The speech was beautiful and elegant, like the descent of sweet nectar.
At that time, the man held his bowl with single-minded focus; his will remained unmoving and he did not look around.
The onlookers all said,
"It would be better to behold this woman's countenance today and never regret it for the rest of one's life than to live long without seeing her!
Although that man heard these words at the time, he remained single-mindedly focused on holding his bowl and did not listen to their speech.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Skillful and composed, her dance is most exquisite;
All people are filled with delight, like the Queen of Māra."
"If one who is capable of moving toward detachment can remain thus, how much more so an ordinary person?
Even as he comes and goes by their side, holding his alms bowl, his mind does not waver.
At that time, there was a large, intoxicated elephant that, in its heedlessness, rushed out onto the royal highway. The people said to one another:

"Now this intoxicated elephant comes, trampling us and causing our untimely deaths; it must be a malevolent spirit (*pūtana*) that has manifested in the form of an elephant, bringing great harm to all without distinction between men and women.

Its body is covered in sores and its skin is coarse and rough, like a massive thigh from which poisonous vapors flow downward. Its tongue is red as blood and its belly hangs low to the ground; its lips hang down as it paces back and forth aimlessly, its body smeared with human blood.

It wanders alone without hindrance, moving forward and backward with ease; when viewed from afar, it is like a mountain. Its violent roars and bellows are like the sound of thunder, and it lifts its trunk in a state of fierce rage."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The great elephant’s strength is formidable and difficult to withstand; Blood flows from his body like a spring source.
Treading the earth, he raises clouds of dust and opens his mouth wide, As if intending to bring harm to the multitude."

"Such is this elephant: it strikes terror into onlookers, causing them to flee in all directions; it breaks through enemy ranks as it charges, and all who behold it desire to die of fear. It can uproot great trees and trample living beings; though it receives the pain of blows from clubs, it feels no dread or difficulty."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"He destroys the multitudes and the herds of elephants; He terrifies people or kills them;
He overturns all dwellings, And rushes about, heedless of being restrained."
His fame reached far and near; he took harshness as his virtue, was arrogant and heedless of all else, and could not endure those of high reputation.

At that time, the merchants and shopkeepers sitting in their stalls along the streets and markets were all terrified; they gathered up their goods for storage, bolted their doors, and fearing their houses would be destroyed, everyone fled.

Furthermore, the elephant trainer had no means of control, and his anger and delusion grew even more intense; he trampled and killed elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, pigs, calves, and other such creatures along the road, shattering all the chariots until they were scattered and strewn in utter disorder.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Those sitting at their market stalls have all closed up their stores; People and livestock are harmed, and carriages are shattered.
Seeing such a sight, they shut their doors and gates, In utter disorder, like a great camp destroyed by bandits."

"Some who see it are seized with trembling terror and dare not move; some cry out in grievance and lamentation as tears fall; others are so bewildered they do not know what to do; some, not yet having put on their clothes, drag them along as they flee; others are so confused they cannot distinguish east from west; and some run away like wind-blown clouds, knowing not where they go!"

Among them, some were terrified and beat their bellies against the ground; others, driven to desperation, drew their bows and fixed their arrows, intending to shoot; some grasped blades with the intent to strike forward; some turned pale and spoke deliriously in a state of confusion; some harbored anger until their eyes became blood-red; and yet others stood back and watched from afar with joy, so that even though they held weapons, they could not bring themselves to strike.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Here some are bewildered and terrified, Others likewise weep with grief;
