Some stand in stunned amazement, unable to act, While others grasp their weapons."
Falling to the ground in distress and confusion, lost in a state of utter oblivion,
they experience this lack of peace and security entirely because of seeing the intoxicated elephant.
At that time, there was a man who understood the incantations for subduing elephants, and he thought to himself:

"I have mastered eight hundred methods for training elephants, encompassing all manner of behaviors, both good and bad. Yet, as I observe this elephant, not one of these traits is present. I must now examine from which lineage it has emerged."
"The superior seeds are of four kinds; are they the middling or the inferior seeds?
Having examined and understood this, he raised his voice and recited a divine mantra.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
The Heavenly King bestowed the vajra; I possess subtle and wondrous words that can eliminate all arrogance and empower the weak and inferior.
At that moment, the man raised his voice and proclaimed:

"Those who possess clear awakening have no self-conceit nor do they give rise to feverish agitation; they cast aside affection and embrace the Dharma, which is brought about by the practice of sincerity and faith!"
"The elephant casts aside its arrogance and subdues its mind to bring it peace.
He then spoke these two verses of a former sage from antiquity:
"Lust, anger, and delusion— These are the three great intoxications of this world."
The Path of Sincerity is free from all defilements, and thus the manifold fevers are extinguished.
By employing that Dharma of ultimate sincerity, one practices in this very manner:
with great intent, one makes offerings to the Elephant King, eliminating delusion and abandoning arrogance.

At that time, having heard this correct teaching, the elephant immediately cast aside its arrogance and subdued its mind; it then followed its original path back to the elephant stable, refraining from offending anyone and causing no harm.
The person carrying the bowl was unaware that the elephant had approached, nor did he realize it had returned.
Why was this? Because his mind was focused solely on the fear of death, with no other thoughts.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Seeing the elephant like a torrential rain, his mind was never once disturbed;
though the rain had already ceased, the sky itself felt no joy."
That person was likewise; unaware of the elephant’s coming and going, he held his mind fixed upon the oil bowl as if guarding a treasure without forgetting it.

At that time, because the onlookers were in a state of commotion, scattering and running hither and thither, a fire broke out in the city, burning the various official palaces, many jeweled houses, pavilions, and high towers. It manifested as a wondrous and towering blaze, spreading and connecting from one place to another; like a great mountain that cannot fail to be seen, the smoke pervaded everywhere and the flames reached their very depths.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"The city is prosperous, joyful, majestic, and beautiful; Its palaces and dwellings are exceedingly spacious and sublime.
Yet smoke pervades everywhere, reaching all places; The fire blazes fiercely as if intentionally set by men."
"When the fire burns the city, the bees all emerge and release their venom to bite people; those who witness it suffer pain and, struck with alarm and wonder, flee in haste.
Men and women, both great and small, have their complexions turn hideous; their hair is disheveled, their clothes come undone, and their precious ornaments fall away.
Stung by the smoke, tears stream from their pupils; seeing the fire from afar, their hearts are filled with dread and terror, and they know not where to go."
Calling out to one another in succession—fathers and sons, brothers, wives and children, and slaves—they instructed each other, saying:
"Avoid fire and stay clear of water; do not fall into the mud pits, and only then will you be safe."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"With hearts filled with sorrow and unaware of themselves, The family, kinsmen, and servants mounted elephants and horses, And went forth in lamentation, saying:
'A great fire has broken out; we must flee and abandon it!'"
"At that time, the government officials and soldiers all arrived to extinguish the fire;
yet that man, with single-minded concentration, held his bowl so firmly that not a single drop fell, and he was unaware of both the outbreak and the extinguishing of the fire."
Why is this? It is because he maintains his mind with single-minded focus, free from other thoughts.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
There were many people who were bewildered, like birds encountering a fire as they flew;
the fire burned the palace halls, and smoke issued forth like drifting clouds.
With disheveled heads and struck with terror, they fled in haste to avoid the flames and smoke.
With his mind focused solely on the oil bowl, he was unaware of the rising and extinguishing of the fire.
At that time, five-colored clouds arose and great thunder and lightning struck from the heavens.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
A great mist has arisen out of season, and the wind rises to blow the clouds into total darkness;
the entire void is devoid of clear sky, just like a herd of wild elephants amidst the clouds.

"At that time, turbulent winds arose, blowing up dust from the earth; sand, gravel, tiles, and stones filled the royal roads, while trees were uprooted, branches broken, and various flowers and fruits cast down.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The wind rises, scattering dust everywhere, Raising clouds and carrying waters, reaching nowhere it does not pervade."
A violent wind suddenly darkened the sky so that they could not see one another; thunder and lightning descended together, causing everyone to be struck with awe.
At that time, great clouds flashed with fiery lightning and thunderbolts crashed down; peacocks all cried out, and the heavens released rain along with falling hailstones.
Yet, despite these portents, the man heard nothing.
"Why is this? Because you must focus your mind solely on the bowl of oil.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
When that elephant of negligence is let loose, it is like a great cloud rising;
with hail, fire, and wind, it uproots trees and destroys houses.
When such a person does not see this, what is good and who is evil?
Unaware that wind and clouds had arisen, he merely observed the oil filling his bowl.
At that time, the man held the bowl full of oil and went to that garden, not letting so much as a single drop fall.

The soldiers, ministers, and officials all returned to the royal palace and related in detail to the King the many hardships they had encountered; yet that man, with single-minded focus, held the bowl without wavering, and without spilling a single drop, he reached the park.
When the king heard these words, he sighed and said:
"This man is difficult to equal; he is a hero among men!
He disregards his kinsmen and the jade maidens; he fears neither the calamities of the great elephant, water, or fire, nor thunder and lightning bolts."

When I hear the sound of thunder, I am struck with alarm and filled with dread; though I may have something to report, I cannot comprehend my own words. Some even suffer their hearts to break and perish, while others, being pregnant, lose their fetuses.

That which the people establish they do not perceive for themselves; though they encounter manifold hardships, their minds do not waver. Such a person as this has nothing that cannot be accomplished; with a mind as steadfast as this, one will ultimately never find it difficult to endure even the interrogations of the King of Hell, who can devour even the diamond!
The king, filled with joy, appointed him as his chief minister.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Seeing my kinsmen weeping, And the intoxicated elephant in its violent frenzy,"
Though he encountered various terrors and hardships, his mind remained unshakable.
Seeing that this man’s heart was firm and unwavering,
the king loved him and honored him greatly, appointing him as a high minister.

"At that time, the mind of this noble being was firm and steadfast; though he encountered both good and evil, as well as various fears and perils, his resolve did not waver. He escaped the penalty of death and attained nobility, longevity, and eternal life!"

The practitioner on the path governs the mind in this way: although various afflictions, as well as lust, anger, and delusion, may arise to disturb the sense faculties, they guard the mind so that it does not follow them, maintaining supreme self-restraint. They observe their own internal body and examine the bodies of others; they do the same for sensations, the mind, and mental phenomena.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a person carrying an oil bowl, Unmoving and without spilling a drop, So too,
with wisdom as subtle as the ocean, One should carry the vessel of oil with single-minded focus."
If a person wishes to study the Way, they should hold their mind in this manner:
harboring within their intent the clarity of all virtues, they eliminate every flaw.
When various forms of desire give rise to anger and delusion, [they must be restrained].
One who is resolute and not negligent, being tranquil and self-restrained;
just as the ailments of the human body are removed by medicine,
so too are the ailments of the mind removed by the four foundations of mindfulness.

If one whose mind is firm and strong can resolve thus, then with their fingernails they could destroy the Snowy Mountains, with the roots of lotuses they could pierce through the Golden Mountain, and with a saw they could cut asunder Mount Sumeru, the mountain of jewels.

Those who lack faith cannot apply themselves with diligence; harboring flattery and deceit, they are negligent and prone to forgetfulness. Even if they remain in the world for a long time, they will ultimately be unable to eliminate the defilements of lust, anger, and ignorance.

If one possesses faith, diligence, uprightness, and wisdom, and their mind is firm and strong, they could even blow away mountains and cause them to shake; how much more so, then, can they eliminate lust, anger, and delusion!

Therefore, a practitioner who wishes to accomplish the Way and its virtue should cultivate faith, diligence, wisdom, and straightforwardness; they must discipline their mind and focus exclusively on the stages of practice.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Upright faith and diligent effort, Wisdom free from flattery and deceit—
These five virtues remove blemishes And leave the mind free from countless defilements."
Having extracted and understood the *Anantavarga-sūtra*, he realized for himself this Buddha-teaching;
taking only its essential words, he analyzed their meanings as infinite.
His merit abides in a realization so lofty and sublime, like a scholar relying on a quiet dwelling for his studies.
With the flowing stream of wisdom and the form of a sublime jewel, I pray to bow my head in homage to the Great Mountain King.
Descending from the heavens, he knows the path and is not deluded;
The Buddha is born without a womb, neither entering nor emerging.
No longer subject to various sufferings and afflictions, unattached and free from inversion, possessing profound virtue and remaining unattached,
I take refuge in the One who delivers us from birth and death.
Those who practice the Path may harbor indolence, claiming that the Dharma is so subtle as to be difficult to comprehend, difficult to understand, and impossible to discern.
One should recognize the root of suffering, sever all habitual tendencies, realize its cessation, and cultivate the path of mindfulness.
Suppose there were a person who took a single hair, split it into a hundred parts, and then rejoined them as they were before without any error—would this task not be extremely difficult?
He replied:
"It is most difficult!
It is most difficult!"
"By means of illusory transformations, medicinal herbs, or divine mantras, one might restore hair to its former state; however, the Way of Nirvana is not established by such matters!
Although one may not yet attain realization of the Way, there must be skillful means."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Always vigorous and diligent, one advances toward the gate of liberation; To desire to awaken to this is difficult, yet even more difficult still.
Exerting effort with joyful encouragement and without retreat, It is like digging deep into the earth until spring water is found."
One should contemplate thus:
"Nothing is as swiftly accomplished as Nirvana; it is not sought from others, but is attained through the cause of one's own mind. That which is obtained from another is indeed difficult!"
"What difficulty is there in attaining what one has acquired through one's own diligence?

One should form this resolve and, using careful observation alone, entice the mind forward—just as one might entice a small child by calling him to come before one to take and eat the object from one's hand;
yet when the child arrives, one withdraws each finger one by one so that he finds nothing at all.
The people of the world thus possess such inverted views: they take the impermanent to be permanent, suffering to be pleasure, what is not-self to be a self, and the empty to be real.
Abandoning the four inversions and practicing the contemplation of original non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*), one then accords with the Buddha’s instructions.
Thereupon, it is said in verse:
If people do not understand original non-existence, They constantly reckon what is suffering to be pleasure and what is impure to be pure.
Just as one uses a puppet to entice a small child,
so do people, in their inversion, conceive the notion of a self;
for them, I shall manifest radiant light, like a lamp lit in the darkness.
"My hair cannot endure forever; it is neither pure nor clean, unstable and devoid of self.
Observing in this way, one sees that all things are likewise.

Encourage the arousal of such a mind as a person with clear vision who, holding a torch, enters an empty room; seeing no person and perceiving nothing at all, so too is it for one who observes with discerning clarity.
Examine the root of form and perceive its impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and non-substantiality; those who hold false views instead bind themselves.
For one who understands the contemplation of emptiness, what difficulty could there be?

One can currently see and hear of those who have attained the fruits of the path—the stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the one who is unattached—as well as those who have attained equal enlightenment. These people and I are the same;
since they have realized the Way, why should my own person alone fail to attain it?
One who cultivates the path should thus exhort the mind: relinquish the four inversions and devote yourself single-mindedly to the stages of practice.
Thereupon, a verse says:
Hair, body hair, nails, flesh, and bones, As well as all images, colors, and forms—
The multitude comes to delude the mind-dharma, Disturbed by the five aggregates;
Impermanent, suffering, and unstable, Selfless and impure.
The body is like an empty, abandoned hut— Thus do the wise contemplate it.
When the Buddha was at the Pāṭali tree, the Lord of Devas offered him food of a hundred flavors;
later, in Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit made offerings to him.
At the Piṇḍola-ārāma, he was served a meal of barley; though the barley rice was sweet in taste, [he ate it with joy].
All received it with equanimity of mind and prostrated to the One Free from Attachment.
Although they had eaten this meal, they were not attached to its form, nor did they give rise to arrogance; they cast away all pride.
Receiving offerings wherever one may be, like crossing a vast wilderness, one does not regard them as sweet or delicious;
for this reason, I bow my head in prostration.
At that time, in practice, one should contemplate food and drink.

Whether it be a hundred kinds of flavors or coarse barley rice, once they are within the belly, there is no difference between them. When food is taken into the mouth, it is chewed and mixed with saliva; this is no different from spittle.
If it enters the stomach (*āmāśaya*), the bodily fire (*tejas*) cooks it and the bodily water (*āpas*) softens it, while the wind (*vāyu*) moves it about.

As it is gradually digested, it falls into the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*); the solid becomes feces, the liquid becomes urine, the froth becomes mucus and saliva, and the essential essence within the intestines moistens and sustains the body.

This essential collection of flavors circulates through the various channels, and subsequently nourishes the hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bones, marrow, blood, flesh, fat, grease, vital essence, brain, and their like. Thus, the four external elements nourish the five internal faculties; these faculties gain strength and develop mental phenomena, giving rise to lust, anger, and delusion.
If you wish to know what this is, it is the root of solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), from which it arises.
Thus, a verse says:
"Countless varieties of supreme flavors, Once fallen into the belly, are no different [from one another]."
Since the body is subject to transformation and other forms of impurity, the practitioner of the Path does not crave food;
though they must eat, they do not seek nourishment for physical plumpness, desiring only to sustain life.
It is like a high official who captures various flying birds, clips their wings, and confines them within a cage; each day he selects the fattest to provide for the official kitchen.
As the days pass, the number of birds gradually diminishes. Among them, there is one bird who thinks to itself:
"Those who are fat die first; if I become fat, I too shall die just as they have."
"If I do not eat, I shall surely die of hunger.

Now I must moderate my diet so that my body is neither too fat nor too emaciated; I shall make it light and agile so that I may move in and out without hindrance, and avoid being seen and slaughtered by the cook. Only then can my wings grow gradually, and once I am out of the cage, I can fly away wherever my heart desires."

The practitioner of the path also calculates in this way: food serves to sustain the body so that it does not become heavy; when food is appropriate, one is light and agile, requires little sleep, and remains at ease while sitting, rising, walking, and breathing; excretions of stool and urine are minimal; the body relies upon practice, and lust, anger, and delusion are thinned.
The practitioner should contemplate in this way:

"I do not crave the body and have eliminated all sensual desires; this body is not essential, being merely a skeleton held together by joints. Now, within this body there is nothing but impurity and no solidity whatsoever."
For example, like a harmful net of enemies who harbor enmity and rob one's kin, one should examine them and serve and honor them as if they were kings.
How should one proceed?

Following the Buddha’s teachings, whether sitting, rising, or walking, one should ensure that no calamities or afflictions arise. One should constantly contemplate the body as foul and exposed, fully aware of its many impurities, maintaining this life merely to advance toward the path of practice.

Just as one would not abandon a close relative, so too is it with the body: one bathes it, feeds it, clothes it, and covers it, constantly protecting it as if it were an only child, ensuring it does not suffer from cold, heat, hunger, or thirst, nor is it allowed to be bitten by mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, or lice.
Suppose there were a rebel who had been arrested and confined in a prison, and the jailer interrogated him with various kinds of torture, asking:
"Whose property did you plunder in the past and present?
Where is your home?"
Where did the thief hide it?
With whom was he in league?
Was he a leader, a member of a faction, or part of a band?
He was treated with the five poisons; though his breath ceased, he revived and immediately reflected:
"By what means can I escape these floggings?
His mind then opened to understanding, and he confessed to the jailer:

"I have calculated from afar that there is a son of a great elder in a certain country named Jinjie (Vinaya). All the things stolen before and after [this incident] were deposited in his place; he resides in his house and consorts with us in our thefts—he is my companion."
Upon hearing this, the prison official seized the elder’s son and bound him together with the previous thief in a single cell using iron shackles.
At that time, a delivery arrived from the elder’s son’s family; he ate it all by himself and did not share any with the thief.

The bandit became greatly enraged; with eyes wide open and teeth gnashing, sweat breaking out and heaving sighs, he intended to harbor evil intent so as to prevent the elder’s son from escaping with his life, let alone eating alone:
"Now that I am in control, I shall force him; he shall not drink water alone, much less eat alone!"

The elder’s son, having been indulged in luxury since childhood, could not bear to be without his attendants for even a moment; wishing to go behind the house, he signaled to the bandits, saying, "Let us go to the latrine together."
The thief replied,
"I cannot go where you intend to go. At that time,
the elder’s son was driven to the utmost desperation and said to the thief:
"You have done me no wrong; it was you who arbitrarily dragged me away and confined me in prison.
Now that I wish to rise briefly, will you not comply?
If we do not go together as prisoners, I shall never repay your kindness."
"I shall feign an offense against you so that you may speak of it; then I shall examine my own faults and apologize for my transgression.
At that time, the bandit replied, "You truly have no fault;
I am the one who has unjustly implicated you."
"You have a large retinue; wishing to exempt yourself from punishment, you falsely accused me simply because I received food and drink while not being subjected to interrogation!
You receive offerings and yet eat them alone, never sharing them with others; for this reason, I did not follow you."
Then the elder’s son replied to the bandits, saying, "I understand what you resent;
from this day forward, we shall never be parted.
If any food is brought, I shall first feed you, and only then eat myself."
"If my life remains, I pray that you will come to the back of my house so that my vital breath may pass through.
The robber then followed her.
On the following day, when the midday meal arrived, she commanded her maidservant:
"Bring the rice you have received and first offer it to my close relatives; only after consuming what remains shall you give me some.
At that time, the maid followed her instructions exactly as she was told, and when the messenger returned, he reported the matter in full to the elder.
Upon hearing this, the elder felt resentment and anger in his heart; the following day, he went to the prison and said to his son:

"You were born into a noble clan, yet you have instead associated with and become intimate with rebellious thieves and wicked men. You were entirely unaware that they have unjustly dragged you away and confined you in this prison."
The son replied: "What my father says is correct;
one should not show respect to such a person as if they were a close friend!
One must recognize him for what he truly is—a thief!"

I wished to go to relieve myself, but being pressed by [the Buddha], I could not comply; my body felt heavy, my abdomen distended, my eyes rolled upward, and my ears went deaf. My head ached, my back felt as if it were splitting, and my ribs seemed ready to tear out. My chest was filled with gas, my breath nearly ceased, and my mind became so agitated and confused that I lost all self-awareness. My joints felt as if they would come apart, my bones and limbs ached with pain, my life-force was on the verge of exhaustion, and as a malevolent adversary stood above me, I broke into a sweat and gasped for breath.
The bandit said to me:
"If you can follow me as a patient follows a physician, only then will it be acceptable!
First feed me, and then eat yourself; only then shall I comply with you."
"It is because of greed for body and life that one treats others as close friends!

Just as the elder’s son fully understands that these thieves are his enemies, yet because they are driven by desperation, they outwardly manifest themselves as if they were close friends while inwardly remaining distant and base;

he knows that the four great elements are transient things, and that with every increase or decrease of the four requisites, there is never any peace or stability—like the venom of a serpent or a viper, like a phantom, a mirage, the moon in water, or an echo in the mountains—and thus he understands the body to be such.

Those who practice this path likewise understand this: they clearly know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all enemies and thieves; they merely provide for and nourish their bodies with food and clothing so as not to cause them harm. Day and night they apply themselves with single-minded diligence as if their hair were on fire; it is not through indolence or negligence that one achieves the Way and its virtue, but by reaching the state of non-action (*wuwei*) and crossing over the afflictions of the beginning and end within the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Chapter Twelve: Subduing the Faculties (*Indriya-vinaya*) (Part Three). In the *Śrāmaṇyaphala-sūtra* (The Stages of Practice), Chapter Twelve, "Subduing the Faculties": The practitioner’s lust, anger, and delusion are attenuated; even if they do not practice amidst sensory objects, they are not afflicted by them. Yet, though they have not yet perfected the Way and its Virtue (*mārga-guṇa*) nor seen the Noble Truths (*āryasatya*), they claim to have attained them!

In this way, the practitioner admonishes his own mind and heart, yet he releases it into thoughts of forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile sensations, becoming attached to the five aggregates; thus, what was to be accomplished remains unfinished.
If one’s mind does not follow the five aggregates or the hindrances, then one knows that the Way has been attained;
if the mind is distracted and follows various sensual desires, then one should immediately become fearful and apprehensive, and apply oneself with renewed vigor.

It is like a cowherd tending cattle in a marsh; if the cattle bolt and trample another's grain, the cowherd, fearing that his master will discover it, leads them back home and beats them with a staff to punish them.
The next day, the ox went out again and returned to the pasture; appearing as though it were not looking about, it knew whether it had again encroached upon the crops of others.
At that time, the ox thought to itself:
"The herder does not see me."
Furthermore, when eating another's seedlings, the owner sees it and beats and whips the ox again; thereafter, out of fear, the ox does not dare to offend again.
In this way, the practitioner admonishes the five sense faculties so that they do not follow sensual desires, and thus the Way is realized!

If one turns back from the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana) and exercises self-restraint, contemplating the suffering of the three evil realms and the hardships of birth and death, one should practice with diligence day and night ten thousand times more than before: that which has not yet been attained should be brought to fulfillment, and that which has already been attained should be maintained without negligence.

Chapter 13: On Forbearance (Part 3). *Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Chapter Thirteen: On Forbearance. Suppose someone were to strike or revile a practitioner; at that time, the one cultivating the Path should form this contemplation: "That which is reviled is nothing but sound.
If one examines it with discernment, it is entirely empty and non-existent; as soon as it arises, it immediately ceases."
For example, although the names of written characters differ from one another, each individual character contains no sound of abuse;
likewise, just as a single blind person sees nothing, even a hundred blind people together would see nothing.
Reproach is also like this: not even a single syllable is established, and even a full hundred or thousand words are entirely empty and non-existent.
Even if my parents, family, and kinsmen were all to praise me together, they too would likewise be empty.
One should contemplate in this way:
"For example, when people from foreign barbarian lands with strange accents come to revile me, it is like the sound of the wind; these sounds are all empty."

Chapter 14: On Abandoning the Infliction of Evil (3). *Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Chapter Fourteen: On Abandoning the Infliction of Evil. Suppose a practitioner is seated in tranquil meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and someone comes to strike and beat him, inflicting upon his body knives, staves, tiles, or stones.
One should contemplate in this way:
"Name-and-form are both empty; that which strikes and that which is struck are entirely non-existent. From what did they originally arise?
Who is it that becomes angry?"
At whom should I be angry?
This affliction has come about because of my own past unwholesome karma.

If there were no name-and-form (nāmarūpa), there would be no conditions for encountering such misfortune. If I wished to retaliate against those who provoke my anger, the number of enemies would be so vast that I could not possibly repay them all.
For example, when encountering venomous snakes, centipedes, fleas, lice, mosquitoes, gadflies, or various types of biting insects, there is no way to retaliate against their harassment.
Even if one could eliminate external afflictions and misfortunes, how could one possibly ward off the four hundred and four diseases and eighty kinds of parasites within the internal body?
For this reason, one should subdue the inner mind, extinguish all defilements, and settle the will in tranquility; therefore, it is called "cultivation. Chapter Fifteen:

Seeing the End and the Beginning with the Divine Eye (*Divyacakṣus*). In the *Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Chapter Fifteen: Seeing the End and the Beginning with the Divine Eye. Even if the practitioner is asleep, they should remain mindful that all things are impermanent and that death approaches before long.

Contemplating the afflictions of birth and death amidst manifold sufferings, one should wash the hands and rinse the face while surveying the four directions; at night, one should observe the stars to govern the mind, casting aside indolence and not thinking of sleep.
If drowsiness does not cease, one should rise and practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*); even if the mind remains unsettled, one should shift one's seat.
Desiring to see light, though the mind is dark, one contemplates the three luminaries to make both the internal and external bright.
Thereupon, it is said in verse:
One should contemplate the suffering of birth and death, Observe transgressions, and gaze upon the four directions.
Examining the external light and shadows, one seeks illumination within the inner mind.
Destroying the darkness of sleep is like the sun dispelling the gloom;
thus, even with eyes closed, what is seen exceeds that of when they are open.
That practitioner constantly contemplates seeing the light, remaining no different by day or night;
they discern the great and the small, the right and the wrong, and their respective destinies; traveling afar, they study universally, such that there is nothing they do not master.
Reflecting thus, one attains the eye of the Path, through which all things are seen with equality; there are no longer the Mīyāna or Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Though his eyes are closed in sleep, they are ever as if open; What is seen through meditative concentration surpasses even the divine eye."
Beholding all classes of sentient beings throughout the world, they penetrate to the heavens without anything unseen;
these practitioners, having perfected the eye of the Way, see clearly all directions and the three evil realms.

It is like this: suppose after a long period of rain, the sky suddenly clears; a person with clear vision standing on a mountain peak gazes upon cities, provinces, districts, towns, villages, people, trees, flowers and fruits, flowing streams, springs, lions, tigers, wolves, elephants, horses, sheep, deer, and various wild beasts—seeing all their coming and going, their advancing and halting.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as in a bright mirror or the empty sky, When the heavy rains have ceased and the sun shines clear,
A person with pure vision standing upon a high mountain Looks down from above and sees everything without exception."
Furthermore, one contemplates city walls, capitals, and provinces;
the practitioner does likewise, beholding the world and its birds and beasts, as well as the abodes of beings in the hells and among the hungry ghosts.

Practicing in this manner, one beholds the three thousandfold world system and perceives the births, deaths, and the destinations of good and evil for sentient beings; this is called the supernormal power of penetration.
Thereupon, a verse says:
"Though there be the unsurpassed flavor of ambrosia, To behold the virtues of the three thousand worlds exceeds that."
Practicing the Way in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, one swiftly attains unimpeded supernormal powers.
The Buddha perceives all things universally pure; out of compassion for the multitude, he has preached this.
He resolves the roots of beginning and end so that they may cross over quickly, analyzing them through the meaning of the infinite.
Consciousness and wisdom form the hub, tranquil and responsive to conditions; unimpeded, they accord with the Right Path.
To those who turn this wheel of the Dharma, the Great Holy One of the Turning-Wheel clan, I prostrate.
Observing and reflecting upon various forms of music and dance, may one maintain a mind of equanimity even in the face of sorrow;
hearing the sounds of devas, humans, and those in the hells, one joins the palms and bows the head to the Honored One of Pure Nature.
As soon as the practitioner achieves the divine ear, they immediately attain the power of penetrating hearing without any confusion or distraction.
It is like a person digging the earth to seek hidden treasure who, having originally intended to find one, discovers other treasures as well;
so it is with the practitioner, who, seeking the divine ear for the purpose of penetrating hearing, subsequently hears all sounds of both the heavens and the world.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Consider that practitioner who, employing skillful means to promote the Dharma,
Through diligent effort attains the divine eye, Beholding the heavens and the world."
Hearing arises spontaneously, and what is heard is likewise limitless;
it is like a person searching for a hidden treasure in the earth who naturally finds other jewels as well.

For example, at midnight while the multitude sleeps, one person alone awakens and ascends a seven-storied tower; in that silence, he listens to and discerns various sounds: the music of songs and dances, the cries of lamentation, and the beating of drums.

The vision attained through the cultivation of the path is likewise thus: while the mind is fundamentally tranquil, one hears from afar the wailing and bitter lamentations of those in hell, and perceives and hears the sounds of music and song from among the hungry ghosts, animals, devas, and the human world; this constitutes the realization of the supernormal power of the divine ear.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when all the people sleep at night, A single person rises and ascends a seven-storied tower;
With a tranquil mind, he listens to the sounds Of all the people’s music, song, dance, and instruments."
The practitioner of the path is likewise: with the divine ear, they hear all sounds clearly;
regarding all forms and colors within the three realms, they fully understand and know their languages.
From the meaning of countless great sūtras, I have obtained their essence and partaken of the nectar;
like a person who, being ill, takes excellent medicine, I now expound the World-Honored One’s teaching of the divine eye.
Wisdom is its sprout, the roots of goodness its source; The sutras and Dharma form its flowers, and virtue its fruit.
Manifesting liberation while remaining immovable— I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Great Tree.

Having cultivated roots of goodness through hundreds of millions of births, And having practiced the tranquil holy life for infinite past eons, He perceives hundreds of thousands of millions of former lives;
The Buddha’s awakened mind is firm, and his heart is settled in concentration.
Suppose one practices and reflects within the mind, asking:
"From where have I come to obtain this human body?
Then, using the divine eye to see clearly and with penetrating insight, one perceives whether one's previous birth was as a human or as a non-human being.
It is, for example, like a person who travels from one district to another and recognizes the places where he previously sat and stood;

so it is with this practice: one reflects upon one's own past lives, recognizing all the bodies one has experienced, as well as one's names and surnames, good and bad fortune, the length of one's lifespan, one's food and drink, and one's clothing.
Passing away from there, one is born here; passing away from here, one is born there. Through such instances, one knows the countless births and deaths undergone.
This is called the supernormal power of knowing past lives, the fundamental source of consciousness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:

"Beholding through the divine eye, one practices the Way; Knowing the births traversed throughout incalculable kalpas, One sees all past bodies that were received, Just as one who, while aboard a ship, gazes at their own reflection."
I clearly remember all the places where the Buddha was born;
having examined the various sūtras, I have excerpted from them what is called "that which was previously experienced," using the mind of wisdom to gather the most essential points.

Incalculable is the proclamation of compassion; knowing the inclinations and thoughts of the multitude, one beholds for oneself what the mind contemplates—whether it be right or wrong, settled or heedless.
With the supreme intent harbored in one’s will, one understands immeasurable wisdom.
Having removed all defilements, I vow to take refuge in the Most Victorious One.

Those practitioners, with the divine eye, behold humans and non-humans—whether they are right or wrong, good or evil, handsome or ugly—and they perceive clearly the mental activities of beings, whether they are bright or obscure. They see that those who rejoice or harbor anger have minds such as these, while those whose wills are harmonious and joyful shall proceed toward their destined goal.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
With the penetrating vision of the divine eye, He beholds all humans and non-humans;
Observing the complexions of the multitude, He likewise perceives what their minds contemplate.
Knowing the fundamental source of their intentions, by what conditions did they attain this practice?
They fully examined their cultivation of the Path, whether harboring anger or feeling joy.
It was like a person sitting by a riverbank who sees within the water various creatures—fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, and countless other kinds of insects.

Practicing in this way, one perceives the thoughts of sentient beings—whether good or evil—with complete clarity and without doubt; this is called the supernormal knowledge of knowing the thoughts of others.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The eye of awakening is clear and the mind is pure; This is obtained by practicing the path of cultivation.
Knowing the thoughts and reflections in the minds of others Is like seeing the roots, branches, and leaves of a tree."
It is like a merchant who, desiring a crystal gem, enters the rivers and seas and obtains that treasure, as well as pearls, diamonds, coral, tridacna shells, and agate.

Practicing in this manner, one abandons sleep and concentrates the mind on clarity; thus, one attains the divine eye as well as the divine ear and supernormal powers, comes to know for oneself where one has come from, and perceives the origins of others. Therefore, in practice, one should cultivate awakening and clarity.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as one who enters the great ocean with a single object Obtains countless precious treasures,
So too does one who practices thus eliminate sleep, Attaining the divine eye and the divine ear to discern the beginning and end of consciousness."
Practicing in this way with a mind of tranquil concentration, what I now proclaim is in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching:
seeing immeasurable forms surpassing the divine eye, and perceiving the thoughts of sentient beings regarding right and wrong.
The power of his patience exceeds that of the earth; he is more supple, peaceful, and harmonious than water;
his resolve is as firm as Mount Sumeru; he transcends all people and surpasses empty space.
Profound wisdom surpasses the Ganges; like the ocean, it is free from anger and resentment.
No one can equal his virtue; I pray to bow my head before the Most Victorious One.
His mind embraces the Way, and he is praised by all the devas.
With a mind held in one-pointed concentration, he does not regard this as a source of joy;
his mind is disciplined, supple, and equanimous, neither increasing nor decreasing;
his brilliant virtue is free from frivolity—I vow to prostrate and pay homage to him.
If, while practicing, the mind becomes frivolous or playful, one should immediately contemplate the nature of sorrow and distress:
"One must inevitably return to death and has not yet attained liberation; the law of impermanence is no time for joy, for all that is cherished through affection must inevitably be parted from."
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Countless rivers flow, filling the waters of the Jia and Yi;
Yet, not having crossed the river of death according to the Dharma, They are distracted and confused, yet instead rejoice."
Immeasurable kindness and affection shall soon be parted from;
the misfortunes of impermanence each follow according to one's own sins and merits.
The practitioner then reflects within his own mind:

"If I should meet my end before attaining the Way or even turning toward it, I fear I may have committed transgressions and failed to follow the teachings of the Dharma, thereby entering the three miserable realms. May I not fail to escape the calamities of the bottomless abyss, falling into various false views and becoming deluded?"
Furthermore, one will enter the womb again and again; surely the accumulated bones will be like Mount Tai!

Perhaps the severed heads will number as many as the blood in the rivers and seas, or the tears shed in weeping will equal the five rivers. Separated from parents, facing the impermanence of wives and children, and witnessing the death of brothers, one’s grief and affliction will be immeasurable.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Before I have attained the Way, I shall not sever the root of the fear of death;
I must undergo hundreds of thousands more hardships, And I shall enter the womb once again."
Not having uprooted the source of sorrow and grief, one encounters immeasurable afflictions;
unable to take refuge in the Noble Path, the three miserable realms naturally open before one.
Thus, one reflects upon one's own practice:

"Having spent the night in fear, lest we fall into the unlawful state of birds and beasts, constantly harboring harmful intent and taking one another's lives without shame, passing from darkness into further darkness—if we have already fallen into such calamity, it will be difficult to regain a human body."
"One may cast a single coin into the sea and retrieve it; yet once the human body has been lost, it is difficult to obtain again.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Enshrouded by greed and lust, blinded by anger and delusion, Driven by the staff of desire, they lack shame and remorse."
Having entered the mists and clouds of the animal realm, one falls into this suffering, and it is difficult to become human again.
The practitioner reflects:
"Will my body not fall into the realm of hungry ghosts?"
I have heard that this person carries an earthenware vessel, filling it with tears, saliva, pus, blood, and human excrement and vomit as food and drink, wandering everywhere to beg for alms.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Using an impure vessel, A cracked earthen bowl,
To hold pus, blood, mucus, and spittle, And consume it as if drinking water."
Constantly greedy and ever quarrelsome, these are the results of evil deeds;
those who act in such a manner will fall into the realm of hungry ghosts.
19. Chapter on the Hells (3). *Caryā-bhūmi Sūtra*, Chapter Nineteen: The Hells. The practitioner reflects within himself:
"Will my body not fall into hell?

I have heard that when sinners encounter one another, they immediately harbor anger and desire to harm each other; their hands and claws become as sharp as blades, and weapons such as spears, halberds, bows, arrows, tiles, and stones appear spontaneously!"

When they face one another, the sound of swords and halberds is like that of breaking bronze; weapons shatter and fall apart, while blades and spears interlace like a net. When the offenders see this, their hearts are filled with sorrow and anxiety.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"These various sinners, harming one another within hell, desire weapons;
as soon as they think of them, they obtain them all."
Holding blades to strike one another, they move like water through a net;
as hot as the midday sun, so too is the heat of these blade-edges. Some, overcome by terror, do not even realize it;

others voice their grievances, harboring poisonous malice and desiring to take each other’s lives, finding pleasure therein. Thus they incite strife and combat, pushing and shoving one another until they wound and harm each other. They are dismembered limb by limb, heads and necks separated from the body; some have their bodies pierced so that blood flows like a spring. With the blades embedded in their flesh, how can the pain ever be described?

From the sites of their sword wounds, fire issues forth; or their bodies are shattered and crushed, like tree leaves blown down by a turbulent wind, lying upon the ground with their bodies reduced to fragments like chaff; yet in an instant, their bodies are restored to their former state.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Pulling hair, punching, and trampling; Tossing about and dragging one another— The sinners gather to fight together, Suffering immeasurable pain."
Their terrors are further compounded;
at that time of great battle, they are like uprooted clusters of trees, being pushed and crushed against one another in this way.
At that moment, the sinners are restored in an instant, as cool breezes blow from all four directions, returning them to their former state!

The ghosts guarding the prison sprinkle water upon the people; though they have already revived and risen, because their transgressions are not yet exhausted, they are made not to die, and as soon as they hear the voice of the prison ghosts, they rise again as before.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Water is sprinkled upon their bodies, And a cool breeze blows over them.
At that time, the prisoners in hell Hear the words of the wardens:
"The bodies of the sinners are shattered and destroyed, yet they are immediately restored with consciousness;
as long as their afflictions and offenses are not exhausted, they must undergo further punishment.

At that time, the sinners, dwelling there, see one another again and immediately conceive feelings of hatred; their lips tremble, their eyes are red as blood, and their entrails fall out as they continue to fight as before.

The days since their enmity began have indeed been long; their bodies were wounded and shattered, falling to the ground with blood flowing like a turbid spring, yet their bodies were restored and they rose from the earth once more, continuing to harm one another as before.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having fallen into the midst of hell, The diligent suffering is beyond description;
Mutually harming one another with great terror— This is brought about by the consequences of past transgressions."
Repeatedly subjected to harm, yet returning to life as before, they turn their evil intentions toward one another; the planting of sins knows no rest.
In this world, people take delight in committing acts of slaughter.
Abiding in the Saṃjñā Hell, one undergoes retribution according to one's original deeds.
Therefore, those who share in such conduct dwell for a long time in the prison of sin;
though they repeatedly take one another’s lives countless times, upon death they are reborn as before.
Those who dwell in the world committing offenses fall into the Saṃjīva Hell;
like the plantain tree, as soon as it is destroyed, it immediately grows back again.

If an offender falls into the Kālasūtra Hell, at that time the hell-wardens seize the offenders and cast them upon ground of glowing iron. Furthermore, taking iron cords and wielding iron saws from which fire spontaneously issues, they straighten their bodies and saw them apart, from head to foot, into hundreds of thousands of pieces, just as a carpenter cuts various wooden planks.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The ghosts who guard the prison receive the King’s command; With iron ropes they bind the body and saw it apart.
The saws blaze with fire, penetrating from top to bottom; They strike the person down upon the ground and dismember them piece by piece."

The wardens of hell further hack at his body with axes; adzes and chisels operate in tandem, just as a carpenter fashions timber, making it square on four sides yet eight-cornered. The treatment of the person’s body in punishment is likewise so.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The assembly of evil deeds of the sinful beings guarded by the spirits, With axes, chisels, adzes, saws, and cords,
They split and dismember the prisoners like a carpenter, Just as someone might build a new house."

At that time, the hell-warden ghosts use flaming iron chains to lash his body back and forth; they cut through the flesh and break the limbs, penetrating to the bone and reaching the marrow, severing the ribs, spine, thighs, shins, head, neck, hands, and feet, each placing them in a different location.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Tortured for a hundred kinds of pain in the Black Rope Hell, Their skin is flayed and their bodies split with axes;
They see themselves being hewn as if building a house."
Each limb of his body is severed, and blood flows like a spring;
bones and flesh are scattered in different places, and the excruciating pain is beyond description.
The wardens of King Yama tear his body apart in this manner.
Their transgressions and offenses being yet unexhausted, pus and blood flow forth in such a manner.

Those who fall into the Saṃghāta Hell due to the defilement of their sins are made to sit down as iron nails are driven into their knees; next, they are nailed all over their bodies until they are shattered and destroyed, with flesh and bone likewise reduced to fragments. Their joints are dislocated and scattered in various places, and their lives are on the verge of ending in an unspeakable agony.

Spontaneously, a wind blows that pulls out the nails and restores them to their former state, only for them to be nailed again; such suffering continues for incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"With hundreds of thousands of countless nails, Descending from the sky like clouds and rain, They crush his body as if grinding flour;
This calamity is brought about by his original transgressions."

Next, iron mallets and iron pestles rain down, and great black elephants and massive mountains press down upon their bodies; they are crushed like sugarcane or squeezed like grapes, so that marrow, brain, fat, grease, blood, flesh, and all manner of impurities flow out spontaneously.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"A black elephant, an iron pestle, and a great mountain of stone; Crushed by an iron hammer, its body is shattered.
Seeing the ghosts of hell, all are filled with dread; Its body is broken and crushed like sugarcane."
They squeeze their bodies with iron pestles and wheels as if pressing sesame oil, and place them within mortars to be pounded with pestles.
Thereupon, a verse says:
"The jailers have no compassion; With iron pestles and mortars,"
Afflicted by their transgressions, they are like those who press sesame seeds for oil.

At that time, the sinners behold Mount Tai from afar; seeing it, they flee in terror into a vast valley, hoping to save themselves but unable to escape. As soon as they enter the valley, they say to one another:
"This mountain has many trees; we shall take shelter here."
At that time, they were each terrified and scattered among the trees; the mountains spontaneously closed together, crushing their bodies.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Because of the accumulation of many sinful calamities, / Which were created by one's own fundamental actions."
At that time, all those sinners entered the mountain valleys;
as soon as they had entered the valleys, the mountains spontaneously closed together.
When the bodies of the sinners were crushed, the sound was most piteous and sorrowful.
Harming oxen, sheep, pigs, deer, and flying birds, and taking human life without compassion, one suffers immeasurable pain in the Saṃghāta Hell;
by endangering the bodies of others, one incurs this torment.
Furthermore, seeing from afar a fire burning, the offenders say to one another:
"This ground is level and vast; the grasses and trees are as green as lapis lazuli. We should go there, for only then shall we find peace and security."
He immediately went against the direction of the flames and sat among the trees.

Fires broke out on all four sides, surrounding his body; as they burned him with agonizing pain, he wailed and lamented in sorrow. He ran toward the east, west, south, and north, seeking to escape this fire, but he encountered it at every turn and could not save himself.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Nails and hair grow spontaneously long; The complexion changes, and there is the agony of being burned and roasted.
The wind blows, drying the body and tongue; Seeing the jailers, one is struck with terror."
Countless multitudes of sinners are scorched by flames;
smoked and burned by the fire, they are like moths entering a lamp.
Furthermore, seeing from afar a forest of trees with iron leaves, they say to one another:
"That tree is most excellent, with its green grass and flowing springs; let us go there together.
Thereupon, hundreds of thousands of offenders, all entering among the trees or sitting beneath them, some standing still, and others sleeping or lying down.

Hot winds rise from all sides, blowing the trees until they sway; sword-leaves fall upon their bodies, stripping the skin, cutting the flesh, breaking the bones down to the marrow, wounding the ribs, chest, and back, severing the necks, and splitting open the heads.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Relying on many forms of faith, they harm living beings;
They fall into the Sañjīva Hell, where hot winds rise from all sides and iron leaves fall, Like one entering a battle and being wounded."

At that time, among the iron trees there naturally appeared crows, magpies, eagles, and vultures with mouths like iron; feeding on flesh and blood, they perched upon people's heads, plucking out their eyes to eat them and splitting open their skulls to devour their brains.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"In his previous lives, that person relied upon faith to harm living beings;
with iron filings smeared upon their bodies, he would dismember and sever them limb from limb."
The vultures and eagles are most fearsome;
they come from all four directions to strike at people, tearing off their heads and gouging out their eyes, then cracking open their skulls to devour them.
Thereupon, within the Great Iron-Leaf Hell, there spontaneously arise many dogs—some pitch black, some white—which run toward the offenders, barking and howling, intent on attacking them.

The sinners wail and flee to hide themselves; some scatter in all directions while others remain motionless in terror. When the dogs run up and catch them, they seize the sinners, sever their heads, drink their blood, and then devour their flesh and marrow.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
With mouth agape and teeth stark white, His roaring cry is terrifying;
Licking his lips with a protruding tongue, He violently coerces and harms others.
With blades they wound their bodies, devoured by birds and beasts;
tormented by bitter poison and harm, this is because they relied on faith to commit killing.
At that time, the sinner is devoured by dogs and harmed by crows and birds; fleeing in terror and panic, he further sees a great road divided into eight paths, all of which consist of sharp blades.
In his mind he thought to himself:
"The living grass is lush green and there are several trees; I shall go there.
As he walked upon the sharp blade, it sliced through the tops of his feet, and blood flowed out and dripped down.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The person who receives the Sūtras and Vinaya Destroys the bridge of the Dharma;
Seeing those who conform to the precepts, He forcibly teaches them to violate them."
They pursued him onto a long road, where blades sliced his feet;
beneath his feet all was wounded and destroyed, leaving him utterly exhausted and without autonomy.
At that time, he saw from afar various thorny trees forty *li* high with thorns sixteen inches long, which were so densely packed that fire spontaneously issued from them.
The sinful people thought to themselves:
"That is a fine tree, with all kinds of flowers and fruits.
They all went together to the vicinity of the iron trees.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"From afar I see iron tree leaves, Their branches and twigs reaching high and far;
Sharp thorns grow like saws, Pointing both upward and downward."
When those sinners see it, they think it is a fruit tree;
this is caused by the sins of their past lives and is the transgression of defiling calamities.

At that time, there are rākṣasas with terrifying countenances, long claws and hair, wearing loathsome garments with fire blazing from their heads; brandishing weapons, they come to strike the sinners and command them to climb the tree.

The sinners were struck with terror, their tears flowing profusely as they all received the teaching; the thorns turned downward and pierced their bodies, wounding their limbs so that blood flowed and dripped.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"His body is massive and his complexion like charcoal;
Coarse and fierce, with eyes wide open in malice, The King of Hell’s henchmen, bearing staves, All beat and strike this man."
The calamities of sins accumulated in previous lives—fools who took pleasure in violating the wives of others—now manifest as their own past transgressions:
blood flows and their bodies are pierced by spears.

At that time, the sinner is struck by the guardian spirits with arrows falling like rain; wailing in bitter grief, he cries out for them to come down, yet the spears point upward, piercing his body like a spit-roasted animal. He calls again for them to go up, [only to find the spears] ascending further.
The sinners joined their palms and all together sought mercy, taking refuge in the evil spirits and praying for pardon.
Thereupon, they recited this verse:
"Having descended from the thorny tree, The hell-king and his guardian spirits met us with thorns to strike and harm."
Struck by arrows, he joined his palms together, seeking pity and compassion in hopes of escaping his punishment.

When the hell-warden ghosts heard and saw him pleading for mercy, they became even more enraged; they beat and pierced him again with renewed violence. They sent him up once more, and when his entire body was completely mangled and ruined, he returned, wailing and sobbing.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The King of Hell’s wardens beat and stab him; Seeking mercy to escape, the wardens only grow more enraged.
At that time, all the thorns pierce his body until it is wounded through; They command him to return to the top once more, just as before."

Beside those iron trees stand two great cauldrons as vast as mountains. The guardian spirits seize the transgressors and cast them into the iron cauldrons; the boiling water surges up and down, just as when small beans are boiled in a large cauldron in the human world and bubble up and down.
Furthermore, within these cauldrons of boiling water, they are subjected to agonizing torment for thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of years.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Even if one attains the position of sovereign of a nation And exercises arbitrary power over the myriad people,
One will eventually reach the realm of hell To undergo judicial punishment for ten billion years."
Falling into the cauldrons of boiling water, they are cooked within the pots;
scorched and boiled by fire, it is as if they were beans being stewed.
Escaping from the iron cauldrons, they see a flowing river in the distance and call out to one another:

“That river is vast and majestic, possessing divine power; its waves rise and fall, and various flowers drift along with the current. Trees grow on both banks, their leaves a lush green shading the river water. The bed consists entirely of shifting sands, and the water is cool and refreshing; one may go there to drink, bathe, and relieve one’s fatigue.”
The offenders, unaware that thorns grow on both sides, enter that river which is entirely boiling ashes.
Thereupon, a verse says:
"In his previous lives, this person harmed aquatic insects; Their flesh and blood all fell away, leaving behind only bones and brains."
What was originally cool water now boils with ash; it is profoundly deep and hot, surging and bubbling.

When a sinner falls into this Hell of Boiling Ash, their hair, fur, nails, teeth, bones, and flesh are each carried away to different places; their skeletal remains, bound by sinews, drift up and down with the current.
Just as they wish to escape, the guardians seize them with hooks and lay them upon the hot ground; when a wind rises and blows upon them, their bodies are restored to their former state.
The hell-demon asked,
"Where have you come from, and where do you intend to go?
The sinner replied:
"I do not know how much time has passed since I arrived; I reckon it has been many hundreds of thousands of billions of years, yet in my hunger, I have found no food.

Because of this hunger and thirst, the wardens seize their hooks and pry open his mouth, inserting glowing iron balls and pouring molten copper into his mouth. It burns his throat, rots all five internal organs within his belly, and passes through his intestines and stomach until it flows out. The agonizing pain is beyond description.
Because their transgressions and evils are not yet exhausted, they do not die!
Not far from the river are two hells:
the first is named Crying Out (Raurava), and the second is named Great Crying Out (Mahāraurava).
The city is made of iron, with watchtowers and battlements a hundred feet high and its parapets strictly fortified; it is entirely covered above with iron nets.
The sinners say to one another:
"This city is magnificent; let us go together to see it."
Having just entered within, they thought to themselves:
"We have escaped danger and difficulty; there are no more afflictions.

They leaped for joy and all cried out, "Ten thousand years! Some struck their faces against the ground, some lay prostrate with their faces upturned, and some fell asleep, striking and injuring their own faces.

On the four walls, fire spontaneously arises from the outside, burning the watchtowers, battlements, and parapets; the various nets and gates are all set ablaze. Within the city, fires burn the bodies of the offenders; as they see one another, it is like brandishing torches, like flashes of lightning, or like scattered embers. The burning of their bodies is so agonizing that it is like being struck by flaming arrows shot at elephants;
their cries of pain are beyond description. After a hundred years have passed, the eastern gate finally opens.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of countless sinners all rushed toward the gate; as soon as they arrived, it was closed, and they jostled one another until they fell to the ground like toppled great trees, piling upon one another like a stack of firewood.
Because their transgressions and evils are not yet exhausted, they are prevented from dying.
Thus, a verse says:
"Arriving at the terrifying and frantic Hell of Wailing, they go there for the sake of seeking rescue and protection."
Just as a great pile of firewood is consumed by flames, so too are these sinners piled together and burned.
Under such scorching agony, they cry out and flee in all directions;
constantly fearing the hell-wardens, they are seized with terror and trembling dread.
If one receives a trust but, being obstinate and aggressive, refuses to return it,
they shall be confined in the Hell of Wailing, where they suffer the agonizing pains of their evil offenses.
Enduring countless bitter torments, they are scorched by fire in extreme distress.
They encounter immeasurable and unspeakable afflictions, as the sinners wail and cry out in great distress.

At that time, the sinners escape from the Hell of Wailing and next enter the Avīci Mahānaraka. The guardians immediately seize the sinners and subject them to the five poisons; they stretch their bodies out like stretched ox-hide, drive large iron nails into their hands, feet, and hearts, pull out their tongues and pin them with a hundred nails, and further flay their skin from their feet to their heads.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Stretching his body like a hide of ox, Nailing it with iron spikes— This is brought about by double-tongued speech; Iron spikes destroy his tongue."
Their skin is flayed and dragged along the ground like the tail of a lion;
if one were to calculate it in this way, the suffering endured would be immeasurable.

Thereupon, the guardians of hell seize the sinner and yoke him to an iron chariot. The guardian drives the chariot, restraining the sinner’s mouth with a bit; holding the reins in his left hand and a staff in his right, he beats him and forces him to run east, west, south, and north.

The sinners, exhausted from pulling the chariot, spit tongues of blood; their bodies wounded by whips and their frames shattered, they all vomit blood and collapse to the ground, their chests bruised.
Thereupon, a verse says:
"The sinners are yoked to iron chariots, Driven by hell-wardens to run and flee."
Beating his body until he vomits blood, like a horse in battle wounded by a spear;
if one lacks faith and treats the virtuous with contempt, committing evil deeds while claiming they accord with the Dharma,
such a person of wicked crime will be led into the Avīci Hell and undergo immeasurable suffering and poison.
In the Avīci Hell, glowing embers spontaneously rise to the knees of the offenders; these flames are vast and immeasurable in extent.

At that time, the offenders give rise to perverse thoughts and, following a crooked path, mistakenly believe it to be a pleasant place. They immediately enter the fire, which burns their skin, flesh, sinews, and blood vessels; yet as soon as they lift their feet, everything is restored to its former state.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"At this time, burning coals rise as high as the knees; Already vast and wide, they are further fanned by the wind.
As the sinner walks upon them, their skin burns and peels away— Such is the retribution for abandoning the right path and entering the wrong."

Having escaped this hell, not far from there lies the Hell of Boiling Excrement. It is immeasurable in breadth and length, and its bottom is exceedingly deep. When the sinners see it, they take it for a bathing pool and say to one another:
"There is a bathing pool over there, filled with blue lotuses and flowers of five colors; let us go together to bathe and drink the water to quench our thirst."

They all enter [the river] and sink to the bottom. Within it are various worms with mouths like iron needles that feed on flesh; they bore into the bodies of the offenders, tearing through their skin and flesh, boring from the feet until they emerge from the crown of the head, and worms likewise emerge from the eyes, ears, nose, and mouth.
Because their primary offenses were not yet exhausted, they were not allowed to die.
Thereupon, a verse was spoken:
"Caused by the fruit of their transgressions, they undergo poisonous agony; at that time, these offenders are in the Avīci Hell."
Crying out in agony and filled with distress, their bodies are stretched out and nailed with iron spikes.
Boiling excrement, foul and impure, fills a vast and immeasurable expanse;
all manner of filth is present there, and its depths are exceedingly deep.
Having committed crimes without a single virtue, they fall into this prison of King Yama;
these multitudes of sinners are devoured by needle-mouthed insects.
They dwell in the charcoal-fire hells and the Avīci hell, as well as amidst all the boiling excrement of impurities.
Falling into the river of transgression arises from the sins they have committed; because of the calamities of their past lives, they do not die.

Therein are two hells named Scorching and Boiling. At that time, the guardians seize the sinners and dismember them piece by piece, placing them upon iron griddles to roast them with fire, turning them over with iron spatulas and broiling them with flames.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having already arrived at great suffering, Being scorched, roasted, and boiled—
Those whose calamities among their offenses have been mitigated Then recognize their own past evil deeds."
Cutting it into pieces with a knife, they break it apart until it is countless;
they roast and scorch it with tongs, frying it upon a griddle.
Being scorched, roasted, and boiled, it becomes loathsome, flawed, and distressing.
Countless people witness his cruelty, as if a kitchen were preparing a meat stew.
Even if one harms a worthy sage or casts them into a great fire,
he who violates the precepts and destroys the Dharma shall be trampled underfoot by a massive elephant.
If one is of a nature that is stubborn and corrupt,
constantly delighting in harming sentient beings and eating without discrimination, one will be reborn as a ghost who guards the prisons of a city.
A practitioner of the Way reflects within his own mind:
"Will my body not, by comparison with this, fall into the eightfold prisons of transgression and the sixteen divisions?
Furthermore, throughout countless previous lives, I have undergone these evil realms; were I unable to reach the ultimate holy path, I would surely enter them once again."

For example, suppose there is a person who has committed a heinous crime against the sovereign. The king issues an order to his border officials that at dawn they shall inflict a hundred wounds with spears, at noon they shall inflict a hundred, and toward dusk they shall inflict another hundred.
That person would receive three hundred wounds in a single day; his body would be utterly destroyed without a single intact spot, and the physical pain and mental anguish would be beyond description.
Although there is this pain, it cannot be compared to the afflictions of hell, which exceed it by hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions of times beyond measure.
The agony of hell is thus exceedingly bitter!
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Committing various evils oneself leads to this; To see such bitter torment and suffering is loathsome.
Beholding these afflictions, one should contemplate them with clarity, And always exert diligent vigor to swiftly attain the Way."

The practitioner established in this stage of training should eliminate excessive joy and stabilize the mind; if the will becomes flighty, one should restrain it, just as a charioteer controls a galloping carriage.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Like burning coals and fire, Never ceasing for a moment,
They constantly encounter such agony, Terrible and immeasurable day and night."
When pierced by various spears and halberds, the pain is a hundredfold;
yet when one calculates these manifold afflictions and harms, they do not compare to the pain of a single hair in hell.
The practitioner reflects within his own mind:
"Since I have not yet escaped this affliction, I ought not to rejoice.
Restraining oneself in this way and no longer engaging in frivolous play, one who stands thus will be able to practice with single-minded devotion and enter into wholesome dharmas.
The practitioner then trembles with awe and alarm, never failing in his practice day or night.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
Beholding such decline and decay, It is like a tree fruit that brings harm to itself.
Furthermore, observe how the dust of afflictions accumulates like Mount Tai.
Seeing this defiled suffering, that people fall into evil realms,
one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence to practice, abandoning both worldly joy and frivolous play.
Contemplating the dark and profound suffering of the evil realms, the Buddha’s sutras and Dharma shine like the sun;
out of weariness with these manifold afflictions, he preached this accordingly, relying on the transcribed volumes of the scriptures to eliminate all contempt.
*Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Three;
*Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 20: Encouragement and Delight (IV) Chapter Twenty:
Encouragement and Delight Relying on wisdom, they deliver the multitudes; The Way accomplished, it flows as a pure stream.
Their wisdom constantly drinks from this, Consuming the nectar of the Dharma.
Its waters flow on without end, Like a leak that never ceases;
I vow to return to the seed of wisdom, Where the Way and its Virtue are already complete.
As for those who are weak and frail, They shall receive this learning and their own minds will attain realization.
He creates the messengers of meditative concentration, establishing his resolve in the dhyāna of the Dharma.
That Buddha, the God among Gods, employs skillful means and expedients, manifesting immeasurable wisdom;
with body and mind, I bow my head in prostration.
Even if, while practicing, one develops a weak and feeble mind, one should think to oneself:
"I have attained a great benefit; I am liberated from the eight difficulties and have gained the freedom of dwelling in leisure."
I have encountered the Teacher of All-Knowledge and take refuge in him; his Dharma is free from desire, and the Sangha is fully perfected.
I have planted the seeds of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and have attained its fruition, as have others who are progressing toward the path.
While the multitude has fallen into error, I follow the Right Path; while others act contrarily, I follow their equal conduct. Now, before long, I shall become a Prince of the Dharma.

My fragrance of precepts and virtue is rare among gods and men; I do not conceal my merits and thus remain free from affliction and fever. Only then shall I dwell in peace, partaking of the flavor of liberation; daily I shall be fully satisfied, attaining salvation and security. Crossing over the evil paths without fear, I shall mount the contemplation of tranquility and enter the practice of the Eightfold Path, reaching the city of Nirvana where there is no terror or hardship.
Thus exhorting oneself, one should follow and practice with diligence.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Even if one's practice is weak, One shall always encounter the benefits of the Dharma."
That I have been able to return to the World-Honored One, the True Dharma, and the Sangha;
that with a mind of skillful means and joy, I encourage those of weak resolve;
and that I always single-mindedly contemplate and reverently follow these—this is called true practice.
Whether a beginner or one who has perfected the Way, people are as diverse as a thicket of trees;
yet by leaving the evil paths, they stand established upon the right path.
Taking the virtue of the precepts as their fragrance, they are like the scent wafting from a forest of trees.
Suddenly attaining liberation, one who has realized the Way manifests everywhere.
From the Buddha arise the tree of the sutras and the Dharma; from the essentials of the multitude, I have compiled this like gathering flowers.
Since the True Dharma may vanish in an instant through negligence, I speak these words so that you may exert yourselves.
He knows the original names of all beings and understands the subtle sufferings of sentient beings, which are like the fibers of a lotus root.
Because he observes with such profound discernment, he is free from the notion of a self.
Among men, he does not cherish his own body; he vows to pay homage to the Honored One Free from Attachment.
His light illuminates the world, like a torch brightening a dark chamber.
That which his mind perceives is entirely devoid of fixed attachments.
I take refuge in that Awakened One, whose mental activity is impartial;
who observes all devas and humans, seeing them everywhere as empty and non-existent.
If a practitioner conceives the notion of a self and does not enter into emptiness, they should reproach themselves:
"I have declined and lack the utility of a mind free from hindrances; failing to accord with the wisdom of emptiness, I take pleasure in the notion of a self.

Grieved by this, he exhorted himself to lead his mind toward emptiness; perhaps admonishing his will, he urged it forward until he reached primordial non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*), wherein the three realms are all empty and all phenomena are impermanent.
For those who harbor such notions, one should admonish them to advance their minds toward non-negligence.
Thus, it is said in verse:
Those who do not understand emptiness and maintain the notion of a self, Their will wavers and arises like a tree being shaken.
Exhorting their minds toward emptiness and non-existence, they shall before long attain ultimate purity.
It is like a king who has a comedian; when the comedian’s mother dies and he remains at home observing the mourning rites, the king, wishing to hear him speak, sends a messenger to summon him.
The King wished to see him, and the jester thought to himself:
"I have recently lost my elderly parents; now the King is stern and urgent. If I do not go, he will surely take my life or punish me with death.
Although my mother has passed away and I possess no other inheritance or estate, I ought to respond to this call and not disobey his honorable command."

Yang performed a comedic play to win the King’s favor; he forcibly suppressed his own grief and no longer thought of his mother, instead adorning himself and appearing before the King with a pleasant countenance and refined attire.
