Outwardly, he made jesting remarks to delight the King, yet in private he reflected upon the loss of his mother, his heart filled with sorrow as if fire were burning through grass: "Alas! How painful!"
"How could I bear to laugh?
Having recently suffered a heavy loss, I was secretly afraid of the King, so I suppressed my grief as one might douse fire with water;
I then resumed my jesting to gradually forget my sorrows, and my laughter grew so intense that it caused the King to leap for joy."

The practitioner should likewise act in this way: they should encourage and advance the aspiration for the Way, causing them to understand emptiness and eliminate the notion of a self; by practicing accordingly, they will eventually enter true emptiness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when a king has a court jester, Who, upon encountering the loss of a heavy sorrow,
Laughs feignly to dispel grief and distress, And thereby his heart becomes joyful and glad."
Cultivation is also like this: gradually inducing the mind toward emptiness, illuminating it so that it approaches the clarity of wisdom, and remaining steadfast without wavering.

Therefore, the practitioner should follow the teaching of emptiness and admonish their own mind; if, in the midst of this, they become distracted and give rise to the notion of a self, they should reflect as follows:
"It is like a person who gathers grass and wood to construct a raft, wishing to cross a broad river, yet the waters are so swift and violent that they drift away and destroy the raft.

For many days I have encouraged and guided your mind with unspeakable diligence and hardship, yet now a distracted will has suddenly arisen; you have violated your single-minded concentration by giving rise to the notion of a self."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a raft constructed from gathered grass and wood Is swept away and destroyed by mountains, rivers, and streams, So too is the river of craving and desire so swift;
One who turns the mind toward stillness moves toward emptiness."
"It is like the grasses and trees scorched by the heat of the summer months, which, upon receiving the drenching rains, flourish once more and yield an abundance of the five grains;
when I contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*), there is no self (*ātman*), but if I do not so contemplate, the notion of a body immediately arises."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when there is a long-lasting rain, All withered grasses and trees flourish and grow;
So too, if one practices the contemplation of emptiness, One casts off the self and is free from conceptual thought."
The practitioner reflects to himself:

"The reason I sit is that I wish to seek nirvāṇa; yet this reality is difficult to seek. If there were a 'self' to be found, one could then seek it; however, I am fundamentally empty and devoid of any self."
"Now, wishing to discern that the body is fundamentally non-existent, what could 'I' possibly be?
Could there even be a body?
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Only when one understands and resolves the notion of a self in that state does one awaken; by constantly and truthfully observing it, one realizes it is fundamentally non-existent.
If one follows worldly conventions without self-comprehension, it is like chasing after a blind man in the darkness.
The practitioner reflects within himself:

"It is this body that constitutes 'me'; though there is an abundance of clothing, food, and offerings, I give them to others. This is what I call 'self,' yet when one calculates its origin, it is entirely empty."
If a difficulty arises, one should first protect oneself and only then rescue others;
if, after sacrificing one's body, further afflictions should occur, one must then provide protection for them.
All human greed arises from the body; there is no other source to be sought.
Therefore, know this: the body is what constitutes "self.
Thus, it is said in verse:
"All those who crave wealth and beauty do so for the sake of the body; if there is fear or danger, they first seek to protect themselves."
Never regarding others and cherishing only oneself—therefore, worldly people cling to "self.
One who practices cultivation reflects thus:
"I should contemplate that this body is originally composed of six elements."
"What are the six?
First is earth, second is water, third is fire, fourth is wind, fifth is space, and sixth is spirit.
What is meant by earth?
The earth has two aspects:
internal earth and external earth.
Regarding this, a verse says:
Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and the soul-spirit—these combined constitute the six.
There are six within the body and likewise six without; the Buddha has expounded this through his noble wisdom.
What is meant by the "earth" of the body?

The solid components within the body are hair, body hair, nails, teeth, filth and impurities, flesh, bones, skin, tendons, the five viscera, the intestines and stomach, feces, and other forms of impurity.
All that is solid is called the "earth-element" of the body.
On this point, a verse says:
The human body is composed of various kinds: Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bones, skin, and flesh.
And whatever else is solid within the body—this is called the earth element of the internal body.
That practitioner then reflects to himself:
"Do I perceive this internal earth as my body?"
"Does the spirit attach itself and merge with the internal?
Or does the body merge [with it] while being distinct from what we call the 'self'?
When one observes the shaving of the head and beard, as each strand of hair is removed before one's eyes, one should examine the mind a hundred times: where is the "self" to be found?
If one hair were the self, where would you place the others?
If every hair were the self, it would be illogical for there to be a manifold body.
Furthermore, from the time the hair is small until it grows long, its growth is difficult to measure; if one were to hold it and burn that hair with fire, the body would immediately perish.
Hair arises from four causes:
first, causal conditions; second, afflictions; third, craving and desire; and fourth, food and drink.
When one reckons that this body is not the self, there is no "I" or "mine"; rather, it is only through the convergence of various conditions that hair and beard temporarily exist as "me."

If a single hair falls to the ground, whether it is cast into fire, discarded in a latrine, or stepped upon by one's foot, there is no harm to the body; nor does its being upon the head provide any benefit.
Viewed in this light, its presence on the head or on the ground is equal and without distinction.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Though there be much hair upon the head, Neither its increase nor its decrease makes a difference;
Whether it is removed or remains, One does not regard it with anxiety."
Having observed this with clear insight, there is no "self" (ātman);
therefore, through thorough discernment, one realizes that each [part] is devoid of a body.
Even if one were to take those hairs as the self, they grow back again even after being cut like scallions or leeks.
Judging by this, there must still be a self. Why is this?
For those scallions and chives destroy themselves and grow themselves; all things are empty, being neither "I" nor "self."

If the hair and beard were united with the spirit (*ātman*), they could still be distinguished just as water and milk can be; yet, if the hair and beard possessed a self (*ātman*), then at the very beginning when one received form and consciousness within the womb, there was no hair or body hair at all—at that time, where would the self have been?
Later, through dependent origination, one knows this: hair has no self; whether hair arises or does not arise, whether it is removed or remains, when reckoned, there is no body.
Viewing it in this way, there is not the slightest difference between the blades of grass and the hair.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"If these whiskers and hair possessed a self, They would surely be visible like scallions or leeks."
The body is like straw that may be cut and chopped; contemplate the physical form as no different from grass.
The practitioner reflects thus:
"Originally there was no 'I,' and now I do not perceive a self."
"Understanding this clearly, one harbors no doubt: as there is no self in a hair, so it is with all things.
Hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bone, marrow, and skin—all have no owner. Contemplating them thus, one sees that the earth has no 'I,' and the 'I' does not reside in the earth."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The body and its hair are of such a nature that there is no self;
If one were to analyze the interior of the body into hundreds of thousands of parts, Seeking within them for a body, none would be found, Just like entering water to search for fire."
The practitioner thinks to himself:
"I have sought within the internal elements and find no self; I shall now examine the external elements.
Might there perhaps be a self that depends upon the external elements?"
"What is meant by external earth?

It is that which is not connected to the body, coarse, strong, and solid, existing apart from the human person; namely, the forms of land, mountains, rocks, sand, stones, tiles, and wood; copper, iron, lead, tin, gold, silver, brass, coral, amber, conch, agate, lapis lazuli, crystal, various trees, grasses, plants, crops, and grains—all such accumulated things."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:

"Mountains, crags, stones, tiles, ground, trees, And all other various forms and species— Each distinct from the body, growing and arising in abundance; These are called the external elements of earth."
When that practitioner contemplates external earth, he knows that within the internal [body] there is no self.
Why is this? Because when the internal [elements] increase or decrease, there is suffering or ease.
Since there is not even a body, how much less could there be a substantial entity in external objects?
Even if they were broken, severed, burned, dug up, or torn apart, one would feel no pain; how, then, could one say that a "self" exists?
Therefore, both the internal and external elements have no place of belonging; they are equal and without distinction.
Thus, it is said in verse:
"Just as within the internal elements there is no self, How much less could there be one existing outside?"
Observing that non-self and so forth are without distinction, one realizes they are identical to emptiness and not separate.
What is called "water"?
Does water exist within me, or do I exist within the water?
There are two kinds of water:
internal water and external water.
What is meant by internal water?

The various soft, moist, and oily substances within the body—such as fat, marrow, blood, vessels, bone-marrow, brain, mucus, tears, spittle, saliva, liver, gallbladder, and urine—all such moisture within the body is called internal water.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The liver, gallbladder, and all the blood vessels, Along with sweat, fat, and their like;
Tears, mucus, and all the urine, As well as all the moist elements within the body."
That which is dispersed throughout the body, supple, not connected to the spirit,
flowing and circulating through the entire body— this is called internal water.
The practitioner first observes the tears and saliva with clear discernment:
"If it were lifted up by means of wood, would I be attached to this?
Even if it were to flow out day after day, being cast away, extinguished, and surely remaining outside, I would not reckon it as 'I,' nor would I protect it."
If this wooden puppet possessed a self, by what name would one call it when placed within a vessel?
One who observes in this way truly knows that there is no body. Why is this so?
In calculating the physical form, there is no plurality; by this analogy, the element of water is manifold, yet water is without self, and so it is both internally and externally.
Thus, a verse says:
"Even if I were like water, when the water is exhausted, I would perish."
Just as the water in the body gradually increases, so too should one regard the "self.
Just as one discards the water within the body and does not greedily cling to it as "this body," so too for one who observes with such discernment, there is no "I" or "self."
The practitioner further examines:
"Having already seen that there is no self within the internal water, one should observe whether there is a self in external water,
or whether the self depends upon water?"
What is called external water?

That which does not belong to oneself: the sap of roots, the sap of stems, the sap of branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits; clarified butter, sesame oil, wine and spirits; mist and dew; bathing pools, wells and springs, ditches and canals, floodwaters, rivers, great oceans, and all waters beneath the earth—these are called external water.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Whatever on earth may be called water, And the various medicinal roots, stalks, and flavors—
When these are distinct from the body and not connected to it, These are what are termed 'external water.'"
The practitioner contemplates external water with such discernment.
Since even the water within one's own body lacks a self, and its increase or decrease causes physical suffering, how much more so for external water—how could it possess a body?
If there is one who takes from me, it causes me no loss; if there is one who gives to me, it brings no benefit to my body.
Viewed in this light, these internal and external waters are equal and without distinction.
Why is this so? Because both are non-existent.
On this point, a verse says:
The various waters within the body have no self; even if there is suffering or pleasure, or increase or decrease, how could such external water possess a body?
Thus, though there is suffering, pleasure, increase, or decrease, there is no affliction.
Now one should examine the various kinds of fire:
Is there a self in the fire?
Or does the self cling to the fire?
What is meant by fire?
Fire has two aspects:
internal fire and external fire.

What is called internal fire? It refers to the warmth, heat, and pervasive fever within the body that sustains the life-consciousness and digests food and drink; these various heats within the body constitute internal fire.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:

"The various heats within the body that digest food and drink, The warming and life-sustaining thermal energies— These are the bodily constituents and the solar radiance; This is what is called 'internal fire.'"
The practitioner should practice equal contemplation:
the various heats or warmth within the body may reside in the head, or in the hands, feet, spine, ribs, abdomen, or back.

When observing in this way, each part is distinct; one should reckon that in a human body there is no "self. To view it thus with precision, nothing belongs to a self; this is the internal fire element.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Discerning and analyzing the human body, the mind examines fire and finds no self.
In all its various constituent parts, each and every one is seen to lack a self."
The practitioner then reflects to himself:
"When I seek the internal fire, there is no body; should I now observe the external fire to see if it possesses a self, or do I depend upon that fire?"
What is called external fire?

That which is not connected to the body, namely fire and its flames, the category of heat and warmth, the light emitted by the sun, moon, and stars, the light from the palaces of the various devas, from the earth’s shores, mountain crags, and fires struck from stone; as well as the heat found in clothing, rare jewels, gold, silver, copper, iron, pearls, necklaces, the five grains, trees, medicinal herbs, clarified butter (*ghṛta*), sesame oil, and all other such things—this is called external fire.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The sun, moon, and blazing fire, along with the stars;
The stones on the earth that possess light and heat, And all other sources of warmth— These are designated as external fire."
When the practitioner contemplates external fire as it appears to him, he knows that external fire is beyond calculation.
Fire has two characteristics:
it burns and cooks things, yet when fire resides within grasses and trees, it does not burn those very grasses and trees.
Their locations are each distinct; if there were a self within external fire, it would not be separate from it.
Therefore, one knows that external fire has no body and does not exist apart from it; internal fire and external fire coexist without distinction.
Why is this so? Because they all ultimately return to emptiness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Thus there is this fire, which burns and heats only to cook;
the various stones upon the mountain crags are accumulated in such a manner.
Each occupies its own distinct place, and they do not blaze forth all at once.
External fire is like this; therefore, one knows there is no self.
Now one should investigate:
do all these winds possess a self?
Am I in the wind?
What is meant by "wind"?
There are two aspects to wind:
There is internal wind and external wind.
What is meant by internal wind?

It refers to the vital energy experienced within the body that moves up and down; the wind that arises transversely between the ribs, in the spine, the back, and the waist; the wind that circulates through all the hundred vessels and between the bones; and the wind that causes the contraction and tension of the sinews and physical strength.
When violent winds suddenly arise and manifest, they cut off human life; these are called internal winds.
On this subject, a verse says:
The various winds that carry the body are like a mechanical device; when these many winds stir, they sever human life.
"Gasping, trembling, and contracting the body—this is what is called internal wind.
The practitioner should contemplate it thus:
'These internal winds all arise due to irregularities in eating and drinking, as well as other causal conditions.'"
Wind does not arise in vain; there are many kinds of wind, each arising and ceasing within every step. If one seeks a "self" therein, it cannot be found.
By this it is said that when seeking the internal wind, no self or ego is to be found.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The winds that move the human body and those that abide within it, Are reckoned to be of various kinds arising from conditions;
Each of these is distinct and lacks a self, Therefore, the internal winds have no body."
The practitioner reflects within his own mind:
"Now, when seeking the internal wind, there is no self; I should further examine the external.
What is meant by external wind?

That which is not connected with the body—the violent, sudden, and turbulent winds of the east, west, south, and north; whirlwinds; cold, hot, and various subtle breezes; winds that raise clouds; the swirling *valāhaka* winds; and the winds that bring about the formation and destruction of the heavens and earth as well as those that sustain the waters—these are called external winds.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The winds from the four directions, cold and heat, The whirlwind that brings both creation and destruction,
That which sustains clouds, dust, and clarity, and the gale— These are what are called external winds."
When the practitioner contemplates the wind in this manner, he reflects to himself:
"External winds are not uniform; they are sometimes great, sometimes small, and sometimes moderate.
At times when it is intensely hot, one holds a fan to fan oneself; or when there is dust and soil, one brushes them away."
A violent, swift whirlwind rushes past, startling all who behold it;

the wind of the swirling storm (Svalana) stands poised in the void, and when the heavens and earth are about to perish, it uproots Mount Sumeru. Striking against one another, they both cause destruction; it lifts them up and casts them down, tossing and shattering them until they are all reduced to dust.

One calculates that the body has but one [wind], whether large or small; yet external winds are numerous and likewise large or small. One contemplates that internal and external winds are equal and without distinction. Why is this so?
"Neither has any fixed belonging.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"If one were to hold a fan to dispel the sweat of summer heat, The internal winds within the human body and the whirlwind-like gales [would remain]."
The various winds in space are likewise without self; these are what are called external winds.
The practitioner is able to discern and understand these four great elements;
yet, although they have not yet abandoned them, failing to understand the functioning of the emptiness of the body, they recklessly conceive of a body existing and speak of a "self" existing as well.
By contemplating that they are originally non-existent, one reckons that the four internal elements and the four external elements are both equal and without distinction.
Form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness are thus at ease within, yet have nothing upon which to rely.
Why is this? Because that mind-consciousness does not abide within, and sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise not connected to the four great elements of the body.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"One should observe these four constituents; those lacking wisdom always harbor doubts.
Form, sensation, formations, and consciousness are not connected within; how could one then become attached to the four external types?"
If a practitioner should harbor doubts, they should contemplate the original source to be able to resolve its root;

thus, they will know it as it truly is. It is like planting a tree that subsequently bears fruit: the fruit is not the original seed, yet it does not exist apart from the seed. All things are likewise:

by reason of obtaining the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), there are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Thus, within the womb, the mind and spirit are formed; when the form is like turbid curd, the fetal mass (*arbuda*) arises; gradually this develops into the body of an infant, and from that small body, one reaches middle age.

These various kinds [of phenomena] originally arise from the womb; once the body is fully formed, it is neither identical to its initial union nor separate from it. Beginning from the fetal essence, they gradually take shape until reaching middle age, when the spirit dwells within them; the transformations of the four great elements grow incrementally day by day.

By contemplating their original non-existence, one realizes there is no self; these four types of dharmas are equal and without distinction. As the spirit dwells therein, the physical frame gradually develops, and even that which lacks spirit likewise grows larger.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Internally, reality arises from the mind, just as a tree emerges from a seed;
the mind is like the tree, and its causes and effects are likewise like external seeds."
The nature of the body is likewise so: because the mind gives rise to various perceptions, how could there be various perceptions in external seeds that possess no intentionality?

It is like external seeds from which gold may emerge; subsequently, a craftsman may produce copper or iron, lead or tin, silver, or perhaps brass, mother-of-pearl, agate, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, beryl, diamond, or refined gold—such various and wondrous treasures as these may emerge from those external seeds.

Consider the formation within the womb when first conceived: when two masses of flesh coalesce, they are termed the "characteristic of the eye. The light within the eye that enables seeing is called the "pupil" (*tāraka*). The black iris within the eye depends upon this internal pupil to perceive external forms; only when the internal and external aspects meet can consciousness arise.
What gives rise to consciousness?
It is feeling, perception, and volitional formations.
Just as feeling, perception, and volitional formations arise from the eye, so too it is with the ear, nose, tongue, and mind.

The various internal and external seeds are likewise without distinction; from the internal seeds arise suffering, perception, and mental formations, which fundamentally originate within and do not depend on the external.
On this point, a verse says:
"There is protection for external seeds, Because they are used to produce gold and silver."
The internal seed is likewise so.
From the eye-faculty one beholds form; conditioned by form, consciousness arises.
From the mind, various perceptions are produced; that which is sovereign within is termed "consciousness."
Should a practitioner have such a doubt as this:
"Is there perhaps something that surpasses what is called the 'inner seed,' that which is the innermost within the inner"?
Or should they say to themselves:

“Those who are deluded do not hear and do not understand; their minds are perverse, and they enter into arrogance. Regarding the body they perceive, they think, ‘This is my domain,’ ‘I am the substantial entity,’ or ‘I am within it. They observe the bodies of others in exactly the same way!”
What is perceived is thus; one cannot transcend it.

The Buddha understands that the human body consists of the four great elements, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the various bases and spheres (*āyatana*); for this reason, it is designated as "body.
Whether "mine" or "another's," these calculations regarding the internal and external are merely the common parlance of worldly people!
"As it is said in the world, 'I wish to follow [this],' yet if one does not follow it, there may arise disputes and litigation; those who study the Way have never reckoned with the physical form.
Thereupon he uttered this verse:
"Am I truly superior? Can I transcend the inner self?"
The foolish are likewise thus: lacking wisdom, they follow false views.
Their speech involves additions and subtractions; it is merely what is spoken by the common vulgar.
Wisdom eliminates such things; in its discernment, there is nothing distinct or extraordinary.

The practitioner perceives and understands this with perfect clarity, thereby accomplishing pure wisdom. If the internal seeds were "mine," they would always be subject to one's mastery; yet, since one can restrain or censure them and their movement depends upon the person, one knows they are not "mine."
What is it that the selfless one cannot control? One is distressed by old age:

the beard and hair turn white, the nails grow long, the teeth fall out, the face becomes wrinkled, the skin slackens, the complexion changes to ugliness, the sinews and veins become flaccid, the flesh wastes away, the bones are exposed, and wind, cold, and heat afflict the body; these conditions clash and are discordant, with pus and blood becoming turbid and disordered. When one calculates the external four great elements, they are likewise thus.
There may be instances where the earth is excavated, mountains collapse, and valleys crumble; or where the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind increase or diminish.
Because one lacks mastery over these, there is no self-existent body. From this it is known that among all internal and external phenomena, there is no "I" and no "mine."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"When birth, old age, sickness, and death arrive, one still lacks self-mastery;
so too it is with external lands, which are constantly subject to collapse, excavation, increase, and decrease."
The internal aggregates form the body, and external seeds are likewise manifold;
by observing them with correct and true insight as they really are, one knows there is no self.
Thus, in practice, one reflects to oneself:
"What is this mind of mine?
Since time immemorial, though the four great elements are entirely empty, you have conversely claimed them as "mine.

It is like the summer heat when the sky is clear and cloudless; wandering through a vast marsh, one sees a mirage from afar. At that time, the ground is as hot as scattered embers; there is no water at all, and the grasses and trees are all withered, like a sandy plain where the midday sun blazes intensely.

There was a merchant who had lost his caravan and was traveling alone at the rear. Above him there was no parasol, and beneath his feet there were no sandals; sweat poured from his body and face, his lips and mouth were parched and dry, and his body was scorched by the heat. With his mouth agape and tongue lolling, he was utterly exhausted and intensely thirsty. Looking around in all directions, his mind became bewildered; seeing a mirage in the distance, he thought it was water. He believed it was not far away, appearing like ripples on a pond, with various kinds of trees growing along its banks where ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks all swam.
"I shall go there and throw myself to the bottom of the pit; once I have emerged, I will rid myself of my bodily filth and heat, as well as my intense thirst and exhaustion, and find relief.

After that person had thought this, he ran with all his might toward the mirage; however, his body was weak, his thirst increased, and he became even more exhausted. His breath failed and his mind grew frantic, so he reflected again:
"I thought the water was near, yet I have run for a *li* and still do not know when I shall reach it. What is this?"
"What is this water that I have seen?
I must have been deluded myself.
He then continued forward; as the sun turned toward evening and the time drew cool, he no longer saw the mirage, and since this water did not exist, his mind immediately realized it.
"This is merely the effect of the intense heat of the blazing sun!
Because I was so overcome by thirst, I saw a mirage from afar and mistakenly took it for water.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Seeing from afar the intense heat of the sun, he thought it was the waves of a flowing river;
because he was so utterly exhausted by thirst, his mind imagined and called it a river.
As evening fell and it became cool, he looked at it again with careful scrutiny.
Then one knows it is but a mirage, yet I was deluded and took it for water.
One practices self-reflection:

"I was originally like this; thirsting for sensual desires, I pursued them without ceasing. Clinging to the love of beginning and end, I burned myself from within. Confused, guarding at doubt and conceit, covered by the net of folly—this was the delusion of seeing a mirage."
For a long time, from antiquity, I have harbored this mind, greedily attached to a self and claiming "this is mine.
Now that I have awakened and clearly realized what is perceived with precision, these mental conceptions regarding the body have been eliminated!

"Now, observing that the six constituents are devoid of a self, and seeing that not even a single hair is ever found to exist, how much less could there be any such thing within the pores of the body?
One understands that a single hair of the body has manifold explanations; how much more so, then, when discussing all the stages [of the bodhisattva path]!"
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"One observes one's own body and says, 'I exist'; The deluded thirst for a mirage is likewise so.
To know that these six constituents are not 'mine'— One who possesses such a mind is endowed with all virtues."
The practitioner should further reflect:
"The fool lacks clarity; he gives rise to thoughts and conceives the notion that 'this is mine' or 'this is my self.
Whatever his mind contemplates, these manifold perceptions are but perverse conduct."
The initial arising is called mindfulness; the subsequent arising is called volitional formations.
Following this, the wind within the mind moves, causing the mouth to speak, while relying upon the body composed of the four great elements, one conceives of a "self" and "mine."

All these things are empty, devoid of "mine" and devoid of a self; they are merely the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*). Therefore, based on the body, one is designated as a person, a man, a male, a sentient being, or a living creature.
The movement of consciousness from within gives rise to the teeth; through the wind [of breath], sound is produced, and by means of the tongue, speech is uttered.
It is like the roar of great waters cascading down from a high mountain, which a traveler hears with a sense of vibration and exhilaration;
it is also like the echo in deep mountains, where a call is immediately answered.
The speech of a person’s tongue originates fundamentally from the mind, and it is just like this.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Relying upon various conceptualizations and manifold dharmas, The mind-attention originally arises from perverse thoughts;
Because of this, the body grows and speech emerges, Producing manifold meanings like mountains and rivers."
The practitioner should further reflect to himself:
"These four kinds of bodies are without self and without a soul, yet they mutually increase their harm.
It is like a person who possesses immeasurable wealth but has four enemies; these four enemies think to themselves:

"This person is immensely wealthy, possessing an abundance of treasures; his fields, houses, and utensils are immeasurable; he lacks nothing in terms of male and female slaves and servants; and his clan, relatives, and friends are all likewise flourishing."
"We are both poor and lack power; we cannot take direct revenge for this enmity. We must use skillful means to bring this man to ruin. By what cause shall we accomplish this stratagem?"
"Only by constantly attending upon them can one repay their enmity.
At that time, the four enemies feigned submission and went to take refuge, each saying:
"We shall serve you as runners and attendants, acting as your slaves and servants; whatever you wish to have done, please command us."
The man accepted him immediately, treating him with full trust and keeping him by his side.

The four enemies were respectful and reverent; they went to bed late and rose early, trembling with awe and joining their palms in reverence. They performed all tasks that required great effort beforehand, never shirking from even the most arduous difficulties.
At that time, the wealthy man saw that those four enemies were respectful, compliant, pure in speech, harmonious, and humble in heart; he loved them deeply and said to these four men:
"These are my kinsmen; none surpass you."
Wherever he sat, he would invariably praise and speak of them, saying:

"These are my close friends; they are like brothers or sons and grandsons to me. There is no difference between them and myself. Whatever these people undertake or whatever they wish to accomplish, I shall never oppose it."
Once this instruction had been given, they shared vessels for food and drink and traveled together in the same carriage.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"By attending upon countless attendants, One removes arrogance and does not disobey commands."
One should humble oneself like a guest in another's house, acting in accordance with their wishes to bring them joy.
How could an enemy perform such a thing? These people are one's fundamental foes;
though they harbor resentment and enmity toward one in this world, one relies upon them as if they were close friends.

At that time, the wealthy man’s heart toward these four enemies remained never distant; subsequently, on a certain occasion, he set out from his native city with these four men, intending to travel to another district.
They deliberated together in secret:

"This man has been our bitter enemy for a long night. Now that he is here, fallen into our hands, and since there are no people in this wilderness, those we have harmed here before and after are not few!"

Now this road is far removed from the city and distant from the district; there are no people before or behind, and no sentries on watch along the way, nor are there any who tend cattle, gather firewood or grass, or hunt for game!
"It is now exactly midday; even fierce beasts rest at such a time, so how much more should a man!
Now you are on the verge of peril.
At that moment, the four enemies seized the wealthy man by his hair, dragged him to the ground, and mounting upon his chest, each recounted his original crime.
The first person complained, saying,
"At such-and-such a time, he killed my father.
The second person said:
"You killed my elder brother," said the third person.
"You killed my son," he said.
The fourth person said:
"You have killed my grandson.
Now that you have fallen into our hands, we shall dismember you limb by limb; we shall cut off your head and slice you apart. Reflect well upon your own mind and what you have done in the past!"
"Reflect upon all this!
Now you, having fled from your life, have arrived at the prison of Yama.
At that moment, the wealthy man finally awakened.

"This is my enemy, yet he falsely claims to be my kinsman. When he first came to join me, I loved and trusted him; I did not begrudge him food, drink, or pleasures, and I looked upon him as a son. Whatever I desired to obtain, I placed it all before him. For a long time he has sought to harm me, but I was simply unaware!"

"Now seize my head and dash me to the ground; lay out my ten thousand crimes before me, cut off my ears and nose as well as my hands, feet, and fingers, flay my skin, and sever my tongue; now I truly know that you are my enemy."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
That person comes along with him, An enemy appearing in the guise of a good friend;
With soft words but a heart harboring poison, Like ashes covering a blazing fire.
Manifesting faith while possessing nothing, he flays me like a butcher slaughtering a sheep;
only then does that person’s mind awaken, realizing that this is an enemy and not a friend.
One who practices should contemplate this meaning in such a manner.

"Originally, I thought that the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind belonged to me; now, having examined them with discernment, I have realized that they are merely a chain of bones linked together like enemies."

Why is this so? When the water element of the body increases or decreases, it gives rise to a hundred and one types of cold-related ailments; originating from the body itself, it returns to endanger the body!

If the fire element of the body undergoes further agitation, it then gives rise to a hundred and one types of feverish afflictions; originating from the body itself, it likewise returns to endanger the body!
If the element of wind arises, one suffers from the hundred and one pains of wind-related ailments!
If the earth trembles, all manner of diseases emerge.
This constitutes the simultaneous arising of the four hundred and four diseases!

"This body composed of the four great elements is entirely a collection of enemies; it is by no means permitted by me and is truly to be loathed and weary of. The wise discard it and never indulge in craving or delight.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Fire originally resides within wood; By rubbing them together, it naturally arises."
The four elements are likewise; when they are in disharmony, they endanger the body.
The wise person constantly observes this with clarity and examines its origin:
these four internal elements are empty; what joy can there be in such an enemy?
That practitioner reflects to himself:
"I observe that the four elements are truly not mine.
I should now examine what kind of thing the empty element is."
"Is emptiness the body?
Or is the body within emptiness?
What is meant by the "element of emptiness"?
There are two aspects to emptiness:
internal emptiness and external emptiness.
What is meant by internal emptiness?

The various voids within the body—such as the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, mind, chest, abdomen, intestines, stomach, and the foul-smelling cavities—as well as the voids within the bones and the throbbing of the various channels;
these are called internal emptiness!
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the various pores of a lotus flower, So too is the body empty in its essence.
The flesh, bones, skin, and moving tendons— The emptiness within the body is no different."
That practitioner should cultivate this contemplation:
"The various cavities within the body are all called 'emptiness. One does not give rise to conceptual thoughts from this emptiness, nor does one unite with emptiness."

Why is this so? Mental consciousness arises from the mind; mental consciousness continues in succession, fundamentally arising from sensory opposition. Regarding these mental phenomena (*dharmas*), one should observe one’s own mind and the minds of others. The mind is non-existent and empty, having nothing upon which to rely.

With the three types of penetrating wisdom (*trividyā*), one examines the past, future, and present and finds that all are non-existent. Through various skillful means, one contemplates internal emptiness and never perceives a self. Therefore, because of internal emptiness, there is no "I" or "mine."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“Observing where the internal seeds reside, I never find a self, even as much as a hair’s tip.
Therefore, body, mind, and consciousness are empty; Like shadows in the dark, they exist as mere names.”
That practitioner should form this contemplation:
"Having already seen that the internal emptiness is entirely devoid of anything, one should further contemplate what kind of thing the external is:
does it possess a self?"
"Shall I rely upon it?
What is meant by "external emptiness"?

It is that which is not connected to the body, which possesses no form or color, which is invisible and cannot be apprehended; it has no physical form and cannot be restrained, nor is it covered by the four elements.

Based on this emptiness, one discriminates the four great elements; and by depending upon coming and going, entering and exiting, advancing and retreating, moving up and down, bending and stretching, lifting and lowering, descending into the deep and ascending to the high;

and by which wind circulates, fire arises, mountains collapse, and the sun, moon, and stars revolve in their orbits—it is through these that movement occurs, and this is called external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Without perceiving their forms or appearances, One is able to endure them without hindrance.
It is because of these that people come and go, Bend and stretch, and perform all actions."
Where all waters flow and converge, where the sun, moon, and winds circulate,
and where mountains crumble or fires arise— this is called external emptiness (bahirdhā-śūnyatā).
The practitioner contemplates it thus with clear observation:
"If even the emptiness within the body is not my domain, how much less can the emptiness without be called 'I'?
Holding the mind with single-minded diligence, one realizes that all internal and external emptinesses are equal and without distinction.
Why is this? Because there is neither suffering nor pleasure!
It cannot be grasped and is devoid of conceptualization; since mind and intention have ceased, there is neither suffering nor pleasure, and one should not conceive of a self.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Since all that is within this body is empty, And its essence is realized to be without self,
How much more so for external emptiness— What could one possibly conceive as existing?"
Examining inner and outer emptiness, they are entirely equal and without distinction;
by not associating with suffering or pleasure, one is free from all conceptualizations.
Now, one should observe as follows:
Regarding the seeds of the mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*): if the mind possesses a self, does the self depend upon the mind-consciousness?
What is meant by "mind-consciousness"?
Mind-consciousness exists within and not without; the mind depends upon internal seeds to perceive external seeds, thereby giving rise to causes and conditions.
The deity has six elements:
the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind!
That practitioner should understand it in this way:
The eye is clarified by forms, just as space follows the mind; for this reason, visual consciousness arises.
Thus, it is said in verse:
"Depending on the internal great elements, And the external fourfold collection,"
Just as fire emerges from two pieces of wood being rubbed together, so does consciousness arise.
Ear, nose, body, mouth, and mind—these six faculties engage in discrimination;
form is the master of both transgression and merit, and these are called the various consciousnesses.
As for this visual consciousness, it does not reside within the eye, nor does it reside in external forms; form does not merge with the eye, yet it is also not separate from the eye.
It arises from the external cause of form and corresponds internally to it; conditioned by these factors, it is called "consciousness."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"For example, if one takes a fire-drill and breaks it into a hundred pieces,
one will not see fire at all."
Observing that fire is not separate from wood, so too should one reckon the seeds of the various consciousnesses.
Consciousness arises because of the six sense-objects; when examined, they cannot be divided.
It is like a king who, while atop a high tower, was assembled with his ministers and officials.

Before he became king, he lived in the mountains as the son of a rishi; when the ministers welcomed him and established him as the king of the nation, he had never heard music. Upon hearing the sounds of drums, *konghou*, lutes, and zithers, their tones were profoundly sorrowful yet soft, harmonious, and exquisite—something he had never experienced before.
He looked back at his ministers and asked, "What kind of sound is this? Its tone is exceptionally beautiful."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as the King of Sages dwelt in seclusion, yet came among men upon hearing the sound of the lute,
the King at that time questioned his ministers:"
"What kind of sound is this that it is so extraordinary?
The ministers said to the king,
"Great King, have you never heard such a sound before?"
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The ministers replied to the king:
'Has Your Majesty not heard this before?'"
“As when the king sees one being tested, his ministers do not utter evil words.
The king addressed his ministers, saying:

‘In my youth I studied; for a long time I dwelt in the Snowy Mountains as the son of a rishi. Because I lived in such seclusion, I was distinct from this [world] and therefore did not hear [of these matters].’”
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“The King explained the matter from beginning to end to his ministers, But they found delight only in the dharma of secluded dwelling;
Because they wandered in solitude, they did not understand, And were unable to discern these sounds.”
At that time, an attendant official stepped forward and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, if you wish to know, this is called a lute.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
The King had never heard this before and did not understand from where the sound originated.
The minister said, "O Honored One among Men, this is called a lute.
The King then addressed his attendants:
“Bring the lute here; let me see what it is like.
Having received this command, he brought the lute.
The King said to him:
"I do not need this; bring me its sound!
A subordinate official replied, "This is called a lute (*vīṇā*);
one must employ skillful means and exert effort to produce its sound."
"For what reason did he raise his voice to show it to the King?
Thereupon, they spoke in verse:
"When the King had a question, the ministers immediately answered him."
“‘That sound cannot be grasped; there is no such thing as a spontaneous tone.
The King asked his ministers:
‘What effort must be exerted to produce this sound?’”
The ministers said to the king:
"This is called a *vīṇā*. Once the master craftsman has finished its construction using dried wood, he adds sinew to bind it and completes the work;
he then tests its tone to ensure it is neither too high nor too low, making it perfectly even and correct."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Crafted from seasoned wood for its construction, Covered with thin plates to leave the interior hollow,
Further fitted with fine strings and tuned to their pitch— Only then does the sound become mournful and harmonious."
The minister addressed the King, saying:

"In playing the lute, one must be skillful so that the rhythms harmonize; neither too hurried nor too slow, neither too tardy nor too rapid; one must know the proper timing and understand the subtleties of the tones, ensuring that the high and low pitches are in their proper place."
Furthermore, once dawn has broken, there are the sounds of rhymed compositions and chants; singing does not lose its rhythm as it is practiced to the beat of drums.
There are the eight musical instruments and the Nine Shao dances, comprising eighteen categories; each category has its distinct melody, and the variations of the strings number thirty-nine.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"His voice is mournful yet harmonious, Proclaiming sounds that are exceptionally elegant;
The voices of the fourfold assembly are soft and supple, And all who sing are proficient."
He understands poetry and song as if they were celestial music;
one who has attained such a state plays the lute with pure harmony.
The ministers said to the king:

"A teacher such as this is like the sound of a lute string: it is only through its adjustment that the sound becomes both mournful and delightful. Just as the sound the King heard earlier has now ceased and vanished, it can never be recovered."
Suppose a person were to pursue its sound in the four directions, seeking its location but unable to find it.
The King said to his ministers:
“That which is called a lute is of no benefit to the world; it has no essential purpose!”
This is what is called a lute; it causes countless people to become dissolute and unrighteous, deceiving and deluding them.
Take this lute away, break it into a hundred pieces, and cast it away in the wilderness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“Various efforts produce this sound; It is a false delusion for worldly folk.
If there were no drum, the sound would not arise; To what end is such great toil and exertion?”
The practitioner reflects thus:
"For example, that lute produces sound only when various efforts are applied;

the eye is likewise: free from wind, cold, or heat, its clarity and brilliance are penetrating, and the mind is not distracted by other thoughts. Because the eye relies on external light, whatever forms it perceives have no distance—whether near or far—and these forms, however subtle, are never obscured."
Consciousness is not of a single kind; through these conditions, visual consciousness arises.
Just as a lute is produced from various parts, the sound is heard by the ear and the mind finds joy in it;
when there are no afflictions and the eyes are clear, and provided there are no other thoughts, this is called visual consciousness.

The causes and conditions from which eye-consciousness arises consist of conditioned factors that are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is because of these that one encounters this affliction through eye-consciousness.
Suppose someone were to say:
"There exists a permanent, blissful life which is mine.
This cannot be found; it is a false statement. How can one say such a thing of oneself?
"One thinks, 'Eye-consciousness is mine.
By this one knows that the body has no eye-consciousness!
Eye-consciousness is impermanent, and the same is true for all mental perceptions."
One who observes with discernment knows its root: all dharmas are not "mine.

It is like a charioteer who plucks a single leaf from a plantain tree and deems it solid; yet as soon as it is in his hand, it is fragile. If he continues to strip away the leaves until he reaches the very root and trunk, not a single part is found to be solid, nor is there any core that could possibly be made firm.
Practicing in this manner, from the time one first resolves upon the aspiration for enlightenment,
one contemplates one's own hair and body hairs:
"Is this mine, or does it belong to another?"
Examining in this manner, he scrutinized the hair and the head; he observed that among all the elements of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, as well as the spirit, there was no body to be found.

As I have heard: "When the sun had set and night was dark, there was a man walking alone without the light of the moon. Having traveled halfway, he saw a tree in the distance and mistook it for a thief. Thinking that the thief would surely endanger him, he drew his sword, strung his bow, and grasped his halberd; filled with terror, he did not dare move forward. He raised his feet to take a step, yet his mind was so overcome with grief and distress that it was beyond description.
When the sky turned toward dawn, the stars vanished and the light of the sun was about to appear, only then did he realize it was not a thief but a tree."
That practitioner should contemplate in this way:

"In the past, I was shrouded by ignorance, thinking there was a self, as well as a body consisting of a head, hands, feet, ribs, spine, chest, and abdomen, which gathered together to perform actions such as walking, stopping, sitting, rising, and speaking."

Gradually attaining self-mastery, his learning became clear regarding the Way and his wisdom grew sharp; the darkness of his ignorance was thus thinned away. Only then did he understand that there is no "self," [realizing] that the body is but a chain of bones connected together and wrapped in skin and leather, which—driven by the winds of the mind—performs walking, stopping, lying down, rising, speaking, and all manner of actions.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a person traveling at night on a path might see a tree in the distance and mistake it for a thief;
so too is the fool, who perceives the body and conceives of a self."
It is understood that there is no self, person, or individual; it is through the accumulation of many factors that a physical form is constituted.
From the skeletal chain, fluids flow through the various apertures, driven by the wind stirred by the mind and spirit.
I have heard this before:

"Once there was a country where a group of young men were playing and enjoying themselves by a riverbank. They built cities and houses out of sand, claiming each as their own and guarding them individually; they distinguished what each was for so that nothing was mistaken, and having finished their work, they departed."

Among them was one son who, with his foot, knocked down another’s sand castle. The owner became greatly enraged; he seized the boy by the hair, struck him with his fist, and cried out at the top of his voice:
“This fellow has destroyed my castle! I pray that you all come to help me punish him!”
The multitude responded at once, all going to assist in beating him and trampling upon his body, saying:
"For what reason have you destroyed the work of another?"
Those people spoke again, saying:
"Since you have destroyed their city, you ought to restore it.
They said this to one another.
"Would you ever see such a person destroy another's city?
Such is the punishment for those who act with such efficacy.
Thus, each remained within their own city, playing and rejoicing, no longer transgressing against one another.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"A child builds a sandcastle; It is destroyed as soon as it is touched.
He builds it with laughter and play, Claiming, 'This is mine.'"
Each held his own thought in his heart: "This is my city and my domain;
I shall take delight within it, just as a king dwells in his royal palace.
At that time, the children played with the sand castle, claiming it was theirs, guarding and cherishing it so that no one else would touch it.

As the sun gradually turned toward dusk, each wished to return home; their hearts felt no lingering attachment, nor did they look back at the sand castle, as each used their hands and feet to trample it into ruin before departing for their own homes.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"A child builds a city out of sand, Spending the entire afternoon in play within it;
When the sun turns toward dusk, he feels no attachment, But immediately abandons his city and returns home."
That practitioner should cultivate this contemplation:

"I have not yet realized the Way; I reckon there is a self, and am attached to affection and love, universally protecting this physical form. Yet old age and sickness are approaching, and the encounter with impermanence has arrived; suddenly it will be exhausted and extinguished!"
Now that I have renounced form and the mind has nothing to delight in, I use the dharma of wisdom to analyze and dismantle the four great elements and the five aggregates.

Having now understood them, I realize that the decay of the sense bases—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—is none of mine; just as the five aggregates are not possessed by a self, so it is for the past, the future, and the present.
"One who contemplates birth and death in this manner is able to fully attain the gates of liberation; those who seek emptiness should practice accordingly.
Thus it is said in verse:
Those who habitually indulge in desire Do not abandon their attachment to affection and love."
One should universally protect one's own body, Just as a person reveres and honors their kin.
If one is free from sensual desires, Like the sun eclipsed by Rāhu,
And knows the body to be like a sandcastle, One no longer calculates "self" or "mine."
The practitioner perceives the three realms as empty and no longer aspires to or delights in rebirth anywhere.
What is meant by "aspirationless" (apraṇihita) and "inclining toward liberation"?
All objective spheres—the defilements of lust, anger, and delusion—even if they should arise, are restrained and not followed; this is called "aspirationless" and "inclining toward liberation."
The state of non-perception is likewise.
One who has thoroughly understood this refers to the three gates of liberation.
It is for this reason that the practitioner applies themselves with single-minded diligence, desiring only to realize emptiness.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"In the three realms, I am not seen; All that is perceived is empty.
How could I seek birth again?"
All shall never retreat.
Even if the mind constantly dwells upon it, through non-conceptualization, wishlessness, and emptiness,
one remains as if in the midst of battle, subduing and eliminating the enemy thieves.
Contemplate that the five aggregates are fundamentally non-existent, yet they depend upon and reside within the human body;
as it was in the past and will be in the future, so it is in the present.
This body, a collection of diligent suffering, is entirely subject to decay and destruction.
The wise contemplate the five aggregates as being like bubbles on water.
If they attain the state of signlessness and wishlessness, they perceive the three realms as entirely empty;
they reach the peace and security of the three liberations and completely transcend all suffering and affliction.
Seeing auspiciousness not far away, as if observing its lines in the palm of one's hand—
this is called being a śramaṇa, free from the afflictions of beginning and end.
Examining and awakening to the various sūtras and dharmas of the Buddha, one acts for the sake of seeking liberation and eternal peace.
He extensively expounds upon the profound and vast meaning out of universal compassion, causing practitioners to understand that he frequently lectures on emptiness.
*The Treatise on the Stages of Cultivation*, Scroll Four;
*The Treatise on the Stages of Cultivation*, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 22: The Chapter on the Supernatural Powers (5) His mind is pure like a flowing spring;
Accompanied by bhikṣus, he is like a flower of virtue.
Wisdom that relieves suffering is as peaceful as a cool breeze; I prostrate with devotion to the Buddha-tree that nurtures all.
Attaining tranquil concentration at the opportune moment, he is immovable like a mountain;
his clear observation is as precise as a scale, removing flaws so that no impurity remains.
Through the profound contemplation of the meaning of the sutras, he illuminates and manifests the world;
with a concentrated mind, he takes refuge and bows his head to the Honored One of the Three Realms.
As for the practitioner, they may first attain stillness and subsequently enter contemplation, or they may first attain contemplation and subsequently enter stillness.

If one practices tranquility (*śānti*) until it reaches meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*), one immediately attains liberation; likewise, if one first enters meditative observation and then reaches tranquility, one also attains liberation.
What is meant by "tranquility"?
When the mind abides correctly, remaining unmoving, undisturbed, and free from negligence, this is the characteristic of tranquility (*śamatha*).

Subsequently, by means of that practice, one contemplates the true Dharma with the mind, examining what has been done and seeing its original non-existence; because of these formal characteristics, this is called insight (*vipaśyanā*).
For example, it is like selling gold: when someone comes to buy it, after seeing the gold they say nothing of its being good or bad; this is called tranquility (*śamatha*).

To see the gold and distinguish that it originates from a certain country, or that it is mixed with silver or copper, identifying its authenticity as genuine *cāmpeya* gold—this is called insight (*vipaśyanā*).

It is like a person mowing grass: the left hand holds the grass while the right hand cuts it with a sickle; the state of tranquility is like the hand grasping the grass, and the contemplation of the Dharma is like the sickle severing it.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
When the mind is free from blemish, Its immovability is called tranquility;
If the mind examines thoroughly, This is termed the contemplation of phenomena.
Holding grass in hand, one should be tranquil; cutting it with a sickle, one takes this as the object of contemplation.
Because of this, one becomes serene and attains subtle liberation.

As for the practitioner, they contemplate the human skeleton—whether in front or behind—as being identical and without difference; whether with eyes open or closed, the contemplation remains the same. This is called tranquility.

He then reflects: that the head and neck are in different places, the hands and feet are each separate, and the bones, joints, and limbs are dismembered and scattered in various locations—this is called contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

This skeletal body grows by means of four things: food and drink, sensual desire, sleep, and the conditions of demerit and merit; it all returns to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. It is an impure accumulation of decay, ultimately possessing nothing at all—this is called contemplation.
To state the essentials: to see without investigating is called tranquility (*śamatha*); to discern their non-existence is called insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Thus, a verse says:
"To see the chain of bones without examining them closely, And for the mind not to be turbid or distracted—this is called tranquility."
To analytically discern the body’s parts—the head, hands, and feet—and to resolve to examine them is what is called "contemplation.
As for the practitioner, by what cause do they single-mindedly and diligently seek to enter into tranquility?
Through countless skillful means one attains tranquility; now, taking the essential words, I shall explain them.
It is brought about by two matters:
first, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
The second is counting the breaths, maintaining mindfulness of the inhalation and exhalation. What is meant by the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*)?

First, one should resolve to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, wishing for them all to be secure and at peace. Having generated this mind, one proceeds to a cemetery and sits to observe the dead. One calculates from the first day up to the seventh day: the body may become bloated and its color turn a dark blue-black; it becomes putrid and decays, eaten by worms until there is no longer any flesh, and it is stained with pus and blood. One observes the bones and joints wrapped in tendons; the bleached white bones scattered about are truly loathsome. Or one may see bones from many years ago, crumbling to dust on the ground, their color like pale turquoise.

Maintaining this in mind and reflecting deeply, whether walking or standing, lying down or rising, or while practicing walking meditation, one should keep it in mind without forgetting. If one goes to a secluded place where no people dwell, one should sit cross-legged and contemplate with single-minded focus the forms of corpses seen among the graves.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Desiring to contemplate impurities, I went to the cemetery;
Arriving at the cemetery, I observed the corpses, In that empty and silent place where no human voice was heard, I beheld my own body as being like those corpses."

If that practitioner should forget this contemplation, they should go back and observe it again; returning to their original seat, they practice the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya*). Whether entering or exiting, advancing or halting, they never let it leave their mind. Without slackening day or night for a month or a year, and even beyond such a period, they remain dedicated and unremitting. Whether walking, sitting, rising, sleeping, waking, standing, or staying still—whether alone or in a group—they never depart from it in their thoughts. Whether in sickness or in health, they should fix their resolve upon it; they do not limit themselves to taking impermanence, suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and non-self (*anātman*) as their sole meditative object.
That which is contemplated is in accordance with reality and does not arise from falsehood.
Thus, a verse says:
"If one forgets the contemplation of causes and conditions, one should return once more to the cemetery to observe it."
Not only does one contemplate exclusively impermanence and suffering, but one turns not from this mind, observing with such clarity as if seeing before one's eyes.
Just as when one sees the forms of corpses in a cemetery, one contemplates them with single-minded attention, never forgetting or abandoning it; so too is the contemplation of one’s own body.

One observes the forms of the dead and one’s own physical frame as being without distinction. Whether seeing others—men or women, large or small, handsome or ugly, naked or clothed, adorned with ornaments and necklaces or otherwise unadorned—one examines them with a single mind and finds them no different from a corpse. By means of this contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one attains profound tranquility.
At that time, one practices by constantly observing the impurities of the body, just as all rivers flow back to the sea.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"My own body, from head to toe, I see its impurities as no different [from those of a corpse]."
The mind is always focused and never abandons its purpose, like the many rivers flowing into the great ocean.
At that time, the practitioner reflects within the mind:
"I have already attained mastery; my mind does not oppose me, nor shall it again be deluded."
Immediately, he rejoiced, finding such sweet delight to be extraordinary; he established and maintained his resolve, no longer following after desire.

If he saw a woman, he regarded her as a chain of bones rather than a beautiful countenance; he examined and discerned with precision that the desires he had previously practiced were defilements. Detached from passion and form, he committed no further evils—this is the first dhyāna.

Having cast off the five hindrances and being endowed with the five virtues, one is free from all discursive thoughts and far removed from various desires, evils, and unwholesome states. With a mind focused and tranquil in single-minded concentration, one joyfully and peacefully practices the first dhyāna; this is called the dharma of serene detachment.
Seeking [the truth] in this manner through the contemplation of impurities (aśubha-bhāvanā),
he then spoke in verse:
"The will is like a bow, and the mind-moments pull one another."
Contemplating the skin and bones of women, one restrains the mind and does not follow desire.
Free from defilement, the mind is pure; the body is liberated from all evils.
Attaining mastery while in the world, one joyfully achieves meditative concentration.

This first dhyāna continues to be permeated by outflows (*āsrava*) as long as those outflows are not yet exhausted; because such a practitioner dwells in the first dhyāna, they are considered an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Although reckoned among the Buddha’s disciples, they are established as being outside [the true fold], for they have not yet exhausted [the defilements] that require entry into the inner chamber;
like the external seers (*ṛṣi*) who remain far removed from desire yet never sever it from beginning to end, they are not true disciples of the Buddha.

Practicing in this manner, the pursuit of the first dhyāna is exceedingly difficult to attain; the remaining three dhyānas are somewhat more accessible as one progresses. It is like learning archery: if one stands at a great distance from the target, it takes a long time of practice before hitting it, yet if one practices without ceasing, one becomes so skilled that one can split a hair.
Likewise, the first dhyāna is attained only through diligent effort when first learned, whereas the other three dhyānas are easy to master once one has studied them.
To study the first dhyāna requires diligent effort and is very difficult to achieve;
as for the remaining three dhyānas, through skillful means one may eventually sit [in them] with ease.
It is like the art of archery: at the beginning, it is extremely difficult to hit the mark.
Having already attained mastery over the central point, he can close his eyes and pierce a single hair.
If one reaches the profound stillness of the first dhyāna, such a person is a worldling who should be subject to reprimand and instruction;
they are not yet a disciple of the Buddha dwelling beyond the realm, for they have already abandoned craving and desire like a rishi.

That practitioner, having already attained mastery and successfully accomplished the four dhyānas, desiring to obtain the supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda), contemplates and perceives everything as empty; he examines the various joints and articulations—the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, neck, nape, ribs, spine, hands, feet, chest, abdomen, and all the pores—as being like empty space.

Having performed this contemplation, one sees one's own body as being linked together like the stalks of a lotus; observing all its pores as being like empty space, one then views the body as being like a leather bag.
Examining it thus in stages, one leaves behind the perception of form and possesses only the perception of emptiness.

Having attained the perception of emptiness, there is no longer any perception of form; or, by practicing the perception of emptiness, one continues to perceive its substance, yet remains entirely without attachment!
If one wishes to see the body, one sees it; if one does not wish to see it, one likewise does not see it.
If one wishes to see empty space, one sees it; if one does not wish to see it, one likewise does not see it.

Body and mind are equal in essence; their intent is focused within like milk and water mixed together. Mind does not depart from the body, nor does the body depart from the mind. Firming one’s resolve, one uses the mind to lift the body, causing it to leave its seat and focus the mind single-pointedly on emptiness. It is like a person holding a scale: once the weights and the hammer are properly settled and the scale is balanced, the hand lifts and suspends the scale.
Practicing in this manner, one supports one's own form while single-mindedly contemplating emptiness.
Thereupon, a verse says:
Those who practice in this way Fly with supernormal power like the gods.
Contemplate the various bones and joints of the body; the pores are all empty.
Having already abandoned the conceit of "I," focus your mindfulness on the joy of emptiness;
just as one weighs objects with a large scale, so too is the entire body.

When the practitioner practices in this manner, they attain accomplishment: at the first lifting of the body, it rises from the ground like a nit; then like a sesame seed; gradually like a soybean; and finally like a jujube fruit.

Practicing such feats of levitation up to the Brahma Heaven, he reached the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa deities; he passed through Mount Sumeru without obstruction. He entered the earth without interval and emerged without leaving a hole;

he wandered through the air, sitting, lying down, walking, and standing. From his upper body he emitted fire while from his lower body he emitted water; from his lower body he emitted water while from his upper body he emitted fire.
From all his pores he manifested various rays of light, with the brilliance of the five colors shining like the sun.
He is able to transform a single body into countless forms, manifesting as oxen, horses, dragons, elephants, mules, donkeys, camels, tigers, wolves, and lions—there is nothing he does not appear as.
In the mere blink of an eye, he travels throughout the Buddha-realms and returns instantly; this is the transformation of the supernormal power of the realm of psychic travel (*ṛddhiviṣaya*).

This supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) is brought about by means of the four dhyānas; those four dhyānas are brought about by means of the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-smṛti). Therefore, in practice, one should contemplate the foulness of the body and cultivate concentration through mindfulness of breathing.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Through the practice of training in lightness of movement, Like the wind, one is free from all obstructions;
The body leaps up to the Brahma Heaven, Thoroughly beholding all the celestial palaces."
Flying through the void, like clouds they are unimpeded;
entering the earth as if entering water, they abide in space as if on the ground.
From their own bodies they emit fire, like the radiance of the sun.
Water falls from his body, like frost and dew descending from the moon.
Having attained supernormal powers through single-minded application, he is sovereign and unimpeded;
if he wishes to touch the Brahma Heaven, he does so at will—how much more so for anything else?
Wishing to reach another realm, one can arrive there by simply lifting the feet lightly;
even faster than Śakra’s hurling of the vajra, one comes and goes in this same manner.
Exercising mastery over transformations, one is able to manifest countless forms.
Just as one enjoys a magical illusion, so too does one delight in the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*).
Roaming in the nectar-pool of the Buddha’s sutras is like a great elephant entering a flower-spring.
To summarize its meaning according to the original teaching, one thus praises and extols this attainment of supernormal power.
His majestic spiritual power shines like the light of the sun; his blazing virtue is so sublime it surpasses that of the Lord of Devas.
His countenance is as upright and beautiful as the full moon, dispelling all darkness and extinguishing every defilement.
The words of Dharma spoken from his mouth are like nectar; His speech issues forth exquisite and wondrous, extolling the ten wholesome paths.
With sincere faith, we join together to take refuge in the Most Honored One; We vow to bow our heads in prostration to the Buddha, who is without equal.
Contemplating and gathering from the various sūtras is like entering the ocean;

having attained meditative concentration free from outflows, who among the Buddha’s disciples could dare to calculate [the extent of their merit]? Therefore, I prostrate to the Most Victorious One, the Peaceful.
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"What is meant by 'being without outflows' up to the first dhyāna?
What is it that entitles one to be called a disciple of the World-Honored One?"
If a practitioner, while practicing dhyāna, suffers from outflows (āsrava), they should give rise to this thought:
"Because I have attained the first dhyāna, there are still outflows; by practicing the first dhyāna with such outflows, I shall be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
However, my merit there will be meager, and when my life ends, I shall fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or among humans."

"Even if such individuals were in the Brahma Heaven, if one observes them closely, they are monks who cannot escape the evil realms; they belong to the class of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana). Why is this so?"
Because they have not yet attained liberation.
Thus, it is said in verse:
"Even if a beginner attains dhyāna with outflows, their practice is like a leaking vessel."
Though one may be born in the Brahma Heaven, one must eventually return, just as rain alters the color of a dyed garment.

It is like a king who has a high minister commit a grave offense; first he is interrogated and punished, and the five types of torture are applied to him. Only then is he shackled and cast into a deep prison, forced to wear tattered clothes and given coarse food. He is provided with a bed of straw mats, forbidden from seeing his family, and placed in a cell near the latrines in a foul and stinking place.
Having received these instructions, the officials immediately carried out the king’s command and interrogated him according to the law.

That man had previously performed some small act of service for the king; the king, remembering this, sent word to the prison officials to release him, allowing him four months of unrestrained pleasure and entertainment together with his kinsmen, during which they congratulated one another. When the four months had ended, he was returned to the prison.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when a minister has violated the king’s law, The king, mindful of his former kindness, releases him from prison;
Allowing him to indulge his desires and enjoy himself at will, Only afterwards does he return him to be locked back in prison."
The jailer, having received the instructions, informed him as the King had commanded.

The man was released; he bathed, dressed himself, and went out with his retinue to sightsee, indulging freely in the five desires. Although they entertained themselves, his mind withdrew in reflection:
"Now I am with my retinue, indulging freely in the five desires; how shall I abandon this and return to prison? Thus he sighed through the three periods of the day.
Furthermore, one must endure being subjected to torture while clad in tattered rags, subsisting on coarse food, and sleeping upon straw, dwelling together with lowly men—how agonizing this is!

One will be devoured by fleas, lice, mosquitoes, and gadflies; living amidst such loathsomeness, one suffers intense heat in summer and bitter cold in winter.
