Mice scurry and cry out through the night in darkness as black as lacquer; one is covered in filth and impurity, with blood flowing to cover the ground, and hair disheveled and matted. Subjected to hundreds of thousands of tortures, some have their ears cut off and noses severed, others have their hands and feet lopped off, defiled and unclean. If one is in a cemetery, the distress is beyond words—one must dwell together with such a host of impurities.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"At the end of the four months of summer, the minister reflected; Together with his loved ones, he enjoyed himself in joy.
But when summer ends, he shall return to prison for interrogation and punishment; The distress of encountering such calamity is immeasurable."

“Furthermore, one shall again see various prisoners bound for their crimes—those who have committed calamitous acts contrary to the Way, such as committing adultery, theft, robbery, or kidnapping men and women; burning down people’s homes and stores of grain; harming others with poison; delighting in acts of contempt; or killing men and women, acting as a butcher of oxen, plundering villages, hamlets, districts, towns, and walled cities, and harboring ill will toward the state.”

Furthermore, one may see them subjected to the five poisons and flogged with whips, their hands, feet, ears, and noses smeared with blood; or see their heads severed, their wounds gaping and torn, from which pus and blood flow out;
or see them severely tortured until their bodies swell up, attracting countless flies that swarm over them as they lie prostrate on the ground like a great bird;
or see those newly entered into prison, whose faces, hands, and feet are all festering, swollen, and scorched, trembling with an unspeakable sorrow, remaining motionless for fear.
Some are emaciated and reduced to mere skeletons, their complexions so hideous as to resemble hungry ghosts;
some have long been in prison, their bodies bloated from the air they breathe, their hair disheveled, and their nails overgrown;
others remain within, looking every day for release.
Or some may think to themselves:
"I am in prison with no prospect of release," and thus they no longer feel despondent.

Those who newly arrive are sometimes strangled to death, or subjected to torture, or beaten; sometimes they are interrogated orally, or their physical forms are bound; sometimes they share a single bed and mat with the dead, or are dragged out and laid upon a latrine; or they are beaten on the roads and in open spaces.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Evil people are exceedingly numerous; Their flaws and impurities are loathsome.
To dwell together with the foolish Is like being with a butcher."
Wailing and weeping with tears falling, suffering as if sharing a house with ghosts, these great ministers are filled with sorrow and anxiety; how can they bear to enter the prison again?
"These various prisoners within the penal halls each speak of the king and the thieves."
Some speak of grains, rice, food and drink, and the like; some speak of flowers, incense, music, dance, and the affairs of men and women;
some speak of past events concerning travels to mountains and seas;
and some speak of the pleasures of others or the art of ambush and capture.
Some lamented the king’s accumulated merits;
some spoke of how the king had governed poorly and failed in statecraft, leading to enemies attacking and thus losing the kingdom;
others said that upon the king’s death a new ruler would be established and issue a great amnesty.
When a lady was carrying her child in this manner and was about to give birth, the prison inmates were released;
when a city fire broke out and much was being consumed by flames, the prison gates opened and we were thus liberated;
or perhaps they consulted together, saying that if they saw an auspicious omen such as the arrival of crows and magpies crying out;

Leaning against the prison gate and standing at the threshold of the cell, he dreamed of making a sound, ascending to the upper hall and climbing a high mountain, entering the palace of the nāgas, falling into a lotus pond, and boarding a boat to cross the sea; he saw for himself that before long he would be liberated from all suffering.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Those who have violated the king’s law converse with one another, encouraging and exhorting each other;
gathering together with joyful hearts, they hope to attain liberation."
Like a herd of oxen plunging into a valley, falling thus into a perilous well;
at that time, the minister contemplated this, and the man of little merit was deeply distressed.
Then the minister reflected:
"How shall I ever again hear such talk from these thieves?
Some instructed one another:

"If the prison officials question you, you should answer thus: 'The most severe interrogation will not exceed fourteen days; once the body has become accustomed to it, it will no longer be a great affliction.'"

Even if your body were dismembered piece by piece with a blade held above your head, do not utter a false word claiming you have committed such an offense; do not speak of the house where you hid, and do not name anyone as your accomplice. Furthermore, if someone attempts to entice you with questions, do not place any trust in them.
"The wardens of hell fear you; be careful not to prostrate yourself. If you see them subjecting you to interrogation and punishment, do not be terrified.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Exhorting one another in turn, Teaching people the methods of humble speech."
Reflecting on the interrogation by the jailers, he considers how he shall answer their words.
Surrounded by his ministers and retinue, he again contemplates the manifold sufferings of the hells;
though accustomed to the five sensual pleasures, his heart is filled with anxiety and distress.
The prisoners said to one another:

"Do you not see how people abandon their parents, brothers, and kinsmen; disregarding their own lives, they leave their native lands and travel through thorns, bamboo thickets, dense forests, desolate wildernesses, and perilous difficulties, even venturing into the sea for the sake of wealth?"
We have acquired these treasures without undergoing the hardships of toil; for this reason, we must endure interrogation and flogging so that we do not lose our wealth to others.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Thieves plunder the wealth of others; What they acquire does not belong to themselves.
One should consider that one must not spare one's life, For having lost one's wealth, one encounters further calamity."
The minister thought to himself:
"How could I bear to see the jailers standing before me, shouting and screaming?
And he said to himself:
"I was born under the three stars of the Weaver Maid (Vaiśravaṇa) and the lunar mansion of Pūrvabhadrapadā, belonging to the King of Hell;

I was born at midnight on the twenty-ninth day. Have you not heard that when I first fell to the earth, the land was beset by manifold calamities and agitated by unrest? Various portents arose: the sky resounded with crashing noises and the earth shook. Looking toward the east and west, all was crimson, and the four quarters suddenly became dark. Vultures, eagles, crows, magpies, foxes, wolves, wild beasts, owls, and screech-owls gathered among the tombs, devouring human flesh.
Ghosts, spirits, various *mārutas*, *kumbhāṇḍas*, *piśācas*, *pratilomikās*, and goddesses all rejoiced together, saying: 'This jailer has been born; he is truly for our sake.'"

"If there were many harmful men and women who followed us about in the prisons and among the burial mounds, we would obtain the flesh, blood, fat, marrow, and brains of the dead for food and drink; for this reason, we protect our children so that their lives may be long."
"Because I had this protection at the time of my birth, I did not fear people.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"One who lacks compassion and whose speech is harsh and urgent, that person harbors resentment for no reason."
Recalling the words of the hell-wardens, my heart was filled with sorrow; though I enjoyed pleasures, I was distressed by this affliction.
The wardens said:
"I possess skillful hands that can strike at anything, and there is no one equal to me—how could there be anyone superior?"

Throughout my past lives, I have used my own hands to kill countless men and women; I have severed their hands, feet, ears, noses, and heads, and plucked out their eyes with my bare hands without using a blade. I have stood over prisoners, pinching, slapping, and striking them;

I have suspended their heads from coarse nooses, bound them in bamboo splints, and subjected them to the fivefold tortures upon the rack. I have wrapped their fingers in cloth, smeared them with oil, and set them ablaze; I have poured fat onto their hair and set it on fire, or wrapped their bodies in straw and burned them. I have cut their flesh into pieces to extract their confessions, slit their mouths, cut their lips, and flayed their faces. I have chewed their fingers as if eating vegetables. Whether it was by whipping or flogging with bamboo or leather whips, the jailers would leap for joy as they pierced their fingers with needles, or strangled their sides and bellies with ropes, binding their heads to wooden stakes.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"The minister does not think of pleasure, fearing he will return to prison; Such interrogation and punishment are truly terrifying.
The wardens come repeatedly to speak of his execution and crimes; One who harbors such anxieties finds no peace."
The jailer spoke again:
"I have neither hatred nor affection; I take no pleasure in sightseeing or listening to the sounds of singing.
Even if there were those condemned to death—beaten with sticks, drummed upon, and surrounded by soldiers as they are led to the marketplace—I would cut off their heads all alike."
Though there be valiant generals, commanders, nobles, or those of high and honored status, they fear my skillful hand as if it were crushing elephant tusks;
whether they be fierce rebels who treat the virtuous with contempt, I shall strangle them all by the neck;
even if their parents, brothers, and kinsmen should weep and beg for mercy at once, I will not listen to them.
Furthermore, another son was shouting and leaping about like the roar of a tiger; I subdued him so that he made no sound.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"I played and enjoyed myself with my attendants, But I now recall the wardens of hell describing the punishments for crimes."
For example, it is like a person drinking pure, clear wine who may become intoxicated, boisterous, and yet joyful.
The hell-warden speaks again:

"I possess a foul breath; from my eyes, poison issues forth as I glare at people. My chest splits and my head cleaves asunder like cracking ice; when men and women see me, none fail to harbor terror, for though I have the form of a human, I act with the conduct of a malevolent spirit."
Having finished speaking thus at the prison gate, he immediately departed.
How could one consider it a joy to dwell in palaces, merely amusing oneself with the five desires, while being subject to the afflictions of such manifold distress?
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Such is this suffering and affliction, Impurity, defilement, and distress—who could find joy in this?
Who could be at peace and free from sorrow?"
Like a criminal facing execution who seeks flowers to wear upon his head,
having obtained a reprieve from the king, he must yet return to receive the lash.
Thus the practitioner reflects to himself:

"Though one may have come from the Brahma Heaven, one must return to the evil realms; dwelling within the womb, above the receptacle for digested food and below the receptacle for undigested food, defiled and impure, bound by the five fetters."
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Practicing to attain the dhyāna of the outflows, One obtains this state that is midway;
Then one is born in the Brahma Heaven, Yet cannot remain there in peace forever."

Thinking thus within their hearts, when their lives end they return to the evil realms, like a person who has briefly escaped from prison, only to be subjected to further punishment once the term expires.

It is like a child who catches a sparrow and holds it so as to distress it; he ties a long thread to its foot and releases it to fly away. The bird thinks to itself that it is free and will no longer suffer misfortune, wishing to go to fruit trees and cool ponds where it may eat and drink at will, dwelling in peace and freedom from anxiety. But when the thread is finally exhausted, it is pulled back again.
He continued to see himself being seized and tormented, no different from before.
Practicing in this manner, he thought to himself:
"Even if I reach the Brahma Heaven, I shall eventually return to the Desire Realm; such is the nature of diligent toil."
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Just as a sparrow with its feet bound by a cord, Soars up only to be pulled back when the string is exhausted;
So it is for one who practices to reach the Brahma-heaven: He returns again to the realm of desire and does not escape suffering."
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"If my body should even attain untainted dhyāna, only then shall I be liberated from the path of toil, suffering, and fear, and be called a Son of the Buddha.

In whatever food and drink I partake, I shall not be subject to delusion or falsehood; being freed from hesitation, I shall abide in the Right Path, attain the first dhyāna, and directly rely upon it to enter the truth of right view."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having attained the first dhyāna, Free from defilement and dwelling extensively in practice,
Yet still finding it difficult to escape birth and death, One should exert oneself with diligence to attain the Way."
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"Observing the various good and evil deeds leads to the attainment of the first dhyāna; it is fundamentally obtained through the chain of bones!
This form is impermanent, suffering, empty, and not-self, arising due to the four nutriments."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:

"The first dhyāna is attained through the body; Understanding that the four great elements constitute the practice of a single mind, One is liberated from impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and the self. Those who contemplate in this way are always diligent."

The mind employed for the contemplation of practice—its very foundation—is likewise impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; it is constituted by four factors and proceeds through the mutual attraction of causes and conditions. Based upon the mental conceptions of calamity and fortune, the physical form returns to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, being produced from these four factors.
Just as I have received this body of the five aggregates, which is empty and non-existent, so too are the twelve links of dependent origination in the past, future, and present.

The aggregates (*skandha*) of the desire realm, as well as those of the form and formless realms—such being the perception of these aggregates—they are all weak and frail. Seeing that the three realms are empty, one realizes their roots are deep; they are characterized by perversion rather than correctness, trembling and burning with intensity.

Beholding that there are no aggregates (*skandha*), all things are utterly tranquil; with the mind set upon serenity and moving toward non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one reaches *nirvāṇa* through the absence of other thoughts.

At that time, the mental activities are harmonious and not rigid; by practicing in this way, one perceives the definitive truth and becomes a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), no longer returning to this world, having attained ultimate liberation from the suffering of the desire realm.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The mind and its thoughts are entirely harmonious; The will relies upon the body as its basis.
To understand that the five aggregates are fundamentally devoid of past, future, and present, And to perceive them all as empty and non-existent—this is called being a sage."
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"Throughout the long night, my body has been covered by the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), deceived by foul odors and impurities.

It is like a man who seizes a wicked and rebellious son, takes a jar, paints it, fills it with impurities, seals its mouth, scatters flowers upon it, perfumes it with incense, and gives it to a country boy.

"Take this jar to such-and-such a garden and pavilion; fill it with rock honey and fine wine, and stay there waiting for us. We shall each return home to prepare offerings so that we may eat and drink together. Hold this firmly without spilling it, and we shall reward you for your labor."
Tianjiazi believed him and, embracing the jar with joy, thought to himself:
"Now I shall indulge myself in food, drink, and entertainment.

He went to his garden pavilion and would not allow even a fly to settle upon it; thus he waited for a long time until after midday had passed. With hunger and thirst in his belly, he marveled at its failure to arrive, his grief and distress beyond words.

As the sun was about to set, he climbed the tree and looked in all directions but saw no one approaching; he descended the tree and took them up again, waiting until everyone had gathered, which finally reached dusk. He thought to himself:
"The city gates have closed and the people will not come; now this rock honey, the fine wine, and the painted jars belong to me!"
"I can become wealthy by selling this; first, I should taste it.
He then washed his hands clean, opened the mouth of the jar, and saw that it was filled with impurities. Only then did he realize:
"Those gamblers must have defrauded me!"
Practicing in this manner, having beheld the Noble Truths, he attained self-awakening, realizing that for a long time past he had been deceived by these five aggregates (*skandhas*).
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Birth and death carry forth the multitude of bodies; The five aggregates have their period of invasion.
Constantly undergoing suffering and pleasure, one falsely claims there is a self, a person, or a life-span.
Practicing the deception of the five pleasures, one later sees oneself harmed,
like a person who obtains a painted jar and, upon opening it, discovers its impurity.

For example, it is like a guide who possesses abundant wealth and treasures; for his son, he brings home a bride who is upright, beautiful, and beyond reproach. He loves and respects her most deeply, never failing to fulfill her wishes; even to be separated from her for a moment, he feels as if his life has come to an end.

At that time, the roads throughout the kingdom were cut off, and for twelve years no one had come. Later, many merchants arrived from afar; they stayed in a neighboring country to rest before proceeding further.
The caravan leader said to his son, "Go to that market, purchase goods there, and return."
Hearing his father’s instruction, the son was filled with grief and distress as if an arrow had pierced his heart;
he said to his close friends, "You do not know how deeply I love my wife, yet now my father has commanded me to leave her behind and go abroad to engage in trade."
"Having just heard this command, my heart is nearly torn asunder; now I shall die, casting myself into the water, or ascending a high mountain to hurl myself into a deep valley.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Young and devoted to his wife, his craving for sensual desire was most intense."
Reflecting on his father’s instructions, his mind was filled with great sorrow and grief;
his heart was so distressed he wished for death—how could he be parted from his beloved wife?
His son’s anguish was extreme, like a mountain elephant caught in a snare.
Upon hearing these words, his close friend immediately replied to him, saying:
"The reason one begets a son is for him to manage the family estate and seek wealth from all directions to provide for his parents; if he does not labor, by what means would he live?"
"Even if one were in the heavens, one would still find no peace, let alone in the human realm!
Having heard his father’s command and received the exhortations of the multitude, he immediately shed tears of sorrow, beat his chest with both hands, and set out on his journey with solemn resolve.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Friends and kinsmen all exhorted him together; Yet he received his father’s instruction with a display of formal conduct.
Wounded by desire as if pierced by an arrow, His heart harbored thoughts of his wife with deep resentment."
His mind constantly thought of his wife, never leaving her from his heart; he went to purchase travel provisions and soon returned to his kingdom, traveling with joy:
"I shall see her now; it will not be long!"
Morning and evening he thought of his wife; as soon as he arrived home, he asked where she was.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Engaged in trade for my livelihood, traveling back and forth, My heart constantly yearns for my beloved wife."

Having arrived home, he first asked: "Where is my wife now? His wife, her heart filled with sorrow for her husband, was one whose merit from past lives was meager; she had fallen slightly ill, her life hanging by a thread.

Her body was covered with various kinds of sores from which pus and blood flowed. She suffered from chills and fever, as well as epilepsy. Her abdomen swelled until it dried up, her upper body gasped for breath and burned with heat, and her face, hands, and feet were swollen. Countless flies settled upon her body; with disheveled hair and emaciated like a hungry ghost, she lay upon a bed of straw in tattered rags.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"He was the sole beloved of his husband’s heart, Yet by the calamity of past karma and meager merit,
He contracted countless ailments and lay upon his bed, Deprived of his fine seat and cast upon the ground."
Thereupon the husband entered the house and asked his people where his wife was.
The maidservant, filled with shame and tears, wept sorrowfully and replied to him:
"O worthy master, your wife is on such-and-such a terrace."
He immediately ascended to the upper gallery to see him; his appearance had changed in a way never seen before!

This countenance was so hideous it could not be beheld with the eyes; all feelings of love, desire, and affection were forever exhausted without remainder, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of pleasure, but only a sense of total weariness and loathing such that he no longer wished to see him again.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Observing her complexion, I find no delight; She is like a corpse abandoned in a tomb, Emaciated and skeletal, devoid of flesh, Like water submerged in sand, having lost its luster."
The practitioner is also like this: weary of and loathing sensual desires, they give rise to the contemplation of impurity and seek to attain tranquility.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The practitioner has already left desire behind; Their weariness with the five pleasures is likewise."
It is like seeing a woman afflicted by many sores, suffering from countless ailments as she lies upon her bed.
What is meant by practicing *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and guarding the mind to seek tranquility?
Now I shall explain the method of counting the breaths.
What is meant by counting the breaths?
What is meant by "peace" (ānā)?
What is meant by *ānāpāna*?
Exhalation is *āna* (in-breath) and inhalation is *apāna* (out-breath);
following the breath as it enters and exits without other thoughts is called counting the inhalations and exhalations.
What is meant by practicing the mindfulness of counting the breath so as to attain tranquility?
There are four practices of counting the breath and maintaining mindfulness, which are free from the two types of defilement and possess the sixteen stages of special excellence.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
“The practitioner who seeks tranquility Should know the inhalation and exhalation of *ānāpāna*.
Free from the two defects and understanding the four matters, They shall possess the sixteen extraordinary transformations.”
What are the four matters?
First is counting the breaths; second is following the breath; third is cessation and contemplation; fourth is returning to purity.
Thereupon, a verse says:
One should employ counting the breaths and following their characteristics; thus one contemplates all the myriad things in the world.
Through the practice of returning to purity, one restrains the mind and stabilizes the intention by means of the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the two defects?
Counting the breaths as either too long or too short constitutes these two defects.
One should abandon these two matters.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Counting the breaths, whether long or short, If inverted and lacking proper sequence, This is merely *ānāpāna-smṛti*;
Only by casting it aside are the two flaws abandoned."

What are the sixteen stages of special excellence? One knows when the breath is long; one also knows when it is short. One knows when the breath moves the body; one knows when the breath is tranquil and relaxed. One knows when joy is encountered; one knows when serenity is met. One knows the direction in which the mind inclines; one knows when the mind is pliant. One knows what the mind perceives; one knows when the mind is joyful. One knows when the mind is subdued; one knows when the mind is liberated. One knows when one perceives impermanence; one knows when there is desirelessness. One knows when one contemplates stillness; one knows when one perceives the path of progress.
These are the sixteen special excellences of counting the breaths.
On this subject, a verse says:
To discern the length and brevity of the counted breaths, And to understand when the inhalation and exhalation move the body.
Harmonizing one’s conduct and establishing its essence, Rejoicing in such experiences as these;
Understanding peace constitutes the sixth, The resolve and practice are called the seventh, which brings the mind to harmony; The bodily practice is named the eighth.
That which the mind perceives and understands, through this one attains joy;
by subduing the mind, one brings it to concentration; with mastery, one causes it to proceed accordingly.
When impermanent desires are extinguished, one should contemplate these three matters.
To know the direction toward which practice leads is the "Sixteen Special Victories.
What is meant by "counting the breaths"?

If a practitioner sits in a secluded place where there are no people, maintains an undistracted mind, and counts the inhalations and exhalations from one to ten—starting from one and proceeding to two—and should the mind become distracted, returns to counting from one to nine, and should the mind again become distracted, returns once more to counting, this is called "counting the breaths."

The practitioner thus practices counting the breath day and night; after one month or one year, they attain the state where ten breaths are counted without the mind becoming distracted in the interim.
On this, a verse says:
"Self-possessed and immovable like a mountain, Counting the inhalations and exhalations until reaching ten."
Day and night, month after month, year after year, without ceasing, one should practice guarding the counting of breaths in this manner.
Once the counting of breaths is stabilized, one should practice "following" (anugata).
It is like a person walking ahead, with another following behind like a shadow.
Practicing in this manner, one follows the inhalation and exhalation of the breath without any other thoughts.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Counting the breath, the mind becomes settled and free; Counting the breath’s entry and exit is the practice."
The mind follows [the breath] without distraction; counting the breaths to subdue the mind is called "following.
When the practitioner has attained this following, at that time they should practice contemplation.
Just as a cowherd stands to one side and watches from afar as the cattle graze;
so too should the practitioner, from the initial counting of breaths until the final culmination, observe them all.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a cowherd goes from afar to observe, Watching over his herd upon the meadow;
So too is the practice of breath-restraint: Guarding the mind as he does—this is called contemplation."
When the practitioner has already accomplished this contemplation, they should further return to purity.
Just as a gatekeeper sitting at the gate observes and recognizes all those entering and leaving;
so too does the practitioner fix the mind on the tip of the nose, observing the counting of breaths and knowing their inhalation and exhalation.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a gatekeeper sits and watches people entering and leaving,
remaining in one place without moving, yet observing and knowing the number of all who pass."
When counting the breath with single-minded focus, observe the mind as it enters and exits;
practice in this same way, and through counting the breath, one will be established in purity again.
What is meant by "counting long"?
To count prematurely before the breath has ceased, or to say "two" before the breath has even reached the nose, is called counting too long.
Thus, the verse says:
Before there has been any response, One counts the incoming and outgoing breaths.
To count one as two—such is not a valid count.
What is meant by a short count?
Two breaths constitute one.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"When the breath reaches the nose and returns again to the navel,
counting two breaths as one— this constitutes a loss in the count."
What is meant by counting the breaths and knowing when they are long?
The practitioner, from the initial counting of the breaths, observes them according to their slowness or speed, examining and weighing their course;
knowing the inhalation and exhalation and knowing their duration—this is what constitutes a long breath.
Counting short breaths is also like this.
Thereupon, a verse says:
When counting long breaths one knows them, The returning of the breath is also thus.
If one reflects in this manner, it is called "observing the length and shortness of the breath.
What is meant by "counting the breath and knowing when the body moves"?
It means observing all the inhalations and exhalations within the body.
Exhalation is also like this.
What is meant by "knowing the body's harmony through counting"?

When first beginning to breathe, if the body is weary and overcome by drowsiness, or if the physical frame feels heavy, one should discard these states and count the breaths with single-minded concentration.
Counting the breath while returning [to the body] is likewise thus.
What is meant by "knowing joy as soon as it is encountered while counting the breath"?
It refers to the state of joy that arises when one is counting the breath.
The breath enters in this manner.
What is meant by "knowing tranquility when it is encountered through counting"?
At the time of first counting the breath, one attains tranquility and stability.
The breath enters in this manner.
What is meant by "knowing the direction in which the mind proceeds through counting the breath"?
One gives rise to the perception of counting the breath and contemplates all mental perceptions.
Inhalation is likewise.
What is meant by "knowing the counting of breaths as the mind becomes pliant"?
One begins by forming the perception of inhalation, discerning that perception, and then counts the breaths accordingly.
The same applies to the inhalation.
What is meant by "the mind being aware of and cognizing the counting of breaths"?
First, one forms the perception of the breath; then, through the consciousness that recognizes all meditative observations (*vipaśyanā*), one counts the breaths.
The breath enters in this manner.
What is meant by "knowing joy while counting the breath"?
When first counting the breath, if the mind is not joyful, one should encourage and inspire it to be glad so as to follow the exhalation.
Inhalation is thus.
What is meant by "knowing the exhalation as the mind is suppressed"?
If the mind is unsettled, one forcibly suppresses it to bring it to stillness and then counts the breaths.
Inhalation is likewise.
What is meant by "knowing the liberation of the mind"?
If, upon exhaling, the mind is unwilling to be liberated, one transforms and subdues it so that it attains transcendence, and thus counts the exhalations.
Inhalation is thus.
What is meant by "knowing impermanence through counting the breaths"?
To see that all breaths lack permanence is what constitutes exhalation.
Inhalation is thus.
What is meant by "knowing immediately that there is no desire for exhalation"?
Seeing the arising and ceasing of the breath, one thus becomes free from desire; this is called observing exhalation with freedom from desire and knowing it immediately.
Inhalation is likewise.
What is meant by "observing cessation and knowing the counting"?
When the breath goes out, one observes its extinction; this is "observing cessation and knowing the exhalation."
Inhalation is thus.
What is meant by "seeing the path and counting the breaths so as to know for oneself"?

One sees the place where the exhaled breath ceases; having observed this, the mind immediately becomes detached from defilements. Through detachment and freedom from desire, one abandons the three bases, and the will is liberated. To guard this intention is what constitutes counting the breaths.
Exhalation and inhalation are thus explained as the sixteen stages of special excellence (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*).

The reason a practitioner contemplates the inhalation and exhalation is to seek tranquility so as to cause the mind to abide in concentration. From that tranquility, two types of persons obtain [the fruit]:
first, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), and second, disciples of the Buddha (*buddha-śrāvaka*).
What is meant by an ordinary person seeking tranquility?
It is the desire to cause the mind to abide and to remove the veils of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-nīvaraṇa*).
For what reason does one wish to eliminate the afflictions of these veils?
It is for the sake of attaining the first dhyāna.
Why does one seek the foremost dhyāna? It is because one desires to obtain the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā).
What is meant by a disciple of the Buddha seeking tranquility?
The reason for seeking it is the desire to attain gentleness. Why seek gentleness?
One who wishes to attain the stage of the Summit (mūrdhan) perceives that the five aggregates are empty and entirely not-self; this is called the stage of the Summit.
For what reason does one seek the stage of the Summit?
Having seen the Four Noble Truths, one proceeds toward the patience regarding the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
For what reason does one seek this patience regarding the Dharma?
It is because one desires to attain the supreme Dharma of the world.
For what reason does one seek the supreme Dharma of the world?
It is because one wishes to know that all phenomena are entirely suffering, thereby gaining the ability to discern the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*).
For what reason does one wish to know the suffering of all phenomena?
Because one desires to attain the eighth station. Why is this so?
The eighth stage of resolve: it is because that person desires to reach the track of the Path (srotāpatti).
What is meant by an ordinary person attaining stillness through the causal conditions of counting the breath?

When the mind is fixed on counting the breath, with single-minded focus, undisturbed and free from other thoughts, by virtue of this, one attains stillness through that counting of the breath; through these skillful means, the five hindrances (pañca-nīvaraṇa) are all eliminated.
At that time, whether his breath enters or exits, it is always accompanied by the mind and takes its mental objects as its condition;
such is the inhalation.

When one observes the destination of the entering and exiting breaths, this is called "application" (*saṃskāra*); the joy within the mind is called "gladness" (*prīti*); that which is agreeable is called "ease" (*praśrabdhi*); when the mind is supreme and attains mastery, this is "concentration of mind" (*samādhi*); having first removed the five hindrances, the mind follows understanding and thereby becomes detached from clinging.
What is meant by "detachment"?
It is to distance oneself from various perceptions, cravings, and unwholesome dharmas.

With such mindfulness and joyful tranquility, the mind attains single-pointed concentration (*ekāgratā*), severing the five hindrances and perfecting the five factors. By means of counting the breaths, one brings forth the five virtues and attains the first dhyāna.

Having attained the first dhyāna, he practices it without abandoning it; the first dhyāna is perfectly peaceful, firm, and immovable. Desiring to seek supernormal powers, he sets his will upon the bases of psychic power: with the divine eye he sees clearly, with the divine ear he hears through, he knows his past lives, he knows the thoughts of others, and he acts with sovereign mastery.
For example, just as a goldsmith can freely fashion from purple-gold ornaments such as necklaces, rings, armlets, and anklets, all of which are produced according to his will;
so too does one who has attained mastery over the four dhyānas act with such freedom—this constitutes the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
What is meant by a disciple of the Buddha counting the inhalations and exhalations to attain tranquility?

The practitioner sits in a quiet, uninhabited place, withdrawing the mind so that it does not scatter. With the mouth closed, they focus their energy on observing the inhalations and exhalations: as the breath enters through the nose, it turns back toward the throat, then reaches the navel, and from the navel returns to the nose.

One should examine this: the exhalation is distinct and the inhalation is different; let the mind follow the breath, entering and exiting in accordance with it, so that the heart is not distracted. By means of this counting of the breath, the will becomes settled and tranquility is attained.

In this interval, he is forever free from other thoughts, contemplating only the virtues of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha, as well as the meaning of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and thereby attains joy; this is called serenity.
It is like a person blowing on a fire to warm their face; the fire does not touch the face, but only its heat.
That heat of the fire cannot be produced by blowing; one should understand that gentleness is just like this.
What are the dharmas of "warmth"?
For one who has not yet perfected the roots of goodness, there are nine matters:

there is mild pliancy, inferior pliancy, and superior pliancy; there is middling [pliancy], middling-middling, and superior-middling; and there is superior pliancy, middling-superior, and supreme-superior pliancy.
To know that which is subtly gentle and softly gentle is called the root of goodness of mildness.
That which is among the lower-middle, the middle-middle, and the upper-middle is called the root of goodness of the Pinnacle of Dharma.
That which is lower-upper, middle-upper, and upper-upper in gentleness is called the truth of the dharma-patience of gentleness.
That which is the upper-of-the-middle is called the honored dharma of the mundane world!
These nine matters constitute the meaning of the roots of goodness; therefore, as these are mundane affairs, the various outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been exhausted.

If one practices and attains a practice of gentleness (*sauratya*), one should fix the perception of counting the breaths and, by means of this, maintain focused mindfulness. If the breath returns, the mind follows that breath without any other thought;

if the breath goes out, one knows the coming and going of the breath. The mind enters into the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha, and regarding suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), its cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*), one remains as if in a state of gentleness.
When that mind becomes increasingly superior, it is called the stage of the "summit" (*mūrdhan*).

It is like a person standing on a high mountain peak observing the four directions: some are ascending the mountain, while others are descending; likewise, some enter the path of the noble ones (*āryamārga*), while others remain in the realm of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*).
If a practitioner has already attained the stage of the "Summit" (mūrdhan) but then falls back into the level of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), it is truly a cause for great concern.

It is like a mountain torrent flowing with such violent speed that it stirs up crooked and crosswise waves; suppose a person wishes to cross it, enters the water to swim toward the opposite shore, but is turned back by eddies and held in the middle of the stream. Becoming exhausted and utterly spent, he eventually sinks into the waves and is submerged at the bottom.
That man thinks to himself that his death is certain beyond doubt, and those staying on the bank feel sorrow and grief on his behalf.

Practicing in this manner, one may have already found an enlightened teacher and awaken day and night while sitting in the full lotus posture, wearing coarse clothing, eating poor food, and sitting upon a mat of grass, thereby afflicting the body.

Yet, if such practice is instead constrained by the surging waves of birth and death, if one is cast into the bonds of affection and unable to remain single-minded, and if one sinks into the flowing pool of manifold thoughts from beginning to end, how can one attain the clarity of the Way?
Therefore, the practitioner should take upon himself the burden of this sorrow.

It is like a guide who, having brought much wealth and treasure, traverses the perilous paths of the wilderness; yet, just as he is about to reach home, he suddenly encounters wicked bandits and loses his property, leaving all the people in deep distress!
One who practices in this way should harbor such anxiety.

It is like a farmer who has sown the five grains; when the stalks and fruit are flourishing and the harvest is imminent, if they are suddenly struck down by hail and frost, leaving nothing but the stubble, that person will be filled with grief.
So it is for one who practices: having attained the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) and yet remaining within the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), one should feel deep dejection.

Having attained the stage of the "Summit" (mūrdhan), one may yet fall back; or, encountering evil friends, one may dwell upon sensual desires, perceiving the impure as pure and the pure as impure. One may delight in wandering far and wide, failing to achieve single-minded concentration. Or, one may encounter chronic illness or face the scarcity of grain, suffering from hunger and destitution such that one cannot even sustain oneself. Or, one may dwell on household matters—parents, brothers, wife, children, and kinsmen—or remain seated amidst the clamor and bustle of the world.

Having attained the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) yet not yet realized the fruit of the Path, old age approaches and his mind becomes deluded. Suddenly afflicted by a debilitating illness, his life hangs by a thread; he no longer has faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, suffering (*duḥkha*), its origin (*samudaya*), its cessation (*nirodha*), or the path (*mārga*) that he once firmly believed in.

He should practice meditative concentration (*samādhi*) but instead abandons it; he should contemplate but fails to do so, and his diligence slackens further. The teachings he originally contemplated never arise again. For these reasons, he falls back and degenerates from that stage of the Summit.

What is meant by the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) from which one does not regress? It is when that which was previously believed increases through daily faith; when the mind of fundamental concentration becomes such that it is no longer shaken; when what is contemplated is not lost; when constant observation and diligence increase further than before; and when the dharmas one contemplates are pursued with single-minded devotion without abandonment. For these reasons, one does not regress from the Summits.

Practicing in this manner, because of their single-minded dedication, their thoughts become unified; each contemplates the ultimate Dharma, never wavering from the beginning and not dwelling on the new or the old. Thus they know that the exhalation is distinct and the inhalation is different;

as these differences in inhalation and exhalation give rise to the mind, they perceive and understand them in such a way that no fear arises. This is called the "supreme among the middling" and the attainment of the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
With a mind free of conceptualization, one performs this contemplation:
"The preceding thought and the succeeding thought have never been confused; how do they distinguish and examine the mind as it moves back and forth?
This is called the lower degree of the superior *anulomikī-kṣānti* (receptive tolerance in accordance with the truth).
If one’s mind is devoted to focused contemplation such that the will does not waver or become disordered, this is called the supreme and middling method of compliant flexibility.
As for that patience, toward what does it accord?
When one proceeds in accordance with the Four Noble Truths and dwells with thorough discernment, the mind thereby attains purity; this is called faith (*śraddhā*).
Nevertheless, although one has obtained this, the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) has not yet been established.
Having attained this faith, the body, speech, and mind become strong; this is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Yet, one has not yet been able to perfect the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
To direct one's aspiration toward all phenomena is called having a mind (*citta*).
When the faculty of mindfulness has not yet been perfected, one unifies the mind; this is called concentration of mind.
When the faculty of concentration has not yet been perfected—
To contemplate all phenomena and discern their meanings is called wisdom (*prajñā*),
yet it does not yet constitute the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
To reckon these five factors as being directed toward the faculties (*indriya*) does not yet constitute the faculty of the path (*mārgendriya*).
Where there is mindfulness and perception, there is still a locus of existence; seeing that one is surrounded by these, the mind has not yet achieved concentration.
This is called the most supreme among the supreme mundane noble dharmas.
The practitioner should know and understand this: the place where form arises and ceases, as well as sensation, ideation, mental formations, and consciousness.
He contemplates the root of arising and ceasing, examining its causes and conditions in the past and the future;
he practices the concentration of wishlessness, entering the gates of liberation to examine the suffering of birth and death;
he reckons that these five aggregates are themselves affliction and distress, free from any doubt.
At that time, one attains the patience regarding the dharma of the cessation of suffering.
Having already seen the root of suffering, one then beholds with the eye of wisdom and eliminates the ten fetters.
What are these ten?

First is attachment to the body; second is the view of a self; third is wrong view; fourth is doubt; fifth is the loss of precepts; sixth is perplexity; seventh is craving; eighth is malice; ninth is arrogance; and tenth is delusion.

Having abandoned these ten fetters and attained this mind, one turns toward the outflow-free state and enters into right view; crossing beyond the stage of ordinary beings, one abides in the Noble Path. One does not incur the offenses of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, and shall never meet with an untimely death. One will surely realize the tracks of the Way, practicing the correct meditative absorption of the wishless samādhi, and is thus already oriented toward the gates of liberation.
Unarisen unwholesome states do not arise again, and all evils naturally come to an end;
one causes the thought of the Dharma that has not yet arisen to emerge, and brings to full completion the wholesome states that have already emerged;
when the mind is as satisfied as if its desires were fulfilled, this is called "self-indulgence" (pāricariyā).
To cause the will to be single-minded is called the samādhi of mastery over the mind.
Following this sequence—faith, mindfulness, diligence, investigation, and guarding the life-force—is what is meant by faith;
contemplating its practice is what is called the samādhi of self-mastery.

To be single-mindedly devoted to the Way and thereby attain the supernormal powers (ṛddhipāda), such that one’s cultivation of body, speech, and mind becomes vigorous—this is called the method of the concentration of diligence (vīrya-samādhi).
To focus the will and concentrate the consciousness—this is called the concentration of the mind (citta-samādhi).
To wish to enter the meaning of the Path is called examining and stabilizing the mind.
By means of this condition, one attains the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Having attained these bases of psychic power, this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The firmness of body and mind is called the faculty of diligence;
the dharmas that are contemplated constitute the faculty of mind;
the one-pointedness of the mind is called the faculty of concentration.
To be able to discern phenomena and know their destination is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
For this reason, one is fully endowed with the five faculties.

That faith which is gentle and mild is called the power of faith (*śraddhābala*); the power of diligence, the power of intention, the power of tranquility of mind, and the power of wisdom are likewise so.
To accomplish the five powers and penetrate all phenomena is the awakening factor of mindfulness;
to discern all phenomena is called the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena;
for body and mind to be firm and steadfast is called the awakening factor of energy.
To have a heart filled with joy and exultation, obtaining what one desires, is called the awakening factor of rapture (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
For body and mind to be mutually dependent, characterized by faith, pliancy, and lack of distraction, is called the awakening factor of faith (*śraddhā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
For the mind to be singularly tranquil is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
When the mind perceives the extinction of the defilements of lust, anger, and delusion, and its aspirations are fulfilled according to its wishes, this is the awakening factor of investigation.
For this reason, the seven factors of awakening are accomplished.
If one contemplates the meaning of all phenomena individually, this is called right view;
whatever thoughts one entertains that are free from deviance, this is right mindfulness;
and when body and mind are firm and steadfast, this is right effort.
To direct the mind toward the meaning of the sutras is right intention;
for the mind to be single-minded is right concentration.
When the karma created by body and mind is purified in these three ways, one then accomplishes the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path.
Within this Eightfold Noble Path, right view, right mindfulness, and right effort—these three factors belong to insight (vipaśyanā);
as for right intention and right concentration—these two factors belong to tranquility (śamatha).
This contemplation and tranquility are like two horses yoked to a single carriage moving forward.

If the untainted mind does not focus on a single dharma but enters universally into the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, then by being fully endowed with these thirty-seven dharmas, one understands suffering;
through such a process, one attains the second untainted mind.
At that time, he reflects:
"Just as the five aggregates in the desire realm are characterized by suffering, so it is likewise and no different in the form realm and the formless realm.
This is called the accomplishment of the wisdom of conforming acceptance regarding the knowledge of suffering; thus, he establishes the third untainted mind.

Having attained this practice and, by means of seeing suffering, having eliminated the eighteen fetters, one transcends the realm of form and surpasses the realm of formlessness; thus, for one whose wisdom is appropriate and compliant, the fourth untainted mind is immediately attained.
Having attained the four untainted minds, he transcended the defects of the arduous suffering of the triple world and immediately realized for himself:
"I have already crossed over affliction; being free from all distress, I have attained liberation from suffering."
He then reflected to himself:
"From what does the root of suffering arise?

It arises from the net of attachment rooted in affection (*sneha*). Having practiced this affection for a long time, I have encountered calamities until now; if I were to forever uproot the root of affection, there would be no further afflictions."
"Once one has abandoned affection and attachment, from what could delight in agreeable things arise?
This is called the patience of understanding, abandoning, and severing the origin of phenomena; this is the fifth untainted mind."

Having eliminated all habitual attachments within the realm of desire, one then casts off the seven fetters; thus, one knows how to uproot the afflictions of the realm of desire—this is called the sixth untainted mind.
The practitioner reflects to himself:
"As for the root of the realm of form (rūpadhātu), from what does it originally arise?
Contemplating its source with discernment, I see that it arises from desire."
To delight in liberation from affection and to find joy in what is agreeable—this is the seventh untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).

By means of this practice, one transcends the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*); as for the twelve fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), the mind follows and cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*) regarding them—this is the eighth untainted mind.
These are called the eight meanings of the Buddha’s first son.
At that time, he thought to himself:
"I have seen the three realms and eliminated the accumulation of suffering; I have no craving for desire—this is what is called peace and security."
Thus, delighting in tranquility and finding it pleasing and sweet, this is the patience regarding the wisdom of the dharma of cessation; this is the ninth untainted mind.
Having attained this realization and seen the fundamental cessation, one eliminates the bonds of the seven fetters within the desire realm; this is the tenth untainted mind.
Then he reflects to himself:
"If one does not cling to the realm of form or the formless realm, this is called tranquility.
This is the eleventh untainted mind.
Thus, having eliminated the doubts regarding the twelve fetters and already transcended these afflictions, one attains the wisdom of total extinction; this is the twelfth untainted mind.
At that time, he thought to himself: "How marvelous!
Such is the way the Buddha, the World-Honored One, understands the Dharma; through this principle of the Path, one comes to know the suffering of the desire realm and thereby abandons it."

Knowing that [suffering] arises from habitual tendencies, one abandons those tendencies and attains their total extinction; through this, one enters the patience regarding the dharma-wisdom of the path—this is the thirteenth untainted mind.

At that time, by perceiving the realm of desire through the Path, one abandons the eight fetters; having departed from these, one shall subsequently attain this flourishing wisdom of the Dharma. This is the fourteenth mind of outflowlessness.

At that moment, he thought to himself that this was unprecedented; through the practice of this path, he understood the suffering of the realm of form and the formless realm, eliminated all habitual tendencies, and realized cessation—this is the fifteenth mind free from outflows (*anāsrava-citta*).

The Path follows from his resolve in eliminating the twelve fetters; having eliminated these fetters within the realms of form and formlessness, he then gives rise to the wisdom of the Path—this constitutes the sixteenth untainted mind.
At that moment, one eliminates the eighty-eight fetters; one should then depart from the ten perceptions of fettering. Why is this?

Just as taking a single drop of water from a great river, the ultimate meaning of the Path is like the waters of the river, while the remainder yet to be eliminated is like that single drop; thus one establishes the track of the Path and attains the state of the Sages and Worthies.
Reborn seven times among the heavens and seven times among humans, they will forever exhaust the root of suffering.
Those who practice in this manner uproot the source of all afflictions and sever the stream of birth and death; their minds are then filled with joy.

Having crossed over the three miserable realms and refrained from committing the five heinous crimes, they remain aloof from heterodox paths. Upon meeting those of like knowledge, they do not seek worldly glory or hope from outside teachers.

The virtue of the Benefactor of the Multitudes does not undergo change from beginning to end; he has never transgressed the precepts throughout seven cycles of rebirth, and beholding countless lights, he rejoices day and night.

It is as if there were a person who, avoiding a land of famine, arrives in a country of abundance and low prices; one who escapes danger to find peace, or one released from prison, or like a patient whose illness has been cured, his heart leaps with joy.
Practicing in this manner, one attains tranquility through *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing); those who seek stillness should practice in this way.
Thereupon, a verse says:
"Awakening from the heavy sleep of indolence, One discerns the moments when the breath issues forth within the body."
Through the practice of mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, one attains realization; this is called the perfection of the practice of body and breath.
*The Scripture on the Stages of Practice*, Scroll Five.
*The Scripture on the Stages of Practice*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four: The Chapter on Contemplation (6). Chapter Twenty-Four: The Chapter on Contemplation.
Regarding the mark of the white hair between the eyebrows, its brilliance surpasses the light of the sun.
Like a crane soaring through the sky, there is nothing far or near that he does not see.
His body is like a lion, surpassing even the elephant of the Lord of Devas;
his shoulders and chest are broad and magnificent—I pray to bow my head before the Honored Buddha.
The arms and elbows are level and perfectly proportioned; the World-Honored One’s navel is like a swirling eddy;
his thighs, knees, calves, and shanks are like pillars of gold—one should take refuge in the Buddha and prostrate before him.
His eyes are long and beautiful like lotuses; his body is covered with fine hair like that of a peacock;
his mind always abides in tranquil stillness—I vow to take refuge in him who transcends all sages.
Regarding the practitioner, what is meant by "contemplation"?
If one goes to a secluded place, dwelling alone beneath a tree, one examines the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and perceives them as they truly are:

the concentrations on suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self. The body of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is fundamentally non-existent; among these fifty-five matters, there is nothing to be craved, nor is there any locus.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"By practicing patience, one attains the contemplation of dharmas;
Examining the origin from which the five aggregates arise, One perceives the past, the future, and the present, And through analytical exposition, explains them in fifty-five ways."
What are the fifty-five matters?
This body is like a mass of foam, incapable of being grasped by the hand; this body is like the ocean, never satiated with the five desires;
this body is like a river flowing toward the deep sea, heading toward old age, sickness, and death; this body is like excrement, abandoned by those of clear wisdom.
This body is like a sandcastle, quickly subject to erosion and destruction; this body is like the borderlands, where one frequently encounters enemies and bandits;
this body is like a realm of ghosts, devoid of any protector; this body is like a wall of bones smeared with flesh and drenched in blood;
this body stands upon marrow bound together by sinews; this body is like a destitute man, the dwelling place of lust, anger, and ignorance.
This body is like a wilderness that deludes the foolish; this body is like a perilous path where one constantly loses wholesome dharmas;
this body is like a tomb of bricks established by the hundred-and-eight cravings; this body is like a cracked vessel that is constantly leaking;
this body is like a painted jar filled with impurities; this body is like a latrine from which nine orifices constantly flow.
This body is like a water channel, entirely filled with filth; this body is like an illusion that deludes the ignorant who do not recognize the true reality;
this body is like garlic, which poisons both body and mind when burned; this body is like a dilapidated house, decaying from the consumption of food and drink;
this body is like a large dwelling infested with many kinds of worms; this body is like a perforated vessel through which purity and impurity pass in and out.
This body is like a withered flower, swiftly approaching decrepitude; this body is like a carriage, accompanied by impermanence;
this body is like dew, unable to endure for long; this body is like a festering sore, from which impurities flow out;
this body is like a blind man, who does not see the nature of forms; this body is like a house, the dwelling place of the four hundred and four diseases.
This body is like a leaking vessel where all manner of impurities and defilements flow; this body is like a chest inhabited by venomous snakes;
this body is like an empty fist used to deceive small children; this body is like a cemetery that strikes fear into those who see it;
this body is like a serpent whose fire of anger burns constantly; this body is like a madman, the source of the eighteen knots.
This body is like an ancient palace dragged away by the demon of death; this body is like a copper coin covered on the outside with gold leaf and wrapped in leather;
this body is like an empty village inhabited by the six sense-faculties;
this body is like a hungry ghost constantly seeking food and drink; this body is like a wild elephant harboring old age, sickness, and death; this body is like a dead dog.
It is constantly covered over; this body is like an enemy whose mind harbors perpetual resentment.
This body is like a plantain tree, lacking solidity. This body is like a wrecked ship, deluded by the sixty-two views.
This body is like a house of lewdness, which makes no distinction between good and evil. This body is like a decaying pavilion, on the verge of collapse, regarding wholesome thoughts.
This body is like a throat obstruction, with impurities and filth within; this body is of no benefit, harboring afflictions both internally and externally.
This body is like a house that has no master, being harmed by lust, anger, and ignorance. This body is without rescue, constantly encountering peril and ruin.
This body is without protection, falling prey to manifold diseases. This body is without refuge, being pressed by the power of death.
This body is like a lute that produces sound because of its strings; this body is like a drum, a covering of leather and wood whose essence is fundamentally empty;
this body is like unbaked clay, lacking any solidity; this body is like a city of ash, destroyed by wind and rain, returning to old age, sickness, death, and decay.

By means of these fifty-five matters, one contemplates the impurities of the body: this body is deceptive and treacherous, harboring no constancy; it does not trust those who are close or affectionate, yet pities them only to abandon them, making no distinction between kin and stranger.
It is like a dream, an illusion, a shadow, an echo, or a mirage that suddenly manifests;

or like an enemy whom one constantly honors, serving and providing for with the hope of gaining his favor—bathing, combing, feeding, clothing, and providing comfortable beds and bedding according to one's convenience—yet it drags a person toward the calamities of poverty, old age, sickness, and death.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"This body is constantly fed and nourished, And the five desires are allowed full indulgence;
One seeks comfort from it as if from a kinsman, Yet when examined with truth, it is a veritable enemy."
Without rescue and without protection, always harboring a lack of reciprocity, it drags people toward calamity and harm, leading them into birth, old age, sickness, and death.
After a person has died, the body shall all rot and decay, becoming food for dogs and beasts; or perhaps it is seen being burned, with the bleached bones scattered upon the ground.

Based on these countless dharmas, one should contemplate this body as being like a festering ulcer, or like an arrowhead lodged in the body that has not been extracted, or like a person condemned to death at the place of execution.
To examine the body and its manifold afflictions as arising from birth and ending in death;
that which one greedily clings to is called form (*rūpa*);
to observe the body as soft and to experience its safety and peril is called feeling (*vedanā*).
That which is clearly known is called perception (saṃjñā);
mental volition is called formations (saṃskāra);
and the differentiation of the various realms of existence is called consciousness (vijñāna).
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The eye perceives forms as its primary object; This body attains its state through fundamental conditions.
Through qualities such as suppleness, one accomplishes practice, And with a mind free of form, one examines all virtues."

For example, suppose there is a stagnant pool by the side of a great river; many elephants enter it to bathe, drink water, and eat the stalks, flowers, and blossoms of the blue lotuses and water lilies therein, and then they withdraw and depart.

At that time, the tracks remained visible in the mud and sand—large and small, wide and long—and hunters, cowherds, and those traveling along the road carrying firewood and grass saw these footprints and said:
"A great herd of elephants has passed through this place."
"Though one does not see the elephant, by observing its tracks, one knows that a herd of elephants has passed through this place.

So it is with the aggregates of non-perception (asaṃjñā-skandha), feeling (vedanā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna); what they have produced is subtle, and the same is true for perception (saṃjñā), formations, and consciousness."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as on a riverbank, where there are footprints in the sand,
By seeing the traces of an elephant's passage, One knows that a herd of elephants has passed."
Thus one calculates [sensations of] smoothness and so forth, up to the mental application of consciousness regarding phenomena;
much is illuminated therein—the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing.
Thus, these various perceptions and thoughts of the formless realm all depend upon form; only then do phenomena possessing form exist.
It is like two bundles of reeds standing leaning against one another.
On this point, a verse says:
The formless depends on much; Form depends on the formless.
Just as branches are attached to and connected with a tree, so too are name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Those formless phenomena depend upon the differentiated existence of form; yet when form exists, there is likewise no dependence on or attachment to the formless.

Just as there must first be a drum before a sound is produced, the sound and the drum are each distinct and different; the drum does not exist within the sound, nor does the sound exist within the drum.
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are likewise distinct and do not coincide; yet, by depending upon one another, they come into being.
The formless aggregates lack autonomy and do not arise through one's own power.
It is like two people, one born blind and the other born lame, who wish to travel to another country.
The blind have eyes that are darkened, so they see nothing forever and do not know where to go;
the lame lack two feet, so they cannot travel.
The blind man said to the lame one:
"I have no sight in my eyes, yet I have feet that can walk; however, my vision is so dim that I cannot distinguish east from west.
You, on the other hand, are lame and crippled, unable to come or go; yet you possess clear eyesight and can see where one advances or retreats, and the direction in which one's steps are taken."
"Now we two shall rely upon one another and travel together to another country.
Thus, the lame man mounted the blind man's shoulders and they set out; this was neither through the power of the lame man nor the virtue of the blind man.
Form-dharmas are thus; they cannot stand alone.
Formless dharmas are likewise; they depend upon one another in succession.
On this point, a verse says:
Contemplate that all phenomena do not arise independently;
whether they are material or immaterial, they revolve within the world by depending on one another, like the blind and the lame riding each other as they travel.
Name and form depend upon one another for their transformation, like the sound of a drum or an arrow released from a bowstring; they rely on each other, neither merging nor separating.

All phenomena are likewise so: they are formed through causes and conditions, lacking inherent power or sovereignty, arising entirely from conditions; it is only when the circumstances are met that things manifest.

If one practices in this manner and examines the root of phenomena, one will know that there is arising and ceasing: that which was originally non-existent suddenly manifests by itself, and then again vanishes and perishes;
that which has no birth arises, and that which has no origination originates—all of these return to impermanence.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
The five aggregates are eternally subject to emptiness; Relying on formations, they are frail and weak.
They are brought together through causes and conditions, Mutually supporting one another in succession.
Arising and ceasing, there is no constancy; flourishing and decline are like floating clouds.
The phenomena of body, mind, perception, and thought—all such things are subject to destruction.
The practitioner constantly contemplates their impermanence through four matters:

First, all things that arise return to impermanence; second, that which is produced has no accumulation; third, though all things perish and come to an end, they do not undergo depletion or diminution; fourth, although persons and things all return to decay and ruin, they do not utterly cease to exist.
For this reason, that which was not born is born, and that which was not exhausted is exhausted.
When observing all phenomena, one should examine their arising and ceasing, their existence and extinction;
by viewing them in this way, there is nothing one does not know, and one is able to perceive everything without anything remaining unclear.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Though sentient beings are born, They neither accumulate nor perish;
Nor do they abandon their manifold forms; Though they pass away, they do not cease to exist."
Although they continue in succession, all arise from four causes and conditions;
observing all things thus, one transcends and passes beyond beginning and end.
Suppose one practices with single-minded reflection:
"All things throughout the east, west, south, and north are subject to impermanence; they are restless and unstable, arising only to perish and all tending toward emptiness.
From the moment of their initial birth, the phenomena of impermanence—the afflictions of old age, sickness, and death—constantly follow them."
"One who practices this contemplation does not cling to the three realms, does not take pleasure in the four modes of birth, and does not dwell within the five consciousnesses.
Their mind does not enter the abodes of the nine spirits; even if they are born again, they eliminate the three fetters:
first, sensual desire; second, violation of the precepts; and third, doubt."
Thus one accomplishes the tracks of the Path and proceeds toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), just as flowing rivers converge and return to the sea.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Observing that all things arise and move, One should realize that they must all pass away."
Bound by the fetters of desire, all things are impermanent.
Those who wish to cross over the world must completely abandon all attachments to desire;
this is called the path to the goal, which flows downward toward the unconditioned.
The practitioner contemplates in this manner, examining his own body as being like a venomous snake.
To employ a metaphor:

suppose a city were to catch fire, and within it there was a wealthy man serving as a leader for the multitude; seeing his house burning and collapsing, he became deeply distressed and thought to himself:
"What plan can I devise to bring out the essential items from within?
He then withdrew to reflect:
"I have a chest containing various treasures hidden in a certain room; it is filled with fine moon-bright pearls and exquisite, rare objects of immeasurable value, beyond all calculation."

Filled with fear and intending to move forward, yet dreading being burned by the fire, he craved the treasure and disregarded his own life and limb; he rushed headlong into the flames and reached the chest containing the jewels, where there was also a chest containing a venomous serpent.

At that time, the guide, fearing the intense fire and having his eyes stung by the smoke, became mentally confused and lost awareness; failing to examine the situation carefully, he mistakenly took a basket containing venomous snakes and fled with it in his arms, while the robbers followed behind him, pursuing him in an attempt to seize it back.
Just as he saw the bandits pursuing him, he fled; the bandits pursued him relentlessly, shouting from afar:
"If you come to us like this, we shall harm and kill you! If you set down the basket, there is hope for your life; if you do not set it down, your life is in jeopardy."
Seeing that the bandits were pressing close to him, the leader thought that he would lose his wealth and treasures and would not even save his life; he then reflected further:
"I shall open my basket, take the most essential items from within, place them in my bosom, leave the rest behind, and then depart in safety."
Upon opening the chest and looking inside, he saw only venomous snakes; he then realized that these were not jewels, but merely vipers!
Practice is like this: having already attained the Truth of the Path, one sees all forms as being just like venomous snakes. For this reason, one attains contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);
those who seek contemplation should conduct their investigation in this manner.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when a blazing fire is burning, a person hastily takes out an essential vessel,
only to clutch it instead within a chest of venomous snakes, mistaking them for precious treasures."
Opening the chest, one sees only worn-out rags and venomous vipers filling its interior;
at that moment, one immediately discards it, for only then does one realize they were not treasures.
Practice is to be reckoned in this way: observe with discernment that, fundamentally, there is nothing to be reckoned as real.
By understanding the Four Noble Truths, one views the body as being like four venomous snakes.
Practicing such contemplation of the truths and constantly mindful of the Way and its Virtue, one attains the unconditioned;
having eliminated suffering, one finally obtains peace.
Having crossed over himself and entered the gate of liberation, he frees others from all defilements;
for this reason, he has explained it in detail, contemplating the dharma of impermanence.
Valiant in the power of goodness, his radiant face is like a golden flower.
With supernormal powers surpassing the swift wind, he travels freely wherever he wishes.
His bodily virtues are perfected and infinite; disciplined and able to practice forbearance, the Buddha delights in the peace of precepts and meditative concentration.
The multitude returns to him with devotion and bows their heads in homage.
His gait is measured and serene, free from the dust of delusion; his virtue is bottomless, and his aspirations are peaceful.
The Buddha is peerless and eternally unattached; I vow to take refuge in the Honored One who is beyond compare.
The Buddha takes the Dharma of skillful means as his bow, With which he subdues the enemies of evil;
Having utterly eliminated the dust of afflictions and all defilements, I vow to take refuge in the Buddha and pay him homage with single-minded devotion.
That practitioner, having already attained the path of entry, perceives that all five kinds of pleasure ultimately revert to impermanence, yet he is unable to eliminate them entirely. Why is this?
Because he still maintains thoughts regarding forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tactile sensations.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Having attained accomplishment as one on the path, Contemplating wisdom, he understands that the five pleasures are non-existent;
He views the realm of desire as a frightened horse, Yet his mind does not cling to form, for the continuity remains unsevered."
For example, it was like the son of a brahmin who, being clean and fond of his own purity, went behind the house and suddenly soiled his finger.
He went to a goldsmith and said, "This finger is defiled and impure; burn it with fire!"
The goldsmith admonished him, saying: "Do not give rise to such a thought.

There are other expedient means to remove this impurity: rub it with ash and soil, or wash it with water. Even if I were to burn you with fire, you would not be able to endure it; the burning pain of the fire would touch your own body even more severely than before."
Upon hearing this, the brahmin’s son immediately conceived anger and reviled the goldsmith:
"Do not judge others by your own mind; unable to endure it yourself, you claim that others cannot bear it either."
I have no desires; yet because my hands are defiled with filth, I dare not walk upon the road, fearing that others might touch me.

Should I happen to draw near to people, I possess learning in the foundations of the Three Classics and knowledge of the Six Arts. I am trained in discourse and fully understand what is appropriate; I can examine the myriad things and distinguish their meanings, sequences, and chapters.
