I am cognizant of the Three Luminaries, as well as celestial phenomena, astronomy, and geography.
He studied the sixty-four marks [of physiognomy] to discern people’s fortunes, lifespans, poverty or wealth, nobility or lowliness, their dwelling places, and their fields and houses;
he understood the cries of a hundred species of birds and could foresee calamities and transformations. He perceived that other lands were filled with vengeful rebels seeking to endanger this realm;

he recognized the portents of solar and lunar eclipses, the irregularity of wind and rain, and the appearance of anomalous stars. He could distinguish the features of beautiful women, those clad in blue or crimson, and the characteristics of men and women, oxen, horses, chickens, and sheep.

He foreknows the abundance or scarcity of the five grains due to drought or flood; he recognizes the movements and positions of the stars and constellations; he distinguishes between water and drought, and the extent of their decline or increase;

he divines great floods and the damage they may cause; he observes the eclipses, risings, and settings of the sun and moon; he discerns whether a fetus in the womb will be male or female; he is proficient in military law and the affairs of combat;
and he possesses profound knowledge of both ancient and modern times.
He observed the positions of the five planets and the movement of Mars; he understood the twelve periods and the hundred *ke* of day and night;
he was proficient in the art of medicine, knowing how to treat wind-cold, fever, sores, and ailments of the young;
and he knew the paths by which the sun and moon travel, as well as what each of their color transformations portended.

Regarding the anomalies of mountain collapses, earthquakes, and falling stars, as well as the deities presiding over the various lunar mansions, the scholars of antiquity were all able to discern them;
there was nothing they could not penetrate. When a comet appeared, how could they fail to calculate what kind of omen it portended!
"For what reason have you defiled my finger with impurity? Do not linger; follow my words and remove the filth from your finger!

Upon hearing this, the goldsmith heated his tongs until they were glowing red and used them to pluck the finger from him. The youth, unable to endure the burning pain, pulled his finger toward his mouth.

The goldsmith laughed heartily and said to the youth, "You pride yourself on being intelligent and widely learned, one who understands the past and the present with complete clarity, pure and without blemish; why then do you now hold a defiled finger in your mouth?"
The youth replied:
"When one has not experienced pain, one perceives the impurity of the finger; yet as soon as one encounters the poison of fire, one forgets the filth of the finger.

The traces of the Way are like this: though one has long practiced amidst the defects of craving and desire through the night, the moment one is separated from sensual passion, the mind of lust is stirred upon seeing beautiful forms."
Why is this? Because his faculties are only partially restrained and he has not yet attained the concentration of exhaustion.
On this point, a verse says:

Having already seen that the desire for forms is what one has long practiced, even if one understands the meaning and reaches the tracks of the Ultimate Way, the mind continues to scent the flowers of conceptualization upon its head;
like a river flowing toward the sea, such is the nature of its will.
The seeker of the path reflected to himself:
"It is not fitting for my person to indulge in sensual desire as do other ordinary worldlings.

He spoke of the defilement of passion and found delight in the absence of desire; he extinguished the blazing fire of craving and practiced the contemplation of impurity day and night without ceasing.
One who practices in this way has diminished lust, anger, and delusion, and attains the path of coming and going; returning to this world only once more, they sever the source of suffering.

Having attained the stage of coming and going, they give rise to no further defilement regarding all sensual desires; lust, anger, and delusion are thin, yet their minds have not yet severed the causes of affliction and distress that stem from existence.

For example, suppose there is a man who has a wife of beautiful countenance and flawless features, her body adorned with various necklaces and ornaments; though the husband loves and respects her greatly for her beauty, she is actually a lust-demon and not a human being!
They subsist solely on human flesh and blood as their food and drink.
Someone said to her husband:
"Your wife is a rākṣasī; she feeds on flesh and blood."
Her husband was a man of no faith; though she spoke to him repeatedly, his mind became increasingly suspicious and he desired to test her.

At night, he feigned sleep and let out a snoring sound as if he were truly asleep. Thinking he was fast asleep, the wife rose furtively and went out of the city to the cemetery. Her husband followed after her and saw her take off her clothes and various precious ornaments, then put on a mask. Her facial expression turned hideous, long fangs protruded from her mouth, flames blazed from her head, and her eyes were red like fire; she was truly terrifying to behold. She approached the corpse and, with her hands, tore away its flesh, which she bit and ate.
Upon seeing this, he realized it was not a man but a ghost; he then returned home and lay upon his bed. His wife soon followed back to her husband’s bed and lay down as before.
When her husband saw that his wife was adorned with ornaments and her countenance was upright and beautiful, he then drew near to her;
yet if he were to imagine her in a cemetery eating the flesh of the dead, his mind would immediately become loathsome and disgusted,
and he would find a way to flee in terror.
If one sees an external form that is upright, handsome, and excellent, the mind of lust is stirred;
if one explains the foul, the impurities, and the lack of purity, the mind of lust is extinguished.
On this subject, a verse says:
The transformed person sheds his human form like armor, assuming the shape of a lustful ghost to go among the tombs;
there he devours corpses as if they were rice—only then does one know him to be a rākṣasa.
One who has attained the path of going and returning reflects within his own mind:
"My three fetters in the realm of desire have already been attenuated, and what remains is but slight!
Having reached the vision of the Noble Truths, I perceive the flaws of sensual craving; since suffering is abundant and peace is meager, it is not fitting to indulge in desire."
Just as the common masses set their minds upon sensual desires, like flies clinging to a corpse, by what skillful means can I eliminate lust, anger,
and delusion so that they are extinguished without remainder, attain the dhyāna of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya), and thereafter dwell in peace like those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens?
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having attained the state of coming and going, and having practiced for one more birth, one then perceives that desire is undesirable;
yet, though one has cultivated this insight, it is not yet permanently severed."
Though the fire of lust be blazing, it cannot endanger the mind;
by practicing the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), one increases [the power to subdue] desire, which is like a *rākṣasa*.
It is like a person in the height of summer who, unable to endure the heat, seeks a fan to fan himself and longs for water to bathe in.
Coming and going in this manner, seeing lust, anger, and delusion as being intensely feverish, he resolved to seek the path of non-returning.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Having accomplished the two auspicious paths, Yet practicing without having eternally eliminated desire.
Having attained untainted dhyāna, his practice is equal to that of the Brahmā heavens.
Whatever heat there is within his body, he removes it with the coolness of water;
seeking the path of non-returning, he attains this state of purity and coolness.

At that time, he practiced the contemplation of the foul, thereby forever liberating himself from desire for form, as well as anger and delusion; he clearly perceived the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates, and their total cessation became his meditative absorption.
Knowing and seeing thus, one severs the five fetters and is free from the hindrances of the aggregates, attaining the path of the non-returner.
No longer returning to this world, one is liberated from craving and desire, and is free from the affliction of the demons of lust that create all obstacles.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having been liberated from the affliction of craving and desire, Constantly contemplating impurity to eliminate all ailments,
Forever free from fear and far removed from suffering and distress, One accomplishes the path of the Non-returner, equal to the third [fruit]."
One immediately attains coolness and is free from all feverish distress; if one beholds forms and desires, one constantly perceives their impurity and thus recognizes their defilement.
It is like a merchant from a distant land who has arrived utterly exhausted;

on the twenty-ninth day, when darkness prevails and there is no moonlight, he arrives at midnight and finds the city gates closed. He wanders around to the southern wall, where below lies a pool of water—the runoff from rain falling from the heavens!

Having set down their belongings on the bank, they saw corpses in human form, as well as chickens, dogs, elephants, livestock, snakes, insects, and other such creatures, all either sinking or floating in the water. Hundreds of thousands of worms leaped and writhed within their bodies, while their hair and body fur floated to the surface; the refuse swept from within the city and the leaking foul waters all converged into this pool.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"It is like a great body of water beside a city, Which cannot even be scrutinized by the eye, let alone drunk;
A man from a distant land arrives only to find the gates closed, And so stays together with the crowd at the edge of this pond."

At that time, among the multitude there were some who were distant travelers who had never before been to this land; being ignorant of what was right or wrong, and exhausted and parched with thirst, they stripped off their clothes, entered the water to wash, drank their fill of water at will, and lay down to rest until they emerged refreshed.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"When that man first arrived in this land, He entered the water to bathe and remove his fever;
He made offerings to the water deity and drank to quench his thirst, But being utterly exhausted, he fell fast asleep."

Tomorrow morning, as dawn was about to break, having risen early and awakened from my fatigue, I saw foul secretions and impurities within the water. Some fled in disgust and closed their eyes, refusing to look; others covered their noses and attempted to force themselves to vomit, only then realizing that the water was filthy and impure.
Thereupon he spoke in verse:
"Having attained the third path, I see that sensual pleasures are unstable;
Entering meditative concentration, I am free from affliction, Beholding desires as water with flaws."
At that time, the practitioner delights in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and examines sensual desires, just as a merchant loathes foul, impure water.
It is like an infant who takes up excrement to play with it; as he grows older, he abandons his former playthings and finds delight in other matters.
When he approaches old age, he completely renounces all such pleasures and finds joy in the Dharma alone.

It is likewise for one who has already attained the path of the Non-returner through practice: they view the pleasures of the five realms of birth and death as merely the play of small children, and thus redouble their diligence, desiring to escape the cycle of beginning and end, without delighting in seeking rebirth.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a young child plays with filth upon the ground,
but as he grows toward adulthood, he abandons that play and takes delight in other things."
Cultivation is also like this: seeking to attain liberation from the three realms, one then exerts diligent effort and fully accomplishes the four paths.
It is like a group of merchants from a distant land who come from the east and stay in a garden outside a city.

At that time, there was in that city a deceitful man, versatile and lacking in faith, who feigned the provision of food, drink, flowers, incense, and fine garments. He went before the Guide and inquired after his well-being, offering many congratulations on his long journey and noting that he had met with no misfortune along the way. "Having been hungry and thirsty for a long time," he said, "I have finally come to meet you in person; please deign to accept this small meal out of compassion."
The Teacher accepted; yet another request was made:

"It would be better for you to enter the city. I have a great residence within which there is a fine palace, fully equipped with soft and smooth furnishings. The house has wells and springs, separate latrines, rows of trees, and all necessary utensils are provided. We pray that you would deign to show your majestic presence and honor us by entering the city."
Having finished speaking these words of deception, he abandoned them and departed.
Thereupon, a verse was recited:
"There was a man harboring flattery and deceit; seeing from afar a great caravan of merchants..."
He welcomed and made offerings to the Teacher, and after the meal, the Teacher said:
"I have a palace, vast, lofty, and magnificent.
But the man lacked sincerity and faith; he spoke deceitfully and then departed.
At that time, there was a great elder in the city who heard that the man had deceived the caravan leader; he immediately went out to meet him and said to the leader:
"Do not trust that man to dwell in this hall."
"Foul and turbid floodwater lies behind this hall, and excrement, urine, and impurities flow everywhere toward the front; for this reason, it cannot be used as a lodging.
Hearing this, the guide replied to the elder:
"Although the hall has an odor, expedient means may be employed—burn incense and scatter flowers to remove its filth."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The elder, harboring thoughts of affection, Therefore went to visit the Teacher;
Beside this hall, he said to him, 'There is foul, putrid impurity.'"
Upon hearing these words, the Guide replied to him, saying:
"Though the offering may be foul-smelling, one should burn incense and scatter various flowers.
At that time, the elder said to the Guide:

"Furthermore, there may arise difficulties when various wicked insects are all within it, using flesh, blood, and sinews as their food and drink; should they become hungry, they will bore through your bag and gnaw to ruin its contents."
The Guide replied,
"I shall provide it for him, so that whatever he eats will not pass through his body.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"There are many foul insects dwelling in this hall, Who feed upon flesh, blood,
and sinews; 'I can provide for them according to their needs,' Thus the Guide replied to the elder."
The Elder said to the Teacher:
"In the four corners of that hall there are four venomous vipers—cruel, harmful, and fond of strife—who must not be approached. By what skillful means can these vipers be pacified?"
The Guide replied, “I am able to understand this;
I shall bestow a divine mantra as medicine so that no transgression occurs.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
There are four venomous vipers in his hall, wicked and malevolent, harboring malice and wishing to cause him harm;
yet with various medicines and divine mantras, he is able to eliminate the knots of poison harbored by those vipers.
Thereupon, the elder spoke again to the guide:
"Furthermore, there is a great peril: the old foundations of the wall are thus about to collapse, and the walls and enclosures are tilting and precarious, such that they cannot be relied upon."
The guide replied:
"Even if such a difficulty were to arise, I would be unable to manage it, nor is there any expedient means by which it could be prevented from collapsing. Why is this so?"
"If there should be danger or ruin, there will be the hardship of losing one's life.
Thereupon, he recited this verse:
"If a hall has stood for long and is about to collapse, even if it should overturn, it cannot be protected."
The guide replied to the elder, saying,
"There is such fear that I will not dwell there.
At that time, having heard of the various defects and difficulties regarding the hall and having also seen them with his own eyes, his mind was immediately repelled and he refused to reside there.

The Non-returner is likewise; having heard the teaching of the World-Honored One and clearly realized the Noble Truths, he takes no pleasure in the afflictions of birth and death from beginning to end.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having attained the state of non-returning and being free from all suffering, In his practice, he seeks immeasurable peace."
One does not long for birth and death even as one would for a hair or a speck of dust, just as a guide does not remain within the hall.
Explanation:
"The hall" refers to the human body.
"Filthy and turbid water" refers to the nine orifices from which impurities constantly flow.
"Water filled with insects" refers to the eighty kinds of worms within the body that constantly consume the flesh, blood, marrow, and bones.
"Leveling the ground and repairing the walls" refers to making offerings to the body by providing it with food and drink.
"The four vipers" refers to the four great elements of the body: earth, water, fire, and wind.
"The hall is dilapidated and dangerous, on the verge of collapsing day and night" refers to old age, sickness, and death.
The practitioner, through skillful means, seeks day and night to escape these manifold hardships.
That guide refers to the path of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

Practicing with single-minded diligence and listening to the World-Honored One’s teaching, he beholds the three realms as all ablaze; whatever forms his eyes examine are seen to be entirely subject to impermanence and inseparable from decay, just as a guide sees a great hall in a state of peril.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Like a venomous serpent harboring poison, Wicked and evil, impossible to approach;
Each dwelling in one of the four corners— These are called the four great elements of the human body."
Decayed, on the verge of collapse, one says the body undergoes increase and decrease;
constantly beset by manifold afflictions, it follows the path of old age, sickness, death, and exhaustion.
The flatterers within the city use this as a metaphor for the wisdom of tainted dhyāna.
That person enters into craving and desire, obstructed by the bonds of affection.
The elder who upholds the prohibitions and precepts is said to be a teacher free from attachment;
through his compassion, he constantly rescues and sustains practitioners, enabling them to cross over all sufferings and hardships.
It is like a great merchant caravan, among whom there is a leader;
the sons of the Buddha partake of the nectar, having attained the path of non-attachment.
The teacher expounds for the practitioners that the body is suffering, empty, and impermanent.
Observing the three realms with discernment, they are turbulent and unstable.
One should seek single-mindedness to reach the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa) and perceive non-attachment with clarity.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
The Buddha, out of compassion for sentient beings, expounded that which can deliver one from all suffering;
I have examined the various sūtras of the Buddha and praised the stage of no-more-learning.
That king released a drunken elephant, its fierce and harmful tusks exceedingly sharp.
The various nāgas harbor poisonous breaths, yet you transform them all to bring them under control.
You rescue and protect beings from fear and hardship, attaining eternal sovereignty.
To the Buddha of Ten Powers, who is without end, and to his disciples, I pay homage.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits serve the Great Sage; Auspicious people all take refuge in him.
All who attain liberation through reverence, And whom the multitude of sages revere—I prostrate before you.

That practitioner, already established in the stage of training, takes no pleasure in beginning or end; having nothing more to delight in, they do not crave the three realms. Transcending the realm of form and the formless realm, they sever all fetters.
With mindfulness, the faculties, the powers, and the factors of awakening, they perceive cessation as tranquility—this is called "eternal stability."
Beholding it thus, one leaves behind form and the formless, and distances oneself from frivolity and arrogance.
Thereupon, a verse says:
The mind already abides in the stage of training, Thoroughly understanding the intent of all trainings.
Restraining the fear of birth and death, one extinguishes dread and finds no further delight.
When all afflictions are exhausted without remainder, what is seen is as it truly is;
playfulness and self-conceit are removed, and delusion is likewise eliminated.
The practitioner reflects to himself:

"I should know that at this time I have become an Arhat, attained non-attachment, and all outflows are forever exhausted; I have cultivated the pure Brahma-conduct, accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, and attained my own benefit; birth and death are ended, I have obtained equal wisdom, and have transcended the moat and trench; I have cleared away the weeds of defilement so that there is no longer any leakage, I have become a banner of the noble ones, and have already crossed over from this shore to that."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Practicing while dwelling on the stage of training, Unshakable, one accomplishes the Noble Path;
Having already attained one's own benefit, One transcends suffering and constantly gains peace."
When the mountain springs of intense heat have dried up, the flow of water is forever exhausted;
one who honors and respects others while remaining free from frivolity is said to be without attachment.
Having severed the five categories [of fetters], such a person is the most eminent among men.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having severed the five grades of afflictions, He has fully perfected the six supernormal powers;
Having cleansed away all worldly defilements, Like water washing the grime from a garment."
Having departed from the afflictions of birth and death, and having attained peace through the perfections, such a person is called a true ruler—a supreme being free from all defilement.

This refers to the Arhat who has attained non-attachment; he is worthy of wearing celestial robes and dwelling in divine palaces. Roaming and residing in the Purple Palace, his food and drink appear spontaneously, and he is constantly entertained by a hundred kinds of music. With great joy and exultation, he rises from his seat and proclaims aloud:
"Now, as I am a son of the One of Ten Powers, having attained this state, I am the refuge for all beings in the heavens and the world;
those who revere and honor me shall increase the lineage of the devas and diminish the asuras."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse: "Sublime,
having perfected the four virtues and the six supernormal powers, Seeking the most supreme through the wisdom of patience,
Following the Buddha’s teaching to reach the ultimate— Therefore, I shall expound upon the stage of No-More-Learning."
Through skillful means, he triumphs over all suffering;
forever liberated from all craving and affection, he has already departed from the afflictions of birth and death, extinguishing all worldly toil.
Like the rising sun dispelling the clouds, the Honored One has left behind the darkness of all attachments.
I take refuge in the Noble Path of the Buddha, which is free from suffering and eternally peaceful.
Having transcended all sense-bases and elements, one is like a person released from prison;
like purple-polished gold, it remains unimpaired even when placed in fire.
Having attained the tranquility of definitive *nirvāṇa*, he has never cherished his own body;
since the Buddha has reached the Deathless (*amṛta*), I vow to prostrate and pay him homage.

As for that practitioner who dwells in the realm of *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*), having exhausted what was past, he creates no new karma and shall no longer receive a body; with a mind focused and single-pointed, never lax, amidst all forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, he is free from all attachment, neither grasping nor rejecting, having brought the root of suffering to its end.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Having attained deliverance into the unconditioned, Forever free from all desire,
Established upon the ground of the 'with-remainder,' He exhausts the old and creates no new."
Not dwelling in forms, sounds, or fragrances, with all tastes and tactile sensations severed—
like a lotus flower, unsullied by dust or water;
with the sense faculties fully stilled, one does not follow the delusions of the sense bases.
Like gold unmixed with iron, one is forever parted from birth and death.
When there is no attachment to causes and conditions, only then is there eternal peace and security;
this is called the practice of dwelling in seclusion, which extinguishes the very roots of suffering and toil.
It is like heating iron until it is glowing red and forging it with a hammer; as the surface impurities are removed and it gradually cools, one does not perceive where the heat of the fire has gone.
Practicing in this manner, even if one attains extinction in the realm of nirvana without remainder, one gradually escapes suffering; for this reason, this sutra is titled "The Practice."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as when iron is forged and heated with a hammer, The flames suddenly flare up and then immediately vanish;
The practice of the Dharma is likewise: Having attained nirvāṇa, its location is unknown."
Just as when it rains from heaven there are bubbles, And once those bubbles have burst, their location is unknown;
so too, if a practitioner attains nirvāṇa, one can never know where they have gone.
The devas, ṛṣis, nāgas, and human beings do not see where those who have crossed over have gone;
for that practitioner, impermanence is emptiness, and through intelligence and wisdom, they attain parinirvāṇa.
Even if a practitioner were to obtain this, there would be nothing that surpasses it in reckoning the nectar of immortality;
only then does one awaken to eternal peace and security, having attained nirvana without remainder.
When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke this parable—
just as sparks fly from iron being forged by a hammer and gradually move toward extinction— the destination of the spirit can never be known.
Having already attained the path of extinction, he understands such equality;
the Buddha, whose wisdom is luminous, has a spirit that is peaceful and unmoving.
Having already crossed over all defilements, he is naturally and greatly liberated from birth and death.
One attains that state of desirelessness, pure and serene as a deep pool.
Those who practice this teaching on the stages of the path will gradually attain liberation and reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Those who seek the unconditioned and desire liberation, Who forever leave behind turbidity and chaos to attain the nectar of immortality—
They should expound this Sūtra of Practice, Following the Buddha’s teaching as a torch found in the darkness."
Should there be anyone who speaks this sutra, and should there be those who listen to it, the Buddha shall show them the path, which is eternally peaceful and without end.

Those who train in this manner attain ultimate realization; practicing the stages of the Way with a mind like empty space, the five supernormal powers arise spontaneously, and they have no fear of beginning or end, remaining forever extinguished like a lamp.
*Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Six;
*Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin Dynasty.
Chapter 28: The Three Grades of Practice for Disciples (7) The Buddha’s virtue is lofty and sublime;
his majestic spiritual power is immeasurable.
He transforms beings according to the times through the Way and its teachings, delivering and liberating all throughout the ten directions.
Beholding the flaws of birth and death, he manifests a bridge for the present life;
he censures the suffering of beginning and end, and extols nirvāṇa.
He distinguishes the joy of his disciples and accordingly demonstrates their proper conduct.
Gradually providing guidance and instruction, one eventually reaches great peace.

If there is one who practices and perceives the afflictions from beginning to end—the poison of hell, the distress of the animal realm, the suffering of hungry ghosts, the anxieties and confusions of the human world, and the impermanence of the heavens—all of which are unbearable!

They revolve and circulate like a chariot wheel, subject to birth, old age, sickness, death, hunger, thirst, cold, and heat; to separation from loved ones, the gathering of grievances, and the pain of sorrowful lamentation—all of which are beyond full description.

Since the beginning of kalpas, they have been at odds with their parents, separated from their brothers, and estranged from their wives and children; the tears they have shed exceed the waters of the four seas, and the milk they have drunk from their kin surpasses the flow of the five rivers and four streams.

Sometimes the father weeps for the son, sometimes the son for the father; sometimes the elder brother for the younger, sometimes the younger for the elder; sometimes the husband for the wife, and sometimes the wife for the husband. With such topsy-turvy relations beyond all order, they plant the roots of diligent suffering—the very source of ignorance.

Practitioners who perceive this are all weary and disgusted by it; they desire only to escape this disease of birth and death, practicing with diligence day and night, never abandoning the Way and its principles as they seek the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

One perceives for oneself that throughout immeasurable kalpas of wandering through birth and death, the accumulated bones of one's bodies would exceed Mount Sumeru; the marrow used to smear the ground would cover the entire world; if one were to count deaths throughout the three thousandfold world system, they would be as numerous as its circumference; and the blood shed and fallen would be more than the rain that falls universally upon the worlds of the past and present.

When a practitioner reflects upon such calamities, even a discourse lasting ten million kalpas would not suffice to exhaust their description; therefore, they abandon the household life, shave their hair and beards, and single-mindedly seek the Way without longing for worldly glory, just as a wise person does not crave a corpse-like body.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Practicing the path, one perceives the beginning and end:
The suffering and affliction of the hells, The calamities of animals and hungry ghosts, And the distinctions within this worldly realm."
The revolving cycle of birth and death is like a chariot wheel;
fathers and sons, brothers drift apart, and wives and children suffer in separation.
The tears shed in weeping and wailing would exceed the waters of the four oceans.
Drinking the milk of one's kin exceeds the waters of the five great rivers;
practicing the path, one leaves home and devotes oneself single-mindedly to the Dharma,
not longing for the honors of worldly custom, just as a wise person abandons poison.

The practitioner reflects within himself: "My bodies have come in countless and immeasurable lifetimes, yet I was unaware of their unions and separations. The pain of my inner distress is like that of a violent intoxication, beyond comprehension; I have falsely spoken superficial words, regarding them as the ultimate truth. My attachment to worldly affection is like glue or lacquer, preventing me from saving myself. Therefore, I shall practice diligence, distancing myself from the mundane and drawing near to the Way."

"It is, for example, like a person who travels far to another country to engage in trade and seek profit. Not long after arriving there, a great epidemic breaks out; many die, and not even one in ten survives. Corpses lie scattered about, their stench beyond description, and there is neither a skilled physician nor good medicine available to treat them."

The man was terrified and regretted having gone to that country; he thought, "Had I not come, I would not have encountered this calamity. Night and day he tossed and turned in grief, unable to describe his sorrow:
"Even if my illness were to heal, once I return to my own country, there will be no time for me to return again."

That person happened upon a great physician who administered medicine, acupuncture, and moxibustion; his illness gradually subsided and his strength was restored. He then returned to his native land to see his family, recounting that he had encountered hardships and distress beyond description, and declaring that from now on he would never again dare to travel there or go to that land.
With but one robe and one meal, what further could one seek?
One merely desires peace for oneself; how could one know the condition of others!
Later, upon hearing the name of that land, one would tremble with fear and dread, unwilling to leave one's dwelling and intent only on preserving one's own body.

A disciple who is thus—seeing the suffering of the five realms of existence, where lust, anger, delusion, illness, birth, and death ceaselessly recur—and who, day and night, applies himself with single-minded diligence to seated meditation and mindfulness of the Way, attaining the teaching of the World-Honored One, extolling *nirvāṇa* and disparaging the cycle of beginning and end: such a person is a true physician.
That one takes excellent medicine and the illness is thereby eliminated refers to the Buddha-dharma sutras removing the three poisons.
That corpses lie scattered in disarray refers to the five aggregates (skandhas) and the six decays (āyatanas).
When those who had repented reached that land, they reflected to themselves:

"Since the beginning of countless kalpas, we have wandered through birth and death; our attachment to affection has been manifold within our minds, and we failed to perceive the Truths of Suffering, Origination, Cessation, and the Path.

Having already attained realization of the Way, we feared suffering and loathed the body, seeking an early parinirvāṇa; we were unable to return and teach others who remain firmly ablaze with afflictions. Only when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, reveals that all is fundamentally non-existent shall we advance forward to attain the stage of non-retrogression, moving freely both advancing and receding."
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Suppose there is a man traveling far on trade, Who reaches a foreign land and encounters an epidemic;
The multitudes die, with only one survivor in ten, And corpses lie scattered with no one to bury them."
Regretting it in my heart as I reached his kingdom, I thought: "Why was I so unfortunate as to meet with this calamity?
Had I found a skilled physician to treat my ailment, I would have returned to my native land and could not have traveled further."
Fearing the afflictions of birth and death is likewise so; beholding the suffering of wandering through the five realms, one reproaches oneself for original faults and failing to perceive the Way.
Enduring hardship from beginning to end brings great distress;
with single-minded diligence, one seeks nirvana, desiring to deliver the world from all terrors and alarms.
Evil persists from beginning to end like a corpse; one must focus the will and turn toward the City of Non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).
One should practice with trepidation, fearing:

"Perhaps my life will end before I attain liberation; I may return to the three miserable realms (*trāya*), from which it is difficult to be extracted. One must not be indolent or harbor the notion of a self (*ātman*), for such a person is like an ordinary worldly being who is alienated from the Three Jewels and remains in profound, dark ignorance.

For example, in the past, there were many merchants traveling far away to pursue their livelihoods. As they passed through a vast wilderness devoid of human habitation, they became utterly exhausted from the journey and fell fast asleep; furthermore, they kept no watch over the time and did not maintain their weapons.

When great bandits suddenly arrive and one is unaware, failing to employ bow and arrow, one will be harmed by the bandits; however, those who possess strength may flee and escape, returning home from their hunger and exhaustion.

Furthermore, he devised a plan to seek out fierce companions; then, following his former path, he traveled as a merchant seeking profit. Whenever night fell and he lay down to sleep, he would rise during the watches of the night, keeping his bow and arrows ready and upright.
When the bandits saw this, they did not dare to advance and resist; knowing they were difficult to overcome, they withdrew of their own accord.

"Profound and obscure" refers to the net of ignorance (*moha*). Because of ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise, which in turn give rise to consciousness and attachment, followed by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), clinging (*upādāna*), becoming (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress.
"Practicing livelihood" refers to the cultivation of practice.
"Exhausted and lying down to sleep" refers to not clearly understanding impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
"Those who do not travel by night" refers to those who do not contemplate the meaning of the profound sūtras.
"Those whose weapons are not formidable" refers to those who do not follow the wisdom of great kindness and great compassion; they seek only to save themselves and do not mind the sentient beings.

When "bandits come to see one in peril," it means that while sitting in meditation and contemplating, one fails to enter emptiness and stillness; instead, being deluded by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six decays (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), one falls into the four inversions: taking the impermanent for the permanent, suffering for pleasure, the non-self for a self, and the empty for the real. When life ends, one is born in the heavens, yet through the exhaustion of merit, one returns to the world, never escaping the three miserable realms (*trividha-durgati*).
Those who, being strong, manage to escape and return home refer to those who have attained Arhatship.

Those who then seek strong companions to further cultivate their livelihood refer to those who reach Nirvana, yet realizing that the limit of Arhatship does not constitute the ultimate goal, they see the Buddha, receive his teachings, and further resolve upon the Great Intention to become Bodhisattvas.
To travel accompanied by a multitude as companions refers to the various practices of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

To carry weapons with solemn correctness while patrolling at night refers to great kindness (maitrī) and great compassion (mahākaruṇā), which distinguish the practice of emptiness (śūnyatā) through neither attachment nor severance.

As for "the thieves retreating," this refers to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and unimpeded wisdom; beholding the emptiness of the three realms, one does not fear birth and death, and all four Māras are thereby subdued.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Fearing that my life may end while practicing, Or that I might enter the three evil realms,
I no longer harbor notions of 'self,' But take refuge in the Triple Gem."
It is like a merchant of old who, traveling far to seek wealth and profit,
fell asleep and was slain by wicked bandits. Among them,
one who was strong and vigorous escaped by exerting all his strength.
Returning home, he spoke of his hardships, saying, "Now at last I have attained peace;
having already realized the path of Arhatship, I know of my own accord that this is my limit.
I cannot enter the cycle of birth and death, for Nirvana has become an obstacle."
Furthermore, joining with fierce companions and marching at night with disciplined troops, the bandits, upon seeing them, did not dare advance; they immediately retreated to their own lands.
Abiding within the realm of non-action, one knows that Nirvana is the ultimate limit.
Thus they give rise to the bodhisattva mind, practicing great kindness and great compassion.
Discerning the practice of profound emptiness, they do not cling and have nothing to sever;
circling through birth and death, they encounter no hardships within the three realms.
To practice and honor the Dharma while entering the four immeasurable minds without possessing great compassion is like a small dragon that can rain upon a single county but not everywhere;
though it provides moisture for the people, it is insufficient to mention. The conduct of an Arhat in the four immeasurable minds is just like this.

Just as the sea dragon sends down rain everywhere across the world so that there is nothing it does not moisten, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with great kindness and great compassion, reaches all sentient beings so that there is none whom he does not rescue.

The Buddha, the God among Gods, seeing their minds thus, immediately manifested for them the limit that nothing may transcend—Nirvana—and gradually led them forward until they reached the Great Way and understood their original delusion.
It is like a man who had three sons; from their youth, the father raised them until they reached adulthood, never failing to provide them with food, clothing, medicine, or medical care.
As the father grew old and his physical strength declined, he said to his sons:

"You are ungrateful! You were raised and nurtured by me until you became men. Now that I am aged, instead of providing for me to repay the kindness of my nursing and upbringing, you instead press me for wealth, food, and clothing. What is the reason for this?"
"We shall inform the local officials to have you executed.
Upon hearing his father's instruction, the sons were immediately seized with terror and took refuge in their father, saying:

"We brothers have been led astray by our own folly and ignorance of righteousness; we failed to heed the virtue of our parents' kindness in raising us, and out of deep attachment and high expectations, we did not examine our own faults. Now that we have heard this stern command, we shall immediately obey it. We will cultivate the way of filial piety to surpass others and, being diligent day and night without slackening, bring no shame upon our ancestors."

At that time, those sons each went forth to manage their livelihoods; they entered the sea to gather treasures and obtained various of the seven precious gems to provide for their parents. Their filial piety was so lofty that they thought only of their two parents and disregarded their own bodies. They obtained a great radiant jewel named "Illumination" and immediately went to present it to their father.

The father saw that his bright hair had turned white and then black again, and his fallen teeth had grown back; he became a great elder to whom people from near and far looked up in reverence. This is what is meant by paternal kindness and filial piety!
To act as a disciple without possessing great compassion is like having a father with three sons—
namely, mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—
who raises an eldest son: namely, attachment to the three realms through lust, anger, and ignorance.
That which provides clothing and food refers to the bondage of the five aggregates, the six sense-bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination.
That the child grows up and continues to seek offerings refers to the various sensual desires that one never knows how to satisfy.
The father’s fear that he might go to the local authorities to lodge a complaint refers to the realization of the extraordinary and the desire to sever the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The son’s acceptance of this instruction and his practice of filial piety refers to taking refuge in the Buddha.
The three sons being even more filial and obedient is the source of giving, observing the precepts, and wisdom.
Entering the sea to obtain the seven treasures is the attainment of the seven factors of enlightenment and the realization of the path of an Arhat.
Those who attain ultimate filial piety know that their disciples' limits extend only to the realm of *nirvāṇa*, yet they further resolve upon the great intention for the path of the Bodhisattva.
As for "obtaining the illuminating pearl and the father becoming even younger," it means that through present meditative vision, one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions without any obstruction.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"In the past there was a man who fathered three sons.
Having raised and nurtured them until they were grown, they now sought clothing and food from their father."
The father said to his three sons:
"I am now extremely old; you ought to provide for me.
Yet you have excessively sought my labor; I tell you, go before the authorities, where you shall be flogged with the five poisons."
Hearing his father’s command, the son reverently practiced the way of filial piety;
he entered the sea to seek the seven treasures to offer to his honored father,
and further obtained the illuminating pearl, whereby his father became younger once more.
The three sons—mind, consciousness, and awareness—were insatiable in their passions;
though their father rebuked them, they became even more filial, practicing giving, precepts, the path, and wisdom.
By adhering to the seven factors of enlightenment, they attained arhatship and nirvana.
Having received the Buddha’s most profound teaching, they further resolve upon the Bodhisattva mind;
their virtue and wisdom are most majestic, and they behold the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Their bodies composed of the four great elements are unimpeded, like space which is without restriction.
For example, in the past there was a turtle that emerged from the sea to wander along the shore, where a large fox pursued it, seeking to end its life.
Perceiving the fox’s approach, the turtle tucked its head and four legs beneath its shell for protection. The fox waited there, thinking:
"If it extends its head and limbs, I shall seize and devour them."
The tortoise remained motionless and did not move; the fox, utterly frustrated, abandoned him and departed.
The tortoise returned to the Great Divine Dragon King and related the beginning and end of his story, requesting to become the body of a dragon king so that he would have nothing to fear.
One who can subdue the five aggregates will not be disturbed by Māra and shall attain the path of Nirvāṇa.
One who attains the state of a dragon enters the bodhisattva path, does not fear the four māras, and rescues and delivers sentient beings.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a turtle withdraws its head and limbs, So too does one who fears not the Arhat;
Having attained flight, they become a dragon deity— Such is the Bodhisattva as well."

For example, suppose there is a person who travels far in search of wealth; enduring cold and heat, they believe they will gain great profit, yet on the way they encounter bandits and lose their enterprise.

Alternatively, there is a wise person who, from within their own land, devises skillful means so that their gains are immeasurable, providing for the four quarters and accumulating merit through successive acts of virtue.

They contemplate impermanence, suffering, the emptiness of formations, and non-self; observing the rise and fall of external phenomena, some attain meditative concentration and achieve the path of an Arhat, yet they further resolve their minds to seek the state of a Bodhisattva.

There may be those who have attained realization, who know that the four great elements are empty and possess neither interior nor exterior; they practice great compassion and extend their pity to the ten directions. Although they deliver beings, there is in truth no one delivered. The Way has no distance, and wisdom is supreme. Having attained equal enlightenment, it is without past, future, or present, being like empty space.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a man goes on a distant journey of trade, So too is the disciple:
accumulating merit, contemplating the foulness [of the body], And observing that all phenomena are impermanent."
The Bodhisattva is like a man of clear vision; seeking his benefit, he does not travel far.
Without [the distinction between] birth-and-death and Nirvana, he attains equal enlightenment.

Those who practice in this way fear birth-and-death and loathe the hardships of the triple world. Fearing suffering and weary of the body, they fail to realize its fundamental non-existence; they seek only to transcend affliction and do not keep sentient beings in mind.
For example, when an army is defeated, those who are weak and inferior desire only to save themselves and do not rescue others from peril.
To those with such a mind, the Buddha teaches the removal of the afflictions of the three poisons, that Nirvana is blissful, and that one should leave darkness for light.

It is like a guide leading a great caravan of merchants on a long journey through a vast wilderness where water and grass are utterly absent; the merchants sigh and lament, saying, "This road stretches on endlessly; how can we reach our destination? We shall surely perish!"

At that time, the guide was intelligent, widely learned, and possessed of spiritual arts; knowing the merchants' thoughts and their weariness with traveling the road, he manifested a kingdom midway along the path, where the cities, people, and lands were prosperous and joyful, and the five grains were abundant and cheap. The merchants were greatly delighted and consulted one another, saying:
"How wonderful! How delightful!"
"I have been here for a very long time; when shall I escape this hardship and reach the human realm?
It was upon having this thought that I arrived at this city, so why should I fear anything further?
At that time, the merchants remained in that land, enjoying themselves with great pleasure, eating and drinking to their heart's content, and resting as they pleased.
Just as when one wishes to become weary of a city, it vanishes and the kingdom is no longer seen,
all the merchants wondered why this was so.
The guide replied:
"You all were weary and disheartened, thinking that the Way was so remote and vast that it could never be reached!
Therefore, I manifested a city of transformation so that the people of the land might find rest; seeing that you were weary, I have now caused it to vanish!"

The Buddha said: "It is so. The practice of the disciples involves fearing the suffering from beginning to end—namely, the afflictions of birth and death—and being terrified of the calamities of the three realms, they desire early extinction; therefore, it was for their sake that this was shown."

It is easy to entice and lead Arhats forward; they cross over birth and death and exhaust the three impurities, attaining the unconditioned path and considering themselves to have reached fulfillment and perfection.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, the Buddha stood before him and revealed the Great Way, saying:

"This is not yet the full realization of the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way; only upon attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena and reaching all-knowledge will one truly have attained it."
"It is like a country that has encountered three calamities.
What are these three?
First is banditry; second is the high price of grain; third is disease."

The multitude dispersed and traveled to other lands; after a long time, when peace was restored in their own country, some returned, while others, fearing the calamities of the three perils, never returned at all.
The Buddha said: "A 'country' refers to the three realms.
'Encountering the three calamities' refers to the defilements of the three poisons.
'Leaving to go to another country' refers to the Arhat."

"Returning to the state of national security" means that a bodhisattva, having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and all profound wisdom, returns to enter the three periods of time to deliver all beings.

Regarding those who encounter the three calamities and do not return: the Arhat, having attained the unconditioned (*asamskrta*), fears the three difficult states and is thus unable to return to deliver sentient beings.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a multitude of merchants, Traveling through a vast wilderness,
Exhausted and fearing they would not reach their goal, The guide conjures a city."
When the multitude dwells in rest, Abiding peacefully for months and days, And the Buddha perceives their hearts have grown weary, He then vanishes and no longer appears.
The World-Honored Buddha is likewise; Seeing the terrors of the perils of birth and death, he [withdraws].
He then manifested the unconditioned for them, enabling them to cross beyond the suffering of the triple world.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he displayed the transformation of the Great Way,
causing them to attain the state of non-arising and extensively saving all beings.
Furthermore, it is like a great kingdom that suddenly encounters three calamities;
its people scatter in all directions to seek refuge in other lands, some returning when the country is secure and others not.
Those who fear the perils of birth and death are called disciples.
Returning to his country without fear, the Bodhisattva transforms the ten directions.
Through the skillful means of expedient wisdom, he brings all beings to their proper place,
like a great navigator who travels back and forth without rest.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is thus: his Dharma-body comes and goes, circulating throughout all things, like the sunlight appearing everywhere.

29. Pratyekabuddha Chapter (7). *Caryā-bhūmi Sūtra*, Pratyekabuddha Chapter Twenty-Nine: Those who follow the path of the pratyekabuddha do not achieve full self-enlightenment; though they have set out for the unsurpassed, right, and true path, they do not receive the true Dharma from virtuous friends, but instead practice exclusively by reflecting upon their own conduct.

Suppose one practices the six perfections according to the teachings yet maintains conceptual attachments, desiring to obtain the honorable title, the thirty-two marks, and the eighty minor characteristics, and to possess majestic and venerable power;
failing to understand skillful means, one regards the manifested form-body of the Buddha as a substantial body and thus falls into the stage of a pratyekabuddha.

It is as if there were a man who, desiring to see the great ocean, traveled to various ponds, lakes, and great rivers; seeking jewels there, he obtained crystal and small moon-bright pearls, yet he imagined that he had attained the sublime radiance of the Vajra.
Those who retreat from the bodhisattva mind do not understand that the Tathāgata’s dharma is without entering or exiting, empty and formless, and that the Way has no past, future, or present.
They claim that seeing emptiness constitutes fixed realization, yet they do not comprehend the practice of conforming to emptiness.
Unable to advance further, they fail to reach the level of a Buddha above, yet they surpass the level of a disciple below; they stop midway.
It is like a person who wishes to see the Lord of Devas but sees instead a frontier king, and thus declares him to be the Lord;

likewise, one who desires to study the mind of perfect enlightenment but sets limits for themselves, failing to understand profound wisdom and falling back into the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, is just like this.
If they possess such a disposition, the Buddha then guides and instructs them in the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas.
It is like an elder who is extremely advanced in years and has many sons; his great mansion has pillars that have long been decayed from age, and a fire has broken out within their cores.
His sons are dissolute, indulging in the five pleasures, and do not perceive this disaster. At that time, the father thinks to himself:
"This house is old, and the fire is burning in the heart of its pillars; I fear the pillars will collapse and destroy the entire palace. What shall we do?

Desiring to employ skillful means to entice and transform them so that they would leave and escape the calamity of the fire, the father performed various musical performances outside and sent people to call his sons, saying:
"I shall grant each of you elephants, horses, carriages, and mani-jewels."

The sons, hearing from afar the sound of the music and being further commanded by their father, all rushed out of the house to where their father was. Their father then bestowed upon each of his sons a precious chariot and a fine vehicle, treating them all equally without partiality.
The sons said, "Just now our honorable father called us out and bestowed various rare treasures upon each of us; why is it that what is bestowed today is of a single uniform kind?
The elder replied:

"My palace is old; the center of its pillars has rotted and fire has ignited within. I fear the pillars will collapse and crush you all. Therefore, I have performed music and called you out so that my mind may be at ease."
"All of them are my children whom I love and cherish; therefore, I bestow upon them all these precious jewels and vehicles.
The Buddha said that his "former palace" refers to the triple world (*triloka*).
"The pillar that is rotten and about to collapse" refers to the afflictions of the three poisons revolving within birth and death.
"Fire burning within the pillar" refers to various discursive thoughts.
"The elder" refers to the Tathāgata.
"The sons being dissolute" refers to their attachment to the desires of the triple world.
"Performing music and dance" refers to the Buddha’s preaching on demerit and merit.
"Calling the sons out and bestowing gifts upon each" manifests the teaching of the three paths.

"The sons all come forth because their father gave them treasures" means that he manifests the Mahāyāna, in which there are no three [inferior] paths; it is only at the time of his final nirvāṇa that they realize this!
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
Suppose there were an elder, Whose sons were exceedingly numerous.
Deluded by the five pleasures, they remained attached to the old palace;
its pillars were rotten and on the verge of collapse, and fire broke out within its heart.
Fearing that the palace would crumble, the father suppressed his sons to prevent their destruction.
Because he performed various musical entertainments and bestowed gifts such as children, the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, likewise attained his realization through the awakening of dependent origination.
At the time of his final passing, the Buddha went before him.
To manifest the teaching of a single Dharma, the Mahāyāna is equal and without distinction.

When those who practice and resolve their minds to seek the Great Way fail to understand that all is fundamentally non-existent, they become attached to the Buddha’s physical body—its thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics—as the most honored among men.

For example, suppose there were a person who heard that in the four directions there was a sovereign named a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin), who ruled over the four continents and possessed the seven treasures; his sons numbered a thousand, all of whom were valiant in strength.
His city was broad and long, measuring four hundred and eighty li from east to west and two hundred and eighty li from south to north.
Within it stood a great palace forty li square, containing thrones made of the four precious substances.

The population was flourishing, the five grains were abundant, and their happiness was beyond measure. There were twelve divisions of musical performances; there were eighty-four thousand ladies of the court and palace attendants, eighty-four thousand kings who ruled over various nations, and the same number of elephants, horses, and chariots.
The King possesses four virtues. What are these four virtues?
Householders, brahmins, commoners, and the general populace all revere the Holy Emperor as sons serve their father;
the King loves and cherishes them as a mother pities her children.
Those whom the King teaches and transforms receive and practice his instructions;
from far and near they take refuge in him, just as people look to the heavens and rely on the earth for their livelihood.
Furthermore, there are four virtues:
There was neither cold nor heat, and from the beginning he experienced neither hunger nor thirst; he never fell ill throughout his life, all due to his original merit.

Upon hearing this, the man desired to go and see the Emperor; yearning for his holy teaching, he set out on his journey. Becoming weary along the way, he encountered a strange path and followed it into a great city. The population was flourishing, with trees and flowing streams whose delights were beyond description. Believing that this city was the realm of the Holy Emperor, he settled there.
Furthermore, although this place is pleasant, it is the abode of ghosts and spirits, yet the person does not perceive it!
At that time, there was a heavenly king named Viśrāma who, seeing the person, explained it to him:
"This is not the dwelling of a sage-king; it is the realm of ghosts and spirits!"
The majestic majesty of the Wheel-Turning Sage King was so sublime that they then joyfully approached and followed him.
Likewise, there are those who resolve their minds to study the Bodhisattva path, yet fail to understand its profound meaning or to discern emptiness;

because there is no Buddha in the world, they dwell in seclusion, entering and leaving their abodes beneath trees, observing that all phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty, and that the body does not endure long. Failing to realize fundamental non-arising, they attain the stage of a Pratyekabuddha and consider themselves accomplished.

When approaching *parinirvāṇa*, the Buddha stands before one and manifests the profound and wondrous teaching of the Great Dharma: that the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are fundamentally rootless!

One understands that both the beginning and the end are empty, devoid of past, future, and present; through great kindness and great compassion, one does not perceive the three realms (*tridhātu*). Only when there is no thought of *nirvāṇa* does one achieve true correctness and deliver all beings.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as someone seeking a Universal Monarch (cakravartin) Sees a single city and thinks it is the capital,
Or as a minor king remembers a Wheel-Turning King And finds great delight in his own domain."
The Heavenly King Viśvabhū went to see him and explained that this was the realm of ghosts and not that of a Great Emperor or a Wheel-Turning King;
thereupon he was struck with terror and realized his error.
I immediately set out for the great imperial realm, where I beheld his majestic power and virtue, vast and towering.
Long have I been in darkness, uncomprehending and deeply deluded; thus I shall serve the Holy King and attend him constantly.
If one desires to study the Great Way but does not attain clarity, one will likewise fall back into the stage of the Pratyekabuddha;
only thereafter will one receive the profound and subtle practice of the Buddha, leading ultimately to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
The Buddha’s majestic virtue shines with light; his merit delivers all sentient beings.
With an impartial mind he bestows grace upon all, eradicating even the names of the three poisons.
They are forever liberated from the suffering of birth and death; the Way is accomplished through wisdom.
Pure like the light of the sun, it thoroughly illuminates the darkness of the three realms.
Chapter 30: On the Bodhisattva (7) The *Caryā-melāyana* Sūtra, Chapter Thirty: On the Bodhisattva. The practitioner reflects within himself: "A person in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is like a wheel;

revolving up and down, it never leaves the ground. From beginning to end it is thus; the suffering of coming and going does not depart from the three realms. All this is due to original ignorance, failing to realize fundamental non-existence, yet claiming that the four great elements exist and clinging to them as truth."
Furthermore, it is like a person who sees a master performing an illusion and calls it a real person, not realizing it is a transformation;
so too is the foolish person, who is greedily attached to a self and reckons there is a body and life, failing to understand that its substance is composed of earth, water, fire, and wind.

It is, for example, like a person who has traveled far away, intending to journey to another country; having long heard that the road is perilous, he constantly harbors fear and dreads bandits. Looking out in all four directions, he sees from afar a cluster of mounds, stones, grass, and trees, and thinks there are many hundreds or thousands of horsemen who are great thieves—what is to be done?
They each fled in all directions, scattering so that no one knew where they were headed.
Among them was a guide who called out to the multitude:

"Do not abandon us yet! We have reached a place of extreme peril where there is neither water nor drink; we may encounter dire straits from which our lives cannot be saved, or we may become so utterly exhausted that only then shall we return. Since the journey back and forth has already taken so long, our fatigue will only increase, and having lost all our wealth and goods, upon whom shall we rely?"
Bare and destitute, starving and freezing, we ought instead to seek reliance upon one another, rather than turning to the wealthy and powerful for refuge and loans.

Furthermore, let us settle our minds and encourage one another to transform ourselves; send scouts to observe the situation—if there are no bandits, you may advance directly; but if they do come, let us maintain firm resolve and fight together so that they shall be driven to flight and defeat.

Why is this so? If one person wishes to die, ten people cannot prevent it; if ten people wish to die, a hundred cannot prevent it; if a hundred wish to die, a thousand cannot prevent it; if a thousand wish to die, ten thousand cannot prevent it; and if ten thousand wish to die, the whole world will fall into chaos.

The multitude accepted these instructions and no longer fled in disorder; they all remained stationed in solemn readiness. When they sent people to scout for thieves, they saw only grass, trees, tiles, and stones—there were absolutely no bandits.

The multitude rejoiced and then stepped forward; they all declared that the Guide was peerless in the world, his wisdom and insight truly beyond anything found in this age, and that in every movement and gesture, they would follow his instructions without daring to disobey or err.

When Bodhisattvas, these great beings, practice in this manner, they act as guides for all, understanding that the three realms are empty, that all things are like illusions, and that the five aggregates are like phantoms; they do not loathe birth and death, yet they bring about the cessation of their own bodies, transforming and instructing those throughout the ten directions to reveal the true path.

I sigh in admiration that the Bodhisattvas are profound and far-reaching, without peer; they traverse the triple world to deliver beings from birth and death. As for us disciples, we are small-minded and constantly harbor fear; we merely seek to extinguish our own bodies, failing to reach the benefit of all, and because we have not attained the ultimate, we shall surely fall back again.

From the initial generation of the aspiration, it is clear that through hearing the teachings of the Bodhisattva, all people have generated the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment!
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices cultivation, Realizing that all bodies are empty and like illusions."
This body is produced through the combination of causes and conditions; If the mind is not upright while sitting, one pursues what is false.
It is like a merchant traveling far away, Who sees trees in the distance and mistakes them for bandits;
Each person in his heart harbors fear and flees in all directions, But when the guide explains it to them, their minds find peace.
The Bodhisattva thus understands that all things are fundamentally non-existent;
as a teacher for all, he expounds the Dharma extensively, revealing the profound Great Way to his disciples, like the rising of the sun when the floating clouds have vanished.

The Bodhisattva, training on the path, gradually advances until reaching infinite wisdom; by means of the six perfections, he discerns the practice of emptiness, accumulating merit and virtue over incalculable eons before finally attaining the Way of the Buddha.

It is like a person who, having entered public service in their youth, begins in poverty but gradually attains great wealth; seeking the office of a vice-governor or magistrate, they eventually become a district magistrate; advancing from the rank of two-thousand-stone official, they reach the position of provincial governor, then the four generals, ministers, and high officials, progressing further to become a sovereign, a wheel-turning sage king, a lord of the devas, and finally a Brahmā.

The student of the stages of the Bodhisattva path is also like this: gradually giving rise to the resolve for generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; binding and restraining the six sense-faculties; removing the three poisons and the hindrances of the aggregates; turning toward the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; reaching the stage of non-retrogression; and drawing near to the fulfillment of all matters as one destined for Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
It is like polishing a mirror or refining flat iron; by gradually making it finer, its brilliance is eventually restored.

Likewise, by gradually practicing the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and accumulating merit and virtue over incalculable eons, one attains Buddhahood by oneself and brings liberation to the ten directions.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as a man begins his official career, Advancing from the rank of Commandant to District Magistrate,
From the Two-Thousand-Stone official to Provincial Governor, And from the Four Generals to the ranks of Duke and High Minister."
The Great Kings and the Wheel-turning Monarchs, The Sun, the Moon, and Śakra, Lord of Devas;
The Bodhisattva is also like this, Gradually accumulating merit and virtue,
Practicing the six perfections (pāramitās), By doing so, one attains Buddhahood.
He transforms and enlightens the people of the ten directions, causing them all to reach great peace.
The Bodhisattva studies meditative concentration with single-minded devotion; gradually casting off all defilements, he advances and refines his resolve.

It is like a person who wishes to travel into the ocean; with the sun and moon leading the way, he proceeds without retreating. Though he encounters hunger and cold, he never wavers; disregarding the hardships of distance and toil, he travels without rest until he reaches the seashore. There, together with others, he boards a ship to enter the sea and gather treasures; though aware of the three perils, he does not feel any dread.
He went to the palace where the Great Dragon King resided and requested from him a supreme, wondrous wish-fulfilling pearl to provide for those in poverty. The Dragon King gave it to him, saying:
"Bestow it upon all; do not be stingy."

"All who are bathed in this light shall not suffer depletion. When that person obtains the jewel and receives its grace, he suddenly returns, so that throughout the entire kingdom there is none who does not attain peace.

It is the same with the Bodhisattva: with an impartial mind he practices the Way, desiring to rescue sentient beings; through loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), he single-mindedly recollects the Buddha. In whatever direction he dwells, he focuses his devotion upon it without ever slackening or abandoning it. For seven days, ten days, three months, or a year, he does not harbor worldly thoughts; with a single mind directed toward the Buddha, he transforms sentient beings as well. Riding upon the Mahāyāna’s boundless teaching, he beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions, receives their instruction, and attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Remaining unmoving in *samādhi*, he preaches for the sake of all.
It is, for example, like obtaining a wish-fulfilling jewel from a dragon king and distributing it widely to the masses.

It is also like a person who hears that there are beautiful celestial maidens in the heavens, exquisite and lovely in appearance; desiring to go and see them, yet lacking the power of spiritual flight (*ṛddhipāda*), they contemplate them day and night, never forgetting them whether lying down or rising, for many years without another thought. Then, within a dream, they are able to go and see them, observing their sitting, rising, advancing, and retreating.

In this way, the bodhisattva focuses the mind in contemplation toward a Buddha in a certain direction, practicing without ceasing for many years until attaining samādhi. Acting without hypocrisy or indolence, they do not grow weary even through successive kalpas, thereby personally attaining Buddhahood;
the bodhisattva practices the path of great kindness and great compassion, bestowing their grace upon all beings.
Once there was a man whose eyesight was impaired; unable to see the light of the sun, he felt deep distress in his heart, thinking:
"Though the sun's brilliance exists, my eyes are blind and dark, and I cannot behold it!"
"What can be done about this? he asked.

He sought out a divine master who gave him ambrosia to drink; his internal ailment was immediately removed, and his eyes became so clear that he could behold the sunlight and perceive all things throughout the eight directions, above and below, as well as all the people.
When one first resolves upon the Great Mind, yet the six sense bases, the five aggregates, and the three poisons have not been eliminated, one cannot perceive the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Once one receives the profound teachings from an accomplished Bodhisattva, practices the four immeasurable minds, and realizes the emptiness of the triple world, one then attains samādhi and perceives the Buddhas of the ten directions; arising from this concentrated state of mind, one rescues and delivers sentient beings.
It is like placing a precious gem upon crystal, or using a vessel to receive lapis lazuli; the color of the lapis lazuli causes the vessel to take on its likeness.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva single-mindedly recollects the Buddha without any other intent, they immediately attain meditative vision and see the Buddhas of the ten directions; it is through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas and the result of their own fundamental virtues that they behold the World-Honored Ones.
Thereupon, he spoke in verse:
"Just as there was once a man who traveled into the sea, Never ceasing his efforts until he reached the dragon king by boat;
From him, he sought the great treasure, the wish-fulfilling jewel."
Bestowing gifts so that none fail to receive them, the Bodhisattva thus practices the four ways of winning over beings;
with great kindness and great compassion, they practice the Great Way, single-mindedly applying diligence to the gates of samādhi.
Just as a person who hears of jade maidens in heaven may contemplate them day and night until they see them in a dream,
so too does the Bodhisattva through such diligence see the Buddhas of the ten directions without exception.
Furthermore, just as one with eyesight in the dark might contemplate the light of the sun, and once a skilled physician treats them, their vision immediately becomes clear;
so too does the Bodhisattva single-mindedly direct themselves toward the Buddha, never ceasing and never regressing.
Just as when precious jewels are placed within crystal, their mutual radiance shines forth so that nothing remains unilluminated;
so too is the bodhisattva’s samādhi-concentration: having received the teachings from the Buddha, they bring about universal transformation through instruction.

The Bodhisattva accumulates merit and virtue, desiring to deliver all beings; he regards them as his father, regards them as his mother, regards them as his son, and regards them as his own body—treating them all with equal impartiality, without distinction.

For the sake of those on the five paths of existence, he undergoes immeasurable toil and suffering without regarding it as arduous; though he passes through the afflictions of birth and death across the five paths—the sufferings of hell, the venom of hungry ghosts, the vexations of animals, and the calamities from beginning to end within the heavens and the human world—his mind remains unshakable.

He practices great compassion and the four debts of gratitude without weariness, rescuing and aiding those throughout the ten directions so that they may be freed from manifold attachments and conceptions.

For example, when the moon first appears, it is like the horn of a young lamb; day by day it gradually grows larger until it reaches fullness, its radiance shining universally and outshining all the stars with its unique brilliance.

The sequential training on the Path constitutes the Dharma of a Bodhisattva: practicing giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom; undergoing arduous cultivation for incalculable eons; ensuring that body and mind are in accord and speech and action are consistent; and regarding the people of the ten directions as one would one's own parents, without distinction of kinship or estrangement.
It is like planting a tree: it gradually produces sprouts, and subsequently develops stems, nodes, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit;

its growth proceeds in this manner. From the first resolution of the mind, one joyfully turns toward the Buddha; by attaining a heart of delight, one finds rest from the evil realms and accomplishes the dharmas of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).
